MESSAGE from His Majesty, by Sir Francis Molyneux, Gentleman Usher of the Black

Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this honourable House to attend His Majesty, immediately, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to attend His Majesty.

And being returned;

Issue of Mr. Speaker acquainted the House, that, in pursu-New Writ*. ance of the Directions of an Act, passed in the Tenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled,

" An Act to enable the Speaker of the House of Commons to issue his Warrants, to make out new Writs " for the Choice of Members to serve in Parliament, in the Room of such Members as shall die during the <c Recess of Parliament," he had issued his Warrants to the Cleric of the Crown, to make out new Writs, for the Election of Members to serve in Parliament, for the following Places; for the Borough of

Morpeth, in the County of Northumberland, in the room of the Honourable William; for the County of Devon, in the Room of Sir Richard Warwick Bampfylde, Baronet; for the Borough of Leominster, in the County of Hereford, in the room of Thomas Hill, Esquire; for the Borough of Camelford, in the County of Cornioall, in the room of Francis Herne, Esquire j for the Borough of Horsham, in the County of Sussex, in the room of the Right honourable Jeremiah Dyson-, and for the Borough of Haselmere, in the County of Surrey, in the room of T Esquire.

Mr. Speaker'reported, That the House had attend- The King’s

ed His Majesty, in the House of Peers; where His Majesty was pleased to make a most Gracious Speech from the Throne, to both Houses of Parliament; of which, Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy; which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz.;

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

Nothing could have afforded Me so much Satisfaction as to have been able to inform you, at the Opening of this Session, that the Troubles, which have so long diffracted My Colonies in North America, were at an End; and that My unhappy People, recovered from their Delusion, had delivered themselves from the Op-prelfion of their Leaders, and returned to their Duty: But so daring and desperate is the Spirit of those Leaders, whose Object has always been Dominion and Power, that they have now openly renounced all Allegiance to the Crown, and all political Connexion with this Country: They have rejected, with Circumstances of Indignity* and Insult, the Means of Conciliation held out to them under the Authority of our Commission; and have presumed to set up their rebellious Confederacies for Independent States. If their Treason be suffered to take Root, much Mischief must grow from it to the Safety of My loyal Colonies, to the Commerce of My Kingdoms, and indeed to the present System of all Europe. One great Advantage,' however, will be derived from the Object of the Rebels'being openly, avowed, and clearly understood; We shall have Unanimity at Home, founded in the general Conviction of the Justice and Necessity of our Measures,

I am

reported*

Address on the King' Speech.

I am happy to inform you, that, by the Blessing of Divine Providence on the good Conduct and Valour of My Officers and Forces by Sea and Land, and on the Zeal and lira very of the Auxiliary Troops in my Service, Canada is recovered; and although, from una-v oidable Delays, the Operations at York could not

begin before the Month of August, the Suceels in that Province has been so important as to give the strongeff Hopes of the most decisive good Consequences: But, notwithstanding this fair Prospect, We mud, at all Events, prepare for another Campaign.

I continue to receive Assurances of Amity from the several Courts of Europe; and am iiling My utmost Endeavours to conciliateunhappy Differences between Two Neighbouring Powers; and I still hope, that all Misunderstandings may be removed, and Europe continue to enjoy the inellimable Blessings of Peace: I think neverthelefethat, in the present Situation of Affairs, it is expedient that We should be in a respectable State of Defence at Home.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I will order the Estimates for the ensuing Year to be laid before you. It is Matter of real Concern to me, that the important Considerations which I have Hated to you mult necessarily be followed by great Expence: I doubt not, however, but that My faitlfful Commons will readily and cheerfully grant Me such Supplies, as the Maintenance of the Honour of My Crown, the Vim dication of the just Rights of Parliament, and the Public Welfare shall be found to require.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

In this arduous Contest I can have no other Object but to promote the true Interests of all my Subjects. No People ever enjoyed more Happiness, or lived under a milder Government, than those nowr revolted Provinces: The Improvements in every Art, of which they boast, declare it: Their Numbers, their Wealth, their Strength by Sea and Land, which they think sufficient to enable them to make Head again!! the whole Power of the Mother Country, are irrefragable Proofs'of it. My desire is to restore to them the Blessings of Law and Liberty, equally enjoyed by every British Subject, which they have fatally and dcfperatcly exchanged for all the Calamities of War, and the arbitrary Tyranny of their Chiefs.

A Motion was made, and the Question being pro- posed. That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, to return His Majesty the Thanks of this House, for His moll Gracious Speech from the Throne.

To assure His Majesty, that, while we lament the Continuance of the Troubles which have so long dif-tracted His Colonies in North America, and of the Calamities and Opprcflions which our unhappy Fellow Subjects are it ill fullering, under, the arbitrary Tyranny of their Leaders, we cannot forbear to ex profs our De-testation and Abhorrence of the audacious and defpe-rate Spirit of Ambition, which has at last carried those Leaders so far, as openly to renounce all Allegiance to the Crown, and all political Connexion with this Country; and, in direct Terms, to presume to set up their rebellious Confederacies for Independent States.

That we consider their Rejection of the gracious and condescending Means of Reconciliation, held out to them under the Authority of His Majesty's Commission, as a fresh and convincing Proof that the Object of thcle Men has always been Power and Dominion; but wre can impute the Circuinftantes of Indignity and In-fult accompanying this Proceeding, to no other Motive than a Resentment of His Majesty’s firm and constant Adherence to the Maintenance of the Constitutional Rights of Parliament, diverted of every possible View of any separate Interests of the Crown: And to assure His 18

Majesty, that the same Attachment of His Majesty to the Parliamentary Authority of Great , which

hath provoked the Insolence of the Chiefs of this Rebellion, cannot but operate, as, it ought to do,- in fixing His Majesty still deeper, if possible, in the Affections of a British Floufe of Commons.

With Reverence and Gratitude to Divine Providence, to express our unfeigned Joy, and to offer our fineere Congratulations to His Majesty, on the Success which has attended the good Conduct and Valour of His Majesty’s Officers and Forces both by Sea and Land, and the Zeal and Bravery of the Auxiliary Troops in His Service, in the Recovery of Canada, and in the important Operations in the Province of New York; which give the strongest Hopes of the most decisive good Consequences.

To assure his Majesty, that we learn, with much Satisfaction, that His Majesty continues to receive Assurances of Amity from the several Courts of Europe; and that we thankfully acknowledge His Majesty’s Goodness and Paternal Concern for the Ilappiness of Flis People, in His constant Attention to preserve the general Tranquillity; and that it is our moll earnest Wish that, by His Majesty’s Interpolation, all Mifun-derstandings and Differences between Two Neighbouring Powers may be happily reconciled, and ill

enjoy the Blessings of Peace.

That we consider it as a Duty we owe to His Majesty, and to those we represent, to grant His Majesty such Supplies as the weighty Considerations, which His Majesty has been pleased to Hate to us, shall be found to require; and we have a well-grounded Confidence, that, at this Time, when the Object of the Rebels is openly avowed, and clearly underliood, the general Conviction of the Justice and Necessity of His Majesty’s Measures mull unite all Ranks of His faithful Subjects in supportingHis Majesty, w’ith One Mind and Heart, in the great National Cause in which he is engaged.

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by leaving out from the Word " that" in the Second Paragraph, to the End of the Question, in order to insert these Words:Animated with the moll " earnest and fineere Zeal for Flis true Interest, and " the real Glory of His Reign, we behold with inexpreflible Concern, the Minds of a very large and " lately loyal and affectionate Part of His People, entirely alienated from His Government; nor can we " conceive, that such an.Event, as the Disaffection and " Revolt of a whole People, could have taken Place " 'without some considerable Error in the Conduct observed towards them; these erroneous Measures, we " conceive are to be imputed to a Want of sufficient " Information being laid before Parliament, and to too " large a Degree of Confidence being repol'ed in those " Ministers, who, from their Duty were obliged, and " from their official Situation were bell enabled, to " know the Temper and Disposition of His Majesty’s " American Subjects, and were therefore presumed moll " capable of pointing out such Measures as might produce the moll salutary Effects; hence the Schemes " which were formed for the Reduction and Chaftisement of a supposed inconsiderable Party of factious " Men, have driven Thirteen large Provinces to Despair: Every Act which has been proposed as a Means " of procuring Peace and Submi!lion, has become a new " Cause of War and Revolt; mid we now find ourselves " almofit inextricably iuvolved in a bloody and expensive Civil War, which, bolides exhauliing. at present " the Strength of all His Majesty’s Dominions, exposing our Allies to the Deligns of their and our Enc-c mies, and leaving this Kingdom in a most perilous " Situation, threatens in its Ilfue, the most deplorable " Calamities to the whole British Race.

" We cannot avoid lamenting, that, in Conseqtience " of the Credit given to the Representations of Ministers, no Hearing has been given to the reiterated

" To represent to His Majesty, that, in Addition to " this Neglect, when in the Beginning of the last Session His Majesty, in His gracious Speech to both " Houses of Parliament, declared His Resolution of " fending out Commissioners for the Purposes therein " expressed " as speedily as possible," no such Commissioners were sent until near Seven Months afterwards; and until the Nation was alarmed by the " Evacuation of the only Town then held for His Majesty in the Thirteen United Colonies: By this Delay, Acts of the mofl critical Nature, the Effect of " which mull as much depend on the Power of imrac- diately relaxing them on Submission, as in enforcing " them upon Disobedience, had only an Operation to " inflame and exasperate.

" But if any Colony, Town, or Place, had been' ihduced to fuhmit by the Operation of the Terrors of these Acts, there were none on the Place of Pow'er " to restore the People so submitting to the common " Rights of Subjection. — The Inhabitants of the Co- Ionics apprized that they were put out of the Protection of Government, and seeing no Means provided for their entering into it, were furnished with " Reasons but too colourable for breaking off their " Dependency bn the Crown of this Kingdom. To " assure His Majesty, that removing our Confidence " from those who in so many Instances have grossly abused it, we shall endeavour to rellore to Parliament, the Confidence of all His People; to this End " it may be advilable to make a more minute Enquiry * into the Grievances of the Colonies, as w-cll as into " the Conduct of Ministers with regard to them. We " may think it proper particularly to inquire how it " has happened, that the Commerce of this Kingdom " has been left exposed to the Reprisals of the Colonies " at the very Time when their Seamen and Fishermen,

" being indiscriminately prohibited from the peaceable " Fixercife of their Occupation, and declared oj)en " Enemies, must be expected with a certain Assurance " to betake themselves to plunder, and to wreak their " Revenge on the Commerce of Great Britain.

" That we under and, that amidll the many Difafters and Disgraces which have attended on His Majesty's Arms in many Parts of , Advantage

" has been gained by llis Majesty’s British and Foreign " mercenary Forces in the Province of , that

" if a wife, moderate, and provident Use be made of " this Advantage, it is not improbable that happy Efsects may result from that Use; and we assure His Majesty, that nothing shall be wanting on our Part " to enable His Majesty to take full Advantage of any " Dispositions to Reconciliation, which may be the Consequence of the Miseries of War, by laying down, on " our Part, real permanent Grounds of Connexion between Great Britain and the Colonies, on Principles " of Liberty, and Terms of mutual Advantage.

" That whilll we lament this EfVufion of English " Blood (which we hope has not been greater or other " than Necessity required and Honour justified) we ' should moll heartily congratulate His Majesty on " any Event leading to the great desirable End of settling «, Peace which might promise to last, by the lleftoration of the ancient Affection which has happily VoL. 36.

Refolivd,'That, if it shall appear that any Person hath procured himself to be elected or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery or any other corrupt Practices^ this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence, the same is declared to be a high Crime and Misdemeanor; and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath given false Evidence, in any Case, before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is a high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons hr Parliament.

Resolved, That, in all Cases of controverted Elections for Counties in England and ales, the Petitioners do, by themselves,. or by their Agents, within a convenient Time, to be appointed by the House, deliver to the Sitting Members, or their Agents, Lists of the Persons intended by the Petitioners to be objected to, who voted for the Sitting Members; giving, in the said Lifts, the several Heads of Objection, and distinguishing the same against the Names of the Voters excepted to;-and that the Sitting Members do, by themselves or by their Agents, within the same Time, deliver the like Lifts, on their Part, to the Petitioners, or their Agents.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from Time to Time, take into his Custody any Stranger, or Strangers, that he shall see, or be in-framed of to be, in the House, or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is Sitting; and that no Person, so taken into Custody, be discharged out of Custody, without the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That the Back Door of the Speaker’s Chamber be locked up every Morning at the Sitting of the House, and the Key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by him; and that he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the House; and that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take Care to clear the Speaker’s Chamber every Day, before the Door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do pre*-fume to bring any Stranger, or Strangers, into the House, or Gallery thereof, while the House is lifting.

His Majesty, that the Committee had drawn up an Address accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the fame; in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read: and is as followeth; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, beg Leave to return your Majesty the humble Thanks of this House, for Your most Gracious Speech from the Throne.

While we lament the Continuance of the Troubles which have so long distrgcted Your Majesty’s Colonies in North America, and of the Calamities and Oppref-

fions which our unhappy Fellow Subjects are hill suffering under the arbitrary Tyranny of their leaders; we cannot forbear to express our Detestation and Abhorrence of the audacious and desperate Spirit of Ambition, which has at lall carried those Leaders so far as to make them openly renounce all Allegiance to the Crown, and all political Connexion with this Country, and in direct Terms to presume to set up their rebellious Confederacies for independent States.

We consider their Rejection of the gracious and condescending Means of Reconciliation, held out to them, under the Authority of Your Majesty’s Com-roiflion, as a fresh and convincing Proof that the Object of these Men has always been Power and Dominion; but we can impute the Circumstances of Indignity and Infuit accompanying this Proceeding to no other Motive, than a Resentment of Your Majesty’s firm and constant Adherence to the Maintenance of the Constitutional Rights of Parliament, diverted of every possible View of any separate Interests of the Crown: And we beg Leave to assure Your Majesty, that the same Attachment of Your Majesty to the Parliamentary Authority of Great Britain, which hath provoked the Insolence of the Chiefs of this Rebellion, cannot but operate, as it ought to do, in fixing Your Majesty still deeper, if possible, in the Affections of a British I louse of Commons.

With Reverence and Gratitude to Divine Providence, permit us to express our unfeigned Joy, and to offer our sincere Congratulations to Your Majesty, on the Success which has attended the good Conduct and Valour of your Majesty’s Officers and Forces both by Sea and Land, and the Zeal and Bravery of the Auxiliary Troops in Y our Service, in the Recovery of Canada, and in the important Operations in the Province of New York, which give the strongest Hopes of the most decisive good Consequences.

It is with much Satisfaction we learn, that Your Majesty continues to receive Assurances of Amity from the several Courts of Europe: And we thankfully acknowledge Your Majesty’s Goodness and Paternal Concern for the Happiness of Your People, in your constant Attention to preserve the general Tranquillity '; and it is our mostearnest Wish that, by Your Majesty’s Interpo-fition, all Misunderstandings and Differences between Two Neighbouring Powers may be happily reconciled, and Europe’still enjoy the Blefiings of Peace.

Your faithful Commons consider it as a Duty which they owe to Your Majesty, and to those they represent, to grant Y’our Majesty such Supplies as the weighty Considerations, which Y’our Majesty has been pleased to stateHo us, shall be found to require; and we have a well-grounded Confidence, that, at this Time, when the Object oi the Rebels is openly avowed and clearly understood, the general Conviction of the Justice and Necessity of Y’our Majesty’s Measures mull unite all Ranks of Y our faithful Subjects in supporting Y our Majesty with one Mind and Heart in the great National Cause in which You arc engaged.

A Petition of Richard Bedford, Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, at an Election, which came on, on or about the ioth l)ay of October 1774, Richard Smith, Esquire? Thomas Brand Hollis, Esquire, James Calthorpe Esquire, and the Pe-

titioner, were Candidates to represent the Borough of Jlindon, in the County of Wilts, in this present Parliament* and that the said Richard Smith and Thomas Brand Hollis*previous to, and during, the said Election, by themselves and their Agents, were guilty of gross Bribery, in corrupting the Voters; and, by those corrupt and illegal Practices, procured themselves to be returned Burgesses, to represent the said Borough in this present Parliament, at the said Election; whereupon the said James Calthorpe and the Petitioner presented their humble Petition to this House, praying such Relief as to the House should seem meet; and that the said Petition was referred to a Committee of the House, and, after the Hearing thereof, the Election and Return of the said Richard Smith and Thomas Brand Hollis were declared by the said Committee to be void; and it was also resolved, by the said Committee, that the said Richard Smith, by his Agents, had been guilty of notorious Bribery, in procuring himself to be elected and returned a Burgeft for the said Borough; and that the aforesaid Resolution of the said Committee was afterwards agreed to by the House; and that afterwards a Prosecution at Law was ordered by the House against the said Richard Smith for the said Bribery, on the Trial whereof the said Richard Smith was convicted of the said Offence; and that a new Writ having issued, for electing Two Burgesses for the said Borough, to supply the said Vacancies, the Election came on the 16th Day of May last, when the Petitioner and the said Richard Smith and Henry Dawkins, Esquires, were.nemed as Candidates; and after some Progress bad been made in the Poll, the said Richard &vtith, in concert with his Friends and Agents, named Joseph Smith, Esquire, as another Candidate; with a view to get a greater Number of Votes, upon the Face of the Poll, for the said Joseph Smith, than might be given for the Petitioner: which, as the said Richard Smith declared, was the only Thing that could serve him, the said Richard Smith, effectually; and that the said Richard Smith procured himself to be, returned a Burgess for the said Borough, at the last Election, by the undue and corrupt Influence of his grols and noto-jious Bribery at the said former Election, in.Consequence whereof the said Richard Smith, (as the Petitioner is advised) was and is incapable of being elected to fit in this present Parliament for the said Borough; and that the said Joseph Smith was an utter Stranger to the said Borough, and unknown to the Inhabitants, and to the Persons having or claiming a Right to vote therein; and that the Votes which were given for the said Joseph Smith, were obtained by the corrupt and illegal influence of the said; and more-

over, that the said Joseph Smith was incapable of being elected and returned a Burgess for the said Borough, he not being, at the Time of the said Election, seised of, or entitled to, such Estate as qualified him for that Purpose; and that John Stroud, Esquire, was also a Candidate at the said last-mentioned Election, and had-only Seven Votes; and that, by the illegal Means aforesaid, and by the Admission of divers Persons to vote for the said Richard Smith and the said Joseph Smith, who had no legal Right to vote; and by the Rejection of several Persons who had a legal Right to vote, and tendered themselves at the Poll for the Petitioner; the said Richard Smith obtained a colourable Majority, and the said Joseph Smith a colourable Equality to the Petitioner, on the Face of the Poll; whereas the Petitioner had a Majority of legal Votes, and ought to have been 16

returned as a Burgess to represent the said Borough in the present Parliament, infteadof the said Richard Smith: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant the Petitioner such Relief therein as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Tuesdaythe 19th Day of this inllant November, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are Enfield thereunto subscribed, being Owners or Occupiers of . Freehold and Copyhold Messuages and Lands in the 11C 0 urCtr several Parishes of Enfield, Edmonton, South Mimms, and Monken Hadley, or some of them, in the County of Middlesex, was presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That His Majesty, in Right of His Duchy of Lancaster, is seised of The of Enfield, lying within the Parish of Enfield, in the County of Middlesex, containing 8000 Acres of Land, and upwards; and that all Freeholders and Copyholders within the aforesaid Parishes, or their Tenants for the Time being, are entitled (amongst other Rights) to an un-stinted Right of Common upon the said Chafe, for divers Kinds of Cattle throughout the Year; and that the said Chafe, in its present State, yields very little Profit, either to His Majesty, or to the said Freeholders and Copyholders, or their Tenants, in Comparison of what it might do if the same was divided and improved; and that, with a View to such Division, a Survey and Admeasurement of the said Ch have been lately made and taken; and a Treaty being set on Foot, between the Officers of His Majesty’s Duchy of Lancaster, on the Part and Behalf of His Majesty, and the Freeholders and Copyholders of the said several Parishes, it hath been proposed and agreed, that certain Parts or Shares of the said Chafe shall be set out and allotted to the several Freeholders and Copyholders of the said Four several Parishes, in lieu of their Rights and Privileges upon the said Cand that other Parts thereof shall be set out and allotted to the Owners of the Tythes arising within the said Parish of Enfield, in lieu and Discharge of the Tythes of certain Parts of the said Chafe; and that the Residue of the said Chafe shall remain the absolute Property of His Majesty, His Heirs and Suqcelfors, in Severalty, freed and discharged from all Tythes whatsoever; and that such Division and Apportionment of the said Chafe will not only manifestly tend to the Benefit of His Majesty, and all Persons immediately interested therein, but, by reason of the Extent of the said Chafe, the Goodness of its Soil, and its Vicinity to the Metropolis, will also be of public Utility: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for dividing, setting out, and allotting, the said Chafe, to and amongst the King’s Majesty, and all other Persons interested therein, under such Regulations, Provisions, and Restrictions, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Sir Charles Whitioorth, Mr. Skynner, Mr. Gilbert, and

Mr. Charles Mellifk, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act was read: And,

Paul Newman, Esquire, the Treasurer, produced to your Committee the Book of Accounts relating to the Trust, whereby it appears, that there is at present no more than Twenty-five Pounds in Hand; that there is upwards of One Thousand Pounds due upon Mortgage of the Tolls} that the limiting the Number of Turnpikes by the said Act has been prejudicial to the Road; and that the Money now owing cannot be repaid, nor the Roads kept in Repair, unless those Limitations are taken off, the Term of the said Act enlarged, and some other Alterations made therein.

A Petition of the honourable Bartholomew Bouverie Shaftefhutjr was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth*

That, at the lad Election of a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Shaftejburin the County of IForfet, George Rous, Esquire, and the Petitioner* were Candidates; and that at the lad General Election many notorious Acts of Corruption were practised within the said Borough, by Francis Sykes, Esquire,

(whose Election and Return for the same were, on account. of the said Corruption, declared void); and many of the Electors of the said Borough, dill continuing eor- > ruptly attached to the said Francis Sykes, by the aforesaid illegal Practices, were, by the personalSolicitations of the said Francis Sykes, influenced to give their Votes for the said George Rons; and that, by Means of these and divers other illegal and unwarrantable Practices, the said George Rous hath been elected and returned to serve in Parliament fyr the said Borough, in manifed Wrong of the Petitioner, who was duly elected, and ought to have been returned for the said Borough; and that the Petitioner apprehends that the was not at the Time of the Election, nor is now, possessed of an Edate sufficient to qualify him to dt and vote in the House: And therefore praying the House to fix an early Day for the Appointment of a Committee, to try the Merits of the lad Election and Return for the said Borough.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Tiuj’day the 28th Dayo next,

at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

Memorandum:

In purl'uance of Two Acts, made in the 10th and 11 th Years of His present Majesty’s Reign, to regulate the Trials of controverted Elections, or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament, the like Notices, as in the former Cafes, were sent to the Parties; accompanied with Orders.for their Attendance, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, at the Time on which the said Petition was ordered to be taken into Consideration.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant, or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records, as shall he thought necessary by the several Parties, on the Hearing of the Matter of the said Petition.

Little A Petition of the Right Honourable William Henry Creffinghanv Lord Viscount Clermont, Lord of the Manor of Little oure. Creffingham, in the County of Norfolk, and Owner of

the greatest Part of certain Common, Open, and Arable, Fields, called Half Year and a certain Tract

of Land called The Heath, certain Closes called Half Year Closes, and certain Meadows called

dows, lying within the said Manor and Parish of Little Creffingham, in the said County of Norfolk, in Behalf of himself and the rest of the Owners and Proprietors of Lands in, and Persons having a Right of Common, upon, the said Fields, Heath, Half Year Closes, and Lammas Meadows, w’as presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Lands of the Petitioner . in the said Fields lie intermixed, and are, in their present Situation, incapable of Improvement; and that, if the said Fields and Heath were divided and inclosed, and specific Parts allotted to the several Persons interested (according to their respective Interests therein) and all Rights of Common and Sheepwalk- in and over the said Fields, Heath, Half Year Closes, and Lammas Meadows, were extinguished, it would be a manifest Advantage to the several Persons interested therein, and of Public Utility: And therefore praying. That I^avg may.be given to bring in a Bill for dividing and inclosing the said Fields, Heath, Ground, and Lammas Meadows, in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill,

pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Sir Edward AJlley and Mr. Coke of Norfolk do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Islington A Petition of the Vicar, Churchwardens, and Over-Poor. seers of the Poor, and other Inhabitants, of the Parish of Saint Mary, Islington, in the County of whole Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Poor of the said Parish are very numerous, and the Expence of their nceossary Support and Maintenance is of late Years much increased, which, the Petitioners apprehend, is occasioned by Want of a proper Place, and sufficient Powers to maintain, regulate, govern, and employ the Poor; and that the said Parish is poU'efl'ed in Fee of a piece of ground within the said Parish, called The Hundred A Piece, containing about One

Acre and an Half, upon which a proper and convenient Workhouse, and other necessary Buildings, might be erected and built; and the Petitioners apprehend, that, if Power was given to build a Workhouse, and to furnish and regulate the fame, for the better relieving, maintaining, employing, and governing the Poor; and also, if a Sum of Money, sufficient for those Purposes, was raised by Annuities, or otherwise, as well as by Rates or Assessments, and if Powers were given for the more easy and equitable assessing and collecting the fame, it. would be the Means, in a short Time, of lowering the Poors Rates, and tend to the Health,

Welfare, and Preservation, of the Poor, and to the Benefit of the said Parish: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effecting the Purposes aforesaid, by such Ways and Means, and in such Manner, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do exa-amine the Matter thereof; and report the fime, as it shall appear to them, to, the House:

And it ‘ is referred to Mr. Penton, Mr. Elives, &c.:

And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Supply. /ORDERED, That Sir Grey Cooper do make the Report from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Sir Grey Cooper accordingly reported from the said Committee, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed to be reported to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth, viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Forty-five thousand Men be employed for the Sea Service, , for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-seven, including Ten thousand One hundred and Twenty-nine Marines.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Four Pounds per Man, per Month, be allowed, for maintaining the said Forty-five thousand Men for Thirteen Months, including Ordnance for Sea Service.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty.

And then the House adjourned till Monday Morning, Ten of the Clock.

Burgesses to represent the said Borough in this present Parliament, when Richard Smith, Esquire, Thomas Brand Hollis, Esquire, James Calthorpe, Esquire, and Richard Bedford, Esquire, were Candidates; and that the said Richard Smith and Thomas Brand were guilty of gross Bribery in corrupting the Voters, and,

> by those corrupt and illegal Practices, procured themselves to be returned Burgesses to represent the said Borough in this present Parliament, at the said Election, whereupon the said James Calthorpe and Richard Bedford presented their Petition to the House, praying such Relief as to the House should seem meet; and that the said Petition was referred to a Committee of the House, and, after the Hearing thereof, the Election and Return of the said Richard, Smith and Thomas Brand Hollis were declared to be yo.id; and it was also resolved, by the said Committee (which Resolution was afterwards agreed to by the House) that the said Richard Smith, by his Agents, had been guilty of notorious Bribery, in procuring himself to be elected and returned a Burgess for the said Borough; and that afterwards a Prosecution at Law was ordered by the House against the said Richard Smith for the said , Bribery, on the Trial whereof the said Richard Smith was convicted of the said Offence; and that a new Writ having issued, for electing Two Burgesses for the

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Letters Patent under the Great Seal of Great , bearing

Date on the ill Day of April 1773, granting to David Hartley, Esquire, the exclusive Privilege of the Invention discovered by him for securing Buildings and Ships from Fire, were produced: And,

An Entry in the Journal of this House, of the 16th Day of May 1774, of a Resolution of the Committee of Supply, for granting £.2,500 to His Majesty, to be paid to the Petitioner, towards enabling him to defray the Charge of Experiments, in order to ascertain the Practicability and Utility of his Discovery of a Method to secure Buildings and Ships from Fire, and that the same be paid without Fee or Reward, was read. — Then,

Mr. Joseph Wyatt, Carpenter, being examined, said. He lives at Bucklebury, in the County of Berks — And

being asked, If he had seen a very great Quantity of Combiiftibles laid in a 1 louse, and let on Fire, that have burnt out without communicating the Fire to the upper Part of the House, or to any other Part than was intended to be confuined, although no Means were used for extinguishing the fame? he said. He had seen many Inch Experiments — that he had built and prepared at Mr. Hartley's Expence Four Houses at Bucklcbury, and One on Common, and

that the Expence of building and preparing those Houses has amounted to £. 1,800 — that he had seen the same Room filled with Combiiftibles Six Times. — And being allied, If he had made any Plans for making further Experiments? he said, lie was, by Mr. Hartley's Directions, making Plans for building a House of Lath and Plailler, and for securing Theatres from Fire, the Expence of executing which would be very considerable; — that he had' seen near Two Hundred Experiments made of Mr. Hartley's Plates in different Houses, One Hundred and Fifty of which Experiments were Inch that he thinks any One would have been sufficient to have burnt down any House that had not Eeen secured by Fire-Plates.

Two Members present informed the Committee, That they had been present at many Trials of the Etlicacy of the said Invention in London and in -

Vol. 36.

cestershire, which mull have been attended with corifi-derable Expence to the Petitioner.

Then David Harder), Esquire, the Petitioner, explained to the Committee, That he conceives, from the Result of Experiments already made, from the Analogy there is between Houses and Ships, and from the Opinion of Persons eminent in the Sea Service, whom he has consulted, that the Invention, for. which he has a Patent, may be rendered materially useful to Shipping. — And,

Mr. Samuel Hartley being examined, said, He had kept the Accounts of the Expences which the Petitioner had incurred (independent of the Expence of the said Experiments) for the tail Eighteen Months; — -that it appeared to him at his first managing the Business for the Petitioner, that he had already expended a very considerable Sum of Money — that since the Commencement of his Management the Expence amounted to £. 3,0.00, or upwards, and that the Petitioner had hitherto not received any Profit from his Invention, but on the contrary has fulfered great Loss.

David Hartley, Esquire, the Petitioner, then further informed your Committee, That there are yet many Experiments to make, and that it will require considerable Time to settle the necessary Correspondencies, to establish necessary Manufactories, and to give the Facts such a Degree of Notoriety, as may introduce the general Reception of the Invention to the Notice of the Public.

Ordered,-That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for vesting in David Hartley, Esquire, his Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, the sole Use and Property of a certain Method, by him invented, of securing Buildings and Ships against the Calamities of Fire, throughout his Majesty’s Dominions, for a Time to be limited: And that Sir George Savile, Mr. Thomas Townshend, Admiral Keppel, Su'Hugh Palliser, and Mr.

The said Report was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, William Hyde, Esquire, being examined,'said. That the Poor of the Parish of Islington are very numerous, and the Expence of their necessary Support and Maintenance is of late Years much increased, and that the Witness apprehends the same is occasioned by the Want of a proper Place, and sufficient Powers, to maintain, regulate, govern, and emptoy, the Poor; that the present Workhouse is too small, and is very inconvenient, and much out of Repair, and is rented at a considerable Expence by the Parish; that the said Parish is possessed in Fee of a Piece of Ground within the said Parish, called The Hundred Acre Piece, containing about Qne Acre and an Half, upon which a proper and convenient Workhouse, and other necessary Buildings, might be erected and built.

And the Witness being further examined, said, That he apprehends, if Power was given to build a Workhouse upon the said Piece of Ground, and to furnish and regulate the same for the better relieving, maintaining, employing, and governing, the Poor, and also if a Sum of Money sufficient for those Purposes was raised by Annuities, or otherwise, as well as by Rates or Assessments, and if Powers were given for the more easy and equitable assessing and collecting the fame, it would be a Means in a iliort Time of lowering the Poors Rates, and tend to the Health, Welfare, and Preservation, of the Poor, and to the Benefit of the said Parish.

Thomas Cogan, Esquire, confirmed the above Evidence. '

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum not exceeding One thousand and Thirteen Pounds Sixteen Shillings and Ten Pence and Three Farthings, be granted to His Majesty, to make good a Deficiency in the Sum voted last Session of Parliament, for the Charge of the Regiment of Foot of Hanau, to the 24 th Day of December One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-six.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum not exceeding Twenty-six thousand and Fifty-three Pounds Seven Shillings and Four Pence, be granted to his Majesty, for, defraying the Charge of Artillery for the Foreign Troops in the Pay of Great Britain, pursuant to Treaties, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-seven.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum not exceeding Five thousand One hundred Fifty-two Pounds Twelve Shillings and Three Pence and Three Farthings, be granted to His Majesty, towards defraying the Charge of Artillery for the Foreign Troops in the Pay of Great Britain, pursuant to Treaties, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-six.

Mr. Benjamin Fellmces, being examined, said, he is Clerk of the Peace for the County of Hertford, and Treasurer to the said Trustees; that he never received or heard of the said Orders relating to Applications for Turnpike Bills, nor, to the belt of his Knowledge, were any of the acting Trustees apprised of them; that there is the Sum of £. 500, together with an Arrear of interest, due on Mortgage on the Credit of the said Acts, bolides considerable Debts to Workmen, and for Materials; that from the Smallness of the Tolls, and Badness of Materials, the Trustees have not been able completely to amend and keep in Repair the Whole of the Roads comprised in the said Acts, in consequence of which a Part of them was in 1775 indicted, and ineffectual Application made to get the Issues respited; that the Term granted by the said Acts, together with the additional one given by the said General Highway Act, Will expire in May 1777; and that, unless the same be further continued, it will be impossible to repay the said Sum due on Mortgage, or discharge the other Debts: And he added, that if the Term of the said Acts is fuftered to expire, the said Roads will very soon become impaftable.

Thames r1 ">HE House being informed that the Sheriffs of Navigation. the City of London attended at the Door; they

were called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House,

A Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, in Common Council assembled.

And then they withdrew.

And the said Petition was read; Setting forth, That, by an Act of Parliament, marie in the Fourteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act more effectually to improve and complete the " Navigation of the River Thames, Westward of London Bridge, within the Liberties of the City of London, and to prevent any Veil'd or Barge from being " moored in Taploxo Stream, in the County of " Bucks," the Petitioners were authorized and impow-

VOL. 36.

ered to improve and complete the Navigation of the said River, between the City of London, and the City Stone above Staines Bridge, and that the Petitioners have proceeded to carry the said Act into Execution, and several necessary and expensive Works have been performed within their Jurisdiction, between London Stone near Staines, and London Bridge; whereby the Navigation

hath been greatly improved, the Passage for Boats and’

Barges rendered more expeditious, and the Expences of navigating considerably reduced; and that the Petitioners have already applied near Ten Thousand Pounds in this Service out of their own Estates, but find that, notwithstanding so large a Sum has been expended, other Works very necessary for completing the Improvement of the said Navigation Hill remain to be done; the probable Expence of which will (as the Petit ioners have been informed) amount to the additional Sum of near Eight thousand Pounds, over and above a considerable Expence that will annually be in- ,

curred, in repairing and supporting the Works; and that the Petitioners are desirous of being enabled to purchase the several Tolls and Duties now collected and taken for Bargesand other Vefibls navigating, and for Horses drawing l’uch Barges and Vessels, within the Limits before mentioned; and propose, that the said Tolls and Duties, so purchased by the Petitioners, shall cease, and be no longer paid, as they apprehend, from the Circumstances and Nature of the said Tolls and Duties, that they are attended with great Inconvenience to the Navigation, and to the Public; and that, if a final!1 Toll in lieu thereof were laid upon the several Barges,

Boats, and other Vessels, navigating the said River, between London Stone, new Staines, and London according to the Quantity of Tonnage, the Petitioners would be enabled more effectually to carry the good Purposes of the said former Act into Execution, to purchase the present Tolls and Duties, and to complete the said Navigation: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant such Relief therein as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House: -

And it is referred to Mr. Alderman Oliver, Mr. A1 derman Hayley, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Sheriff of the County of Devon; and the Petitioners are informed, that, as such, he was disqualified from being elected a Member to serve in Parliament; and that, at the Place of Election, and before the taking the Poll, the Returning Officer and the Electors had public Notice, that the said Mr. Baring, being Sheriff of Devon, M as incapable of being chosen to represent the said City in Parliament, and that all the Votes given for him would be thrown away; notwithstanding which, the Returning Officer persisted in proceeding to take the Poll, and the said Mr. Baring M as returned as duly elected; the Petitioners therefore think themselves aggrieved, and apprehend that the said Election and Return of the said Mr. Baring is an undue Election and Return; and hope that the said Mr. Cholzvich, the only Candidate capable of being elef ted, will be considered as having been duly elected, and will be permitted to fit in the House, as one of the Members for the said City, in the room of the said Mr. Baring; and that the Returning Officer admitted in Favour of Mr. Baring the Votes of several Persons who had no Right to vote, and rejected to the Prejudice of Mr. Cholwich the Votes of several Persons who had a Right to vote; and that the said Mr. Baring and his Agents, after Mr. Walter had vacated his feat in Parliament, and during the said Election, did give and lend, and promise to give and lend, divers Sums of Money and other Rewards^ and did also openly and publicly, and otherwise, give and allow Meat, Drink, Provision, and Entertainment, to many of the Electors of the said City, who had, or claimed, a Right to vote at the said Election, in order' to corrupt and procure them to vote for the said Mr. Baring, and to refrain giving their Votes for the said Mr. Cholwich; and the said Mr. Baring and his Agents were guilty of other notorious Acts of Bribery and Corruption, and divers flagrant Attempts to bribe and corrupt the Electors of the said City; and by Means thereof, and divers other illegal Practices, the said Mr. Baring procured a Majority of Votes, and caused liimfelfto be returned as a Member to serve in Parliament for the said City, notwithstanding the said Mr. Cholwich had a Majority of legal, undoubted, and uncorrupt Votes upon the Poll, and ought in Justice, for the Reasons aforesaid, to have been returned, although the said Mr. Baring had been eligible at the Time of

A Petition of William Owen, Esquire, and of several other Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Owners of Lands and Estates within the Township of Rednal, in the Parish of West Felton, in the County of Salop, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That there are, within the said Township, certain Moors, Commons, or Waste Lands, belonging to the Petitioners and others, which, in their present State, are incapable of any Improvement; and that it would be advantageous to the Petitioners, and the several other Persons interested in the said Moors, Commons, or Waste Lands, if the same were divided and inclosed, and specific Allotments made to them, according to their several and respective Rights of Common, and other Rights and interests therein, and if the Petitioners were enabled to make Exchanges of any of their Lands and Estates within the said Parish of West Felton'. And therefore praying. A Petition of the Lord of the Manor, Rector, and other the Owners of Lands, Grounds, and Tythes, in the Open and Common Fields of Cclvile, in the County of Cambridge, on Behalf of themselves, and other Owners and Proprietors of the said Lands, Grounds, and Tythes, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the said Open and Common Fields and Commonable Lands contain 1970 Acres, or thereabouts, but that the said Lands are very inconveniently situated with respect to the Farm Houses of the Occupiers thereof; and the Properties of the said Owners and Proprietors in the said Fields are so dispersed in small Pieces and Parcels, that, in their present Situation, they are incapable of much Improvement; bhtdhat it would tend much to the better Cultivation of the said Lands and Grounds, and to the Interest of all the said Owners and Proprietors, if the said Fields were divided, and specificShares and Allotments thereof made to the said several Owners and Proprietors, in lieu of their respective Rights and Interest therein; and that such Divisions, Allotments, and Inclosure, would be for the mutual Advantage of all Persons Having a Right to Lands, Tythes, Commons, and Comr mon of Pasture, and other Interelis, in the said Fields: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for dividing, allotting, and inclosing, the Open and Common Fields, Commonable I^ands, and Waste Ground, within the Manor of WeJlonColvile, in the County of Cambridge; and for exonerating, as well the said Open Fields, as the Old Inclosures lying within the said Manor and Parish, from the Payment of Tythes, Modules, or Compositions for Tythes, and for ascertaining and settling an Equivalent to the Rector and other Owners and Proprietors of Tythes within the said Parish in lieu thereof, or otherwise to grant, unto the Petitioners such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Sir Charles Bunbury, Sir John Hynde Cotton, and Sir Sampson Gideon, do prepare, ancTbring in, the fame.

Estates belonging to the said Governor and Company in Scotland are now let at £.6,573. is. "j{d. and which Rent is capable of being considerably advanced; and that the Rents of the said Estates have, ever since the Year 1728, been received by the Trustees for the said Annuitants, or some Persons acting for them; and in as much as such Rents have for a considerable Number of Years pall greatly exceeded the Annuities payable thereout, the Persons so in Receipt of the said Rents for such Annuitants mull have a considerable Sum of Money in their Hands, which ought to be applied towards Payment of the Demands of the Petitioners, and the other Creditors under the said Deed of Trust of the 18th of January 1731; and that the Governor and other Persons who formerly undertook the Management of the said Company’s Affairs, did abuse the Trust in them reposed, and did affix the Seal of the said Coxnpany to divers and sundry Bonds, some whereof were issued for a small, and others for no real Consideration, and by other Mismanagement contracted, or suffered to incur, a great variety of Debts and Demands on the said Company’s Estates and Effects, but to what Amount is at present unknown; and the said Company long since became Insolvent; and that all the Persons who were originally named Trustees for the said Annuitants, and Trustees for the Creditors under the Deed of the 18th of 1731, are long

since deceased, and the Trust is now devolved on the

l9

Heirs of the surviving Trustees; and that (lie Petitioners, or those under whom they claim, and all other the Creditors of the said Company under the said Deed of Trust of the 18th of January 1731, have brought Actions of Ranking and Sale in the Court of Sefiiuii in Scotland, against the Company and their Creditors, which have been depending several Years; but as the Law of Scotland requires that, in all Actions for Sale of Bankrupt Estates, the Ranking of the Creditors shall proceed and fil'd be concluded by Decreet, before the Lands can be exposed to Roup or Sale, the same cannot be obtained by the'ordinary Process in a long Course of Years (especially as many of the Company’s Creditors defer the Production of the Grounds of their Debts) although the Rank of the Creditors under the said Deed of Trust of the 18th of January 1731, as among themselves, is altogether immaterial, in as much as the Value of the said Estates, after appropriating Lands sufficient to securethe subsisting Annuities, is far beyond the whole Amount of all the Debts due to such Creditors; and that the expediting the Sale of such Part of the Company’s Estates as shall remain after appropriating Lands sufficient to answer the subsisting Annuities, according to the-Provisions made in the said Deed of the 26th of 1725, will be the

Means of the Petitioners, and all other the Creditors under the said Deed of the 18th of January 1731, in a little Time, receiving their just Demands, and will be of great Benefit to all the subsequent Creditors of the said Company, in as much as the w hole Expence of the various Processes neetflary to bring an El’tate to a judicial Sale by the Law of Scotland are paid out of the Estate itself, and the Fund for the Payment of the Creditors thereby diminished; and the Lands and Estates of the said Company, which have been long neglected and uncultivated, while remaining in the Hands of an insolvent Company, will, by transferring them to Purchasers, be improved, to the great Benefit of the Public; The Petitioners, therefore, on Behalf of themselves and all other the Creditors of the said Company, under the said Deed of Trust of the 18th of January 1731, pray, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for a Sale of the Company’s Estates in Scotland, or so much thereof as shall remain after an Appropriation of a Fund sufficient for answering the subsisting Annuities, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet; and that the Petitioners may have such further and other Relief in the Premises as shall seem just and expedient.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Sir Charles Whitworth, Mr. Waljh,&c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber: and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records; and all who tome to the Committee are to have Voices.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow', One of the Clock in the Afternoon.

THE Hour, appointed for taking into Consideration the Petition of Richard Beckford, Esquire, and also the Petition of the several Persons whose" Names are thereunto subscribed, who respectively have a Right to vote in the Election of Members to represent the Borough of Hindon in Parliament, complaining of the undue Election and Return of Richard Smith, Esquire, for the said Borough, being come;

T he House proceeded to the Appointment of a Select Committee, to trjr and determine the Merits of the said Petitions.

The Serjeant at Arms was directed, by Mr. Speaker; to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent, and require the immediate Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House.

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and 120 Members being found to be present;

The Counsel and Agents for the several Parties, who attended at the Door, were called in to the Bar.

And the Door of the House being locked;

And the said Counsel being ailked, by Mr. Speaker, for whom they respectively appeared; One of them informed the House, That he appeared at the Bar on the Part of Joseph Smith,- Esquire; who is stated in both the said Petitions now taken into Consideration, as having been a Candidate, and as having had an Equality of Votes with the Petitioner, Mr. Beckford, at the said EJeftion; and who had also received a Notice, signed by Mr. Speaker, accompanied with" an Order to attend the House, by himself, his Counsel, or Agent, on the faking the said Petitions into Consideration.

And thereupon One of the Counsel for the said Petitioner, Mr. Beckford, objected to the said Mr. Joseph Smith's being admitted to appear, by his Counsel, as a Party on the Appointment of the said Select Committee; as he was neither a Sitting Member for the said Borough complained against, nor had presented any Petition to the House, nor had any Petition been presented to the House, on his Behalf, complaining of the said Election or Return.

And the said Counsel further objected to the said Mr. Joseph Smith's appearing by his Counsel in the Manner before mentioned; he not having delivered in to the Clerk of the House, a Particular of his Qualification, according to the Dire&ion of the Standing Order of the House, of the 21st Day of November 1717; such Qualification having been expressly objected to by the said Petitions respectively.

And the said Counsel was heard thereupon.

And both the said Petitions were read.

And the said Standing Order of the House, of the 2.1st Day of November 17x7, was also read.

And the Clerk of the House, being called upon, acquainted the House, that he had not received any Particular of the said Mr. Joseph Smith's Qualification.

And the other Counsel for the said Mr. Beckford was heard in Support of the said Objections. And the Counsel for the said Mr. Joseph Smith was heard in Answer thereto.

And one of the Counsel for the said Mr. Beckford having been heard by Way of Reply;

The Counsel and Agents were directed to withdraw some Way from the Bar.

A Petition of the Committee *of the Company of Merchants trading to Africa, being offered to be presented to the House;

The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have laid before the 1 Ioufe, an Account of the Money granted for the Year 1775, examined and passed by the Cursitor Baron of the Exchequer, as required by an Act of the Twenty-third of George the Second, intituled, "An Act for " extending and improving the Trade to /* and

that they have inverted the Money granted in 177 6, for the Support and Maintenance of the Forts ana Settlements on the said Coast; and that, the said Forts and Settlements having been delivered to the Petitioners in a very bad State by the Royal African Company, and the Sums annually granted by Parliament being nearly expended in the tivil and Military Establishments, leaving very little for the Repairs of the said Forts, several of them still remain in a very ruinous Condition; and that the I Ioufe, in the Year 1772, granted the Sum of £.2,400 to finish the Repairs of Cape Coast Castle; but, in the Progress of the Work, the Walls of the Fort were found in so very decayed a State, and so many Defects difc&vered, that the Petitioners have been unavoidably led' into the Expence of a much larger Sum, and the Repairs of the said Fort still remain unfinished, nor can the Petitioners proceed therein until the House shall enable them; and that, at the End of December 1775, the Officers and Servants in Africa had advanced for the Public Service about £.7,000 more than the Petitioners have been enabled to repay them; and that the said Officers have further advanced about £. 1,200 to the Inhabitants of Lagoeand Two prin-

cipal trading Towns on the Coast of Africa, in order to preserve the Commerce of those Towns to the t

Nation, which Advance the said Officers pray may be repaid them; and that the Expence of Freight and Insurance on the Goods and Stores sent to Africa this Year will amount to near /. 1,000 extraordinary; and that the Petitioners, being sensible of the great Regard shewn by the House for the British Forts and Settlements on the Coast of Africa: Therefore pray the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant such Sum for the necessary Support and Maintenance of the said Forts and Settlements, for repaying the Officers and Servants the several Sums of Money advanced by them, and likewise for the Repairs still wanted, as shall feein meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Sir Grey Cooper accordingly reported from the said Committee, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed to be reported to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the'Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as follow? eth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred and Five ThousandTwo hundred Seventy-nine Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Nine Pence, be granted to His Majesty, upon account, towards defraying the Charge of the Out Pensioners of Chelsea Hospital, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-seven.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Ninety-three thousand Six hundred and Sixteen Pounds Eight Shilling6'and Four Pence, be granted to His Majesty, upon account of the reduced Officers of His Majesty’s Land Forces and Marines, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-seven.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Seven hundred Fifty-four

l7

Pounds Twelve Shillings and One Penny, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge for Allowances to the several Officers and private Gentlemen of the Two Troops of Horse Guards reduced, and to the superannuated Gentlemen of the Four Troops of Horse Guards, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-seven.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Three hundred and Seventy Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, for the paying of Pensions to the Widows of such reduced Officers of His Majesty’s Land Forces and Marines, as died upon the Establishment of Half Pay in Great Britain, and were married to them before the.Twenty-fifth Day of December, One thousand Seven hundred and Sixteen, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-seven.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Six thousand Nine hundred Ninety-seven Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Seven Pence, be granted to His Majesty, upon account of the Expences of the new Roads of Communication, arid, building Bridges, in the Highlands of North Britain, in the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-seven.

.Lucre, introduced large Quantities of false counterfeit Halfpence, and artfully and industriously circulated them in the Town of Nottingham, and the adjacent Country, in direct Opposition to the lawful Coin of this Realm, and to the manifest Injury and Distress of the fair Trader, and the Public in general; and that the Petitioners, well knowing the fatal Tendency of such illicit Practices, have endeavoured, by all lawful Means in their Power, to suppress the Currency of such counterfeit Money, and to bring the Offenders to Punishment, but have found all their Attempts fruitless and ineffectual, and have bf en informed, that the Laws in their present State are inefficient for that Purpose; and the Petitioners daily find, that the Introduction of the said counterfeit Halfpence is a growing Evil, and loudly calls for Redress, which, the Petitioners are advised, cannot be obtained without the Intervention of the Legislative Authority: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to provide such Remedies and Relief as the House may think proper.

Hcfle Caflirll. Copy of a Convention between His Majesty and the Landgrave of Hejfe Csigned at nth De-

cember 1776; and Translation.

And the Titles of the said Copy and Translation Were read.

The said Copy is preferred amongst the other Papers of this Session; and the said Translation is as followeth;

Translation of a Convention Between His Majesty and the Landgrave of Hejfe Cajfell, concluded and signed at Cajfell the 11 th Day of December 1776.

His Britannick Majesty having desired that the Corps 17

of Hejfian Chasseurs, now in His Service in should be augmented. His Minister Plenipotentiary, Colonel William Faucitt, and the Baron Martin de Schliejfen, Minister of State and Lieutenant General of H is Molt Serene Highness the Reigning Landgrave of HqffeCajfell, furnished with the full Powers of their

respective Mailers, have agreed upon what follows:

1.

The Corps of Chasseurs, including those already in America, Avail- be augmented to One thousand and Sixty-seven Men, instead of Two hundred and Sixty-two Men, of which it at present consists. In the room of Two Companies, of which it is now composed, Six shall be formed; Five of which shall serve on Foot, and One on Horseback, on the Footing of Hussars: His Majesty Avail cause them to be provided with Horses and-Forage; His Moll Serene Highness Avail equip them with every Thing necessary besides for the Service on Horseback.

2.

The Pay of the Chasseurs, as well Foot as Horse, Avail be higher than that which his Majesty allows to the IJeJJian Infantry, in the same Proportion as it was during the last War.

3’

The said Pay for the new Augmentation shall commence from the Day of the Signature of this Coven tion. But as the Number of Men stipulated is not yet entirely collected, the Deficiency shall not be paid for but in Proportion as the Men shall be enlisted, according to the Returns which shall be made with the utnvoll Exactness, and duly certified.

4*

This Augmentation Avail be composed only of experienced Chasseurs, all well-trained Marksmen; and if it is not poffvble to find the Number demanded of these Ikilfiil Marksmen, His Majesty will content himself with a less Number, rather than accept of Men not having the Dexterity requisite; and although i£ is impossible to fix exactly the Time in which this Augmentation may be entirely completed, seeing that Hejfe alone has not so many of these Chaflfeurs by Pro-session, and that they must be engaged in the neighbouring Countries, it is promised, that all that is poffvble shall be done, in Order to assemble them in a very short Time, and to cause them to march, without Delay, for their Destination.

5’

Every Thing that has lately been agreed upon in the Treaty of the 15th of January, in the present Year, with respect to the Corps of in general,

now in His Majesty’s Service, shall extend to this new Augmentation of the Corps of Chasseurs: The Subsidy Avail be proportionably augmented: Thirty Crowns Banco per Head, Levy Money, shall be paid for the Companies of Foot; and Forty-five Crowns Banco per Head Avail be paid for the Troop of Horse, as their Equipage is a great deal more expensive.

6.

This Convention shall be ratified by the High contracting Parties, and the Ratifications thereof Avail bp exchanged as soon as possible.

In Testimony whereof. We, the undersigned, being furnished with the full Powers of His Majesty the King of Great Britain on the one Part, and of His Most Serene Highness the Reigning Landgrave of Hejfe Cajfell on the other Part, have signed the present Convention, and have caused the Seals of our Arms to be affixed thereto.

Done at Cajfell this nth, of December, in the Year

Poor, See. of the Poor, and other the Inhabitants and Parishioners of the Parish of Kensington, in the County of -/ex, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the said Parish hath, of late Years, greatly increased in Buildings and Inhabitants, whereby the Poor are become very numerous, and the Poor Rates are daily increasing, and the Parish Officers are under greatDilficulties in providing proper Accommodations for their Reception; and that the Petitioners conceive, if a sufficient Workhouse was provided for the Parish, and put under the Management of proper Persons, to be from Time to Time appointed, the Poor of the said Parish would be better provided for, whereby the Petitioners would be greatly eased in the Poor Rates; and that the purchasing of Ground in the said Parish, and building such a Workhouse for the Reception of the Poor, would not, as the Petitioners believe, cost more than /. 4,000; and that, by Indentures of Lease and Relealc, dated the 31st Day of May, and ift Day of June 1757, certain former Trustees, therein named, conveyed to Robert Phillimore, Esquire, Stephen Pitt, Esquire, Edward Lloyd, Esquire, Robert Pilkington, Thomas Bird, and John Clarke, and Ten others (ftnee dead) as Trustees, certain Pieces or Parcels of Land and Premises therein mentioned, in Trust, to let the same for the Benefit of the Poor of Kensington, in such Manner, and according to the Directions of the Wills of Lord and Lady Campden; which Estates are now let upon Leases for short Terms of Years, nearly expired, at the annual Rent of £.54 only in the whole; and, that the Petitioners and the said surviving Trustees are offered, and could now let the said Parcels of Land ami Premises, at very considerable improved Rents and Fines, provided they were enabled to grant long building Leases thereof, and to dig for Brick Earth, Loom, and Gravel; und, that the Vicar, Churchwardens, and Parishioners, of Kensington aforesaid, are desirous that the same Estates, and all other their Estates, should be let out upon I^eases, for such Terms of Years, and at such reserved Rents, and in such *5

Manner, as shall be thought most beneficial to the said Trull, and that Three-fourths of the reserved Rents be, from Time to Time, applied in Aid of the Poor Rates, for paying Interest of Monies to be bor-Towed on Annuities to be granted, for raising Monies for purchasing Ground, and erecting a Workhouse, for the said Parish; which, the Petitioners conceive, will be of real' Benefit to the Poor, as lyell as to the Parishioners in general; and, that the remaining One-fourth may be applied for putting out poor Boys Apprentices; and that, by an Act, made in the Twenty-ninth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act to empower " the Churchwardens, Overseers of the Poor, and " Vestry, of the Parish of Kensington, in the County " of Middlesex, to make a Rate or Rates for the Relie

" of the Poor, repairing the Highways, and dcanling " the Streets, within the said Parish," the Rates for 'the Relief of the Poor, repairing the Highways, and cleansing the Streets within the said Parish, are directed to be made equal Pound Rates or Assessments; and by the said Act it is also directed, that all the Rates to be thereafter made for the Relief of the Poor, and all other the Parochial Rates to be thereafter made in the said Parish, should be made according to the Land l ax Books of the said Parish for the Time being; and that, for many Reasons, no fair or equal Pound Rates can be made in the said Parish, according to the Poor Laws, so long as the Parochial Rates continue to be governed by the Land Tax Books;' and that, if lb much of the said Act of Parliament, as relates to the making of the Parochial Rates by the Land Tax Books was repealed, and if the Petitioners were empowered to make fair and equal Pound Rates, according to the true Rents, or Fines in lieu of Rents, actually paid by the Occupiers of Houses and Lands in the said Parish, and the Petitioners and the said Trustees were enabled to let the said Charity Estates in Manner aforesaid, and to appropriate the said Three-fourths of the Produce thereof, and of all other the said Estates, in Aid of such R°tes, and to raise Monies upon the Credit of such Rates, the Petitioners would thereby be enabled to purchase Land, and to build or provide such Workhouse and Accommodations for employing the Poor as aforesaid; and, if proper Powers were given to the Parishioners, to appoint a fit Number of Trustees, to be annually added to the Vicar, Churchwardens, and Overseers, for the Time being, for carrying the said Act into Execution, it would tend to the more easy Execution thereof: And therefore praying. A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Gentlemen, Merchants, Tradesmen, and principal Inhabitants, of the City of Gloucester, and of several Gentlemen, Clergy,

and others, redding near, or resorting to the said City, whose Names are thereunto subscribed* was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, about Sixty Years ago, a Bridge was built with Brick, by voluntary Subscriptkra, across the River Severn, at Maijemore, near the City of Gloucester, in the Road leading to

Worotfer, but, for Want of a proper Fund to keep it in Repair, the same has been for some Time in a ruinous State; and, by the late Equinoctial Tides, and great Fall of Rain, the said River swelled so high, and became so rapid, that a Vessel was driven from its Moorings against the said Bridge, and broke down one of the Arches thereof, by which Means the Remainder of the Bridge was blown up and totally destroyed; and that immediate Communication between the Cities of Gloucester, Bristol, and Bath, the Western and Southern Parts of England, the City and County of the Counties of Hertford and Salop, and the Northern Parts of the Kingdom, was thereby intirely (lopped, until a temporary Wooden Bridge was, through abfo* lute Necessity, let up by private Persons at their own Expence, and which can answer the Purpose but for a short Time; and the want of a substantial Bridge there will be attended with great public Inconvenience; and that the Causeway, called Ove leading from the City of Gloucester, towards the said Bridge, and also towards the City of Hertford, Town of Monmouth, and all South Wales, containing in Length abqut 800 Yards, and being a raised Road, to avoid the Floods, upon 25 Arches, for the Passage of Water from the adjacent Meads, during the Time of Floods, is very narrow in general, and over the said Arches in particular, so that Carriages cannot pass each other thereon, and the Passage along the some is extremely dangerous, especially in high Floods; and that the said Causeway has been raised Time immemorial, but no Fund appropriated for the Maintenance and Preservation of the fame, except a (mail charitable Donation of £. 5 per Annum, which is very inadequate for that Purpose; and that the Bridge over another Branch of the said River Severn, at the West Gate of the City of Gloucester, and immediately leading from thence to the said Causeway,

*7

is much out of Repair, and, in its present State, very inconvenient for Vessels and Barges, and many Delays and Damages are occasioned thereby; and that, if a Drawbridge was made, for the more easy and expeditious passing of Barges and Vessels through the fame, without lowering their Malls, it would be of great Service to the Trade and Commerce of the said City, and of public Utility; and that the several Streets in the City of Gloucester are very ill paved and cleansed, and the Passage through the fume rendered inconvenient, and obstructed by many Nuisances* and Annoyances, and the present Methods prescribed by Law for removing such Annoyances, and for enforcing the proper paving and cleansing the said Streets, and keeping such Pavements in sufficient Repair, are ineffectual; and that if Power was given for effecting these Purposes, it would tend greatly to the Advantage of the Inhabitants of the said City, and fofety of all PeiJans passing through the fame, and be of Public Convenience: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for erecting the said Bridge at Maifemore aforesaid, for repairing and widening the said Causeway and Arches, making the said Drawbridge at the West Gate aforesaid, removing and preventing Nuisances and Annoyances, and enforcing the more effectually repairing and cleansing the Streets and Ways in the said City, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Pechell and Mr. Fames:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to a Bill, intituled, An Act for the better Relief and Employment of the Poor of the Parish of Saint Mary, I, in the County of Middlesex, and for building a Workhouse for the said Parish; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for vesting in David Hartley, Esquire, his Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, the sole Use and Property of a certain Method, by him invented, of securing Buildings and Ships against the Calamities of Fire, throughout His Majesty’s Dominions, for a limited Time; with some Amendments; to which Amendments the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House.

And then the Messenger withdrew.
