Bailiffs, and Conservators; and that Numbers of large Engines or Mills have; within the last Thirty Years, been erected for throwing the Waters of the Fens into the RivCrs, which, throwing great Quantities of the Mo6r which combs into the Mill Drains dHTolved by the Water, as weH as the said Water, into the Rivers, hath Ocoafioned die Beds of the said RiVers to grow iip, and hath much decreased the Depth of the fame; that* from the Causes above stated, and others, the ( Works already made are now insufficient for carrying the Waters through and off The Great Level; apd -that the same is continually liable to be overflowed, and The Great River Banks in general want deepening, repairing, heightening, and strengthening, and will, from Time to Time, require great Sums for the continuing them in a proper State to preserve The Great Level from being overflowed, as also to furnish proper Haling Ways for the Navigators through the said Rivers, and other considerable Works are still wanting for the Preservation of the fame; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that the Loss of The Great River Banks, and in Consequence the Loss of the . whole Level, will be attended, in a great Measure, with the Loss of the Navigation through the fame, from the Ports of King's Lynn and into

Mr. Barrow reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Gentlemen, Merchants, Tradesmen, and principal Inhabitants, of the City of Gloucester, and of several Gentlemen, Clergy, and others, redding near, or resorting to, the said City, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

To prove t he Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. John Wilkins Jepfon, Deputy Clerk of the Peace for the County of Gloucester, and Partner with Mr. , the Town Clerk of the City of Gloucester, informed your Committee, That several Years ago a Brick Bridge *7

was built by Subscription across The Severn, at Maise-moor, near tike said City, and in the Road leading to Worcester;that for Want of a Fund to maintain the said Bridge, the same has been for some Time in a ruinous State, and that by the late equinoctial Tides, and great Fall of Rain, the said River was swelled so high, and became so rapid, that, a Vessel was driven from its Moorings against the said Bridge, and broke down One of the Arches; in Consequence whereof the Remainder of the . Bridge was blown up, and totally destroyed, and the Communication thereby stopped, between the said City of Gloucester and the Cities of Bristol and , and the Western and Southern Parts of England, the City and County of Worcester, the Counties of Hereford. ana Salop, and the Nortlkem Parts of the Kingdom.

That, in order in some Degree to remove so great a" public Inconvenience, a Right Wooden Bridge was soon after set up in the room of the former by private Persons, at. their own Expence, but which cannot’ be expected to last long.

That th^rc is a Canfeway, called Overs,

leading from the said City towards the said Bridge, and and also towards Hereford, Monmouth, and,

mid which is 800 Yards long, raisedupon 25 Arches, for the Passage of the Waters, from the adjoining Meadows in the Time of Floods; — that the Road along the said Causeway is. in general very narrow, and that the Passage over the said Arches is not more than Seven Feet wide, which makes travelling along the said Causeway very dangerous: and he informed your Committee* That about Two Years ago a Person was drowned by missing the Track over One of the said Arches.

Then, a Member present confirmed the above Evidence; inilanced the dangerous Situations that several Persons had been in; and said. That he himself had heen in the utmost danger of losing his Life in passing over the said Causeway and Arches.

Mr. Henry Wilton corroborated the forgoing Evidence with respect to the State and Condition of the said Bridge at Maifcmoor, of the said Causeway, and of the said Arches.

The said Member informed your Committee, That the said Causeway was raised by a Donation about 200 Years ago: And Mr. Jepfon said. That there is no other Provision for supporting and repairing it than the very inadequate Sum of £. 5 per Annum, which, it appears, by the Records of the Corporation of Gloucester, was many Years ago appropriated to that Purpose.

And he said, That it does not appear by the Records of the County of Gloucejl, that the said Bridge at Mafemoor was a County Bridge, or ever repaired as such.

The Witness then informed your Committee, That the Bridge over another Branch of the River,

at the Well Gate of the said City of Gloucester, and leading from thence immediately to the aforesaid Causeway, is much out of Repair, and in its present State very inconvenient; that if Part of the said Bridge was made a Draw Bridge, for the passing of Vessels, without their Masts being lowered, many Interruptions, Delays, and Damages, which now frequently happen, might be prevented.

That the several Streets in the said City are very ill paved and cleansed, and the Passage through the same rendered inconvenient, and obllrucled by many Nuisances and Annoyances; and that the present Methods prescribed by Law for removing such Annoyances, and for enforcing the proper paving and cleansing the said Streets, and keeping such Pavements in sufficient Repair, are ineffectual.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for rebuilding the Bridge over the River Severn, at

Mafemoor, near the City of Gloucester; for repairing and making commodious Overs Causeway, leading from the said City, towards Mafemoor aforesaid; for amending and altering the Bridge over another Branch of the

That a very extensive Trade is carried on in the said Parishes, particularly in Wapping Street, which is very narrow, and liable to be obstructed by Carriages, being near a Mile in Length, and there being no Way into the same but at the Ends thereof; — that the Communication between Ratcliffe Highzcay and the said Street is exceedingly incommodious; and it would be a great Advantage to the Inhabitants of the said Parishes, and to Trade in general, if proper Communications were opened from napping Street to Rat Highway, between Old Gravel Lane and Little Hermitage Street, by widening . the South Well End of Bird Street, and by building a new Street from Bird Street across certain Fields to John's Hill, and another new Street from Wapping Street aforesaid through Globe Yard, through Gardens, and across certain Ground to Hill,

and another new Street from Old Gravel Lane through Johnson’s Street, and across certain Fields to Virginia Street, in the said Parish of Saint George.

And the Witness added. That in order to accomplish the fame, it will be necessary to take down some Houses, and other Buildings, in Yard, and also

in Bird Street, which the Proprietors of the said Houses and Buildings have oonfonted to.

And the Witness further said, That Hermitage Street, Sampson's Gardens, Artichoak Lane, Virginia Street, Pennington Street, John's Hill, Artichoak Hill, and Bird Street, together with the Footway of Caiuwn Street, and the Pafl’ages leading into the said Streets, are very badly paved, and incommoded by Annoyances and Incroachments; and that the Opening the said new Streets, and making Provisions for paving the fame, and the other Streets and Places before-mentioned, and for removing all Incroachments and Annoyances therein, would be beneficial to the Inhabitants of the said Parishes, and be of public Utility.

In Support of the Second-mentioned Petition, Mr William Hondo, being examined, laid, That Princes Square, with the Avenues leading thereto from Highway, are very ill paved, and incommoded by Polls and other Annoyances and Incroachments, and that it would be very convenient to the Inhabitants of the said Square, and the Avenues leading thereto, if the same were properly paved, and such Annoyances and Incroachments removed.

Mr John Hopkins and Mr. John confirmed

the Whole of the foregoing Evidence.

Birmingham Mr. Skipwith reported from the Committee, to whom ’*'t*trt* the Petition of Richard Yates, Gentleman, and also the Petition of many of the principal Inhabitants of the Town of Birmingham, in the County of Warwick, were severally referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the first-mentioned Petition, and had considered the last mentioned Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition, Mr. Thomas Falco being examined, said.

That Birmingham is a large and populous Town; that a great many Persons of considerable Property reside there, and in the Neighbourhood thereof, who are desirous of having a Theatre established in the said Town, under proper Regulations.

The Witness also said. That a commodious Building has been erected by Subscription within the said Town, for the Purpose of performing Plays, and other En-

tertainments, of the Stage; and that Mr. Yates has, at a very great Expence, fitted up the said Building, and provided all Things necessary for the Performing of such Entertainments.

And the Witness added. That when the said Theatre is established, it will be of Advantage to the said Town.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for enabling His Majesty to licence a Playhouse in the Town of Birmingham, in the County of Warrvick .* And that Mr. Skipwith and Sir Henry Bridgeman do prepare, and bring in the fame.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act was read: And,

Mr. I!ri llicmFranks-, Clerk to the Trustees, being examined, said. That in pursuance of the said Act, £.6,000 was borrowed, at £. 4 per Cent. — that he filled up the Ronds.'

And he produced to your Committee, an Account of Money raised and expended towards building the said Church; and also, an Account of Bills unpaid, and Work contracted for; whereby it appeared, that the Sum of ,£.7,719. 11 s. 6d. was raised towards building the said Church; that £.7,686. 2 2d. has

been already expended in the Building; and that .£.1,368. i8a\ id. now remains due for Bills unpaid, and Work contracted for, in order to complete the Whole. — Then,

Kenton CovJ'c, Esquire, who w'as employed as Sur*

veyor, being examined, informed your Committee, That a Contract was entered into with John Ilanfcomb, for building the Church at £.5,000. — that he was present when it was agreed upon, but not at the Signing.

And being asked. Whether any other Olfers were made for building the Church besides Mr. he said. Several; that when the Church was agreed to , be built, it w'as advertised for People to deliver in Proposals; and, in Consequence, several were delivered iii; that they were very wide from one another, and M first were delivered in Part; that, upon the Whole, Mr. Ilanfcomb's, tho’ not the lowest, was thought by the Trustees to be the moll eligible.

That there W’ere some Exceptions in the Contract — that in case the Ground should require a deeper Foundation, the extra Work was to be paid for at a certain Price; and also, if Piling or Planking was necessary, it was to be paid for separately; that the Common is all a Flat; and the Consequence was, that when the Spot of Ground was fixed upon exactly, and the Contractor began to dig, it was found to be of all Sorts of Soil — Part of it was a hard Rock of Gravel, some Part of it Clay, and some Part a Sand; the Whole was exceedingly full of Springs; that the Witness informed the Truliees of it, and many of the Gentlemen were there, and had a View; — that they directed the Witness to give such Orders as he thought proper for the Security of the Building^ which he did, by directing the Foundation to be piled and planked; that it was raised higher titan was proposed, in order to get above the Springs; and the Witness said. That was one of the chief Articles for exceeding the Expence; — that there was besides an Exception in the Contract, of the Pulpit, Altar, and Reading Delk; — and in the Church Yard, Drains were to be made, which were not then thought of--that Locks to the Pews were not mentioned in the Contract — that about Two Thirds of the Foundation of the Church was piled, and the Whole of it planked.

Mr. Franks being again examined, said. He never heard that Mr. Ilanfcomb offered to contract for less than £. 5,000.

And being asked. Whether any Objection was made to the Contractor who offered for less, viz. to his being capable or responsible ? he said. He did not know that there was.

And being asked. If Mr. Ilanfcomb acts in any Capacity in the Parish ? he said. He is one of the Assessors of the Land Tax; — that he was, and, at first, aided as a Trullee, but not since the Contract.

And being asked. Whether the other Contractors did not offer proper Security for the Performance of their Contract ? he said. He did not recollect, —

And,

Mr. Couse being again called, was asked. Who gave the Orders for the extra Works ? he said, The Committee.

And being asked, Why Mr. Hanfcomb was preferred to the lower Contractors ? he said, He wras asked by fijme of the Trustees, Whether he thought that Mr. llanfcomb's Proposal of £.5,000 was extravagant? that he told them, Nof upon which they then determined to take Mr. Ilanfcomb.

And being asked, Whether he gave any Reason why they should prefer Mr. Ilanfcomb's Proposal of£. 5,000

to the other of £.4,750? he said, He had no Reason for preferring Mr. Hanfcomb's Proposal.

And being asked, Whether he thought that Carrick and Burton, who offered to contract for £.4,750, could

afford to do it in a proper Manner for that Sum ? he said. He thought not; he thought they would be out 1 of Pocket by it,-but he did not tell the Trustees, so.

And being asked. Whether he ever gave an Estimate of the Expence of Building the new Church previous to the Contract? he said, No; but he had formed one in his own Mind; and when the Drawing was approved of by the Gentlemen, he believes he told them it would come to about £.5,300.

And being asked. Whether the £.5000 contracted for was to complete the Church in such a Manner as that Divine Service might be performed in it? he said. No; the Pulpit, Delk, and Altar, were postponed.

And being asked, Whether painting, glazing, and every other Necessary, were not to be done ? he said.

Yes.

A Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of Loin Conunon Council

assemblerf.

And then they withdrew.

And the said Petition was read: Setting forth, That the Petitioners have seen a Bill depending in the House, to empower His Majesty to secure and detain Persons charged with, or fuipetted of, the Crime of High Treason, committed in North , or on the High

Seas, or the Crime of Piracy; and that, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, the Petitioners are appre-lienfive it will create the greatest Uneafmefs in the Minds of many of 11 is Majesty’s good Subjects, and tend to excite the most alarming Ditlurbances, all Persons indiscriminately being liable, upon the Ground of Suspiciou alone, without any Oath made, and without convening the Parties, or hearing what, they can alledge in their own Jollification, to be committed to a remote Prison in any Corner of the Realm, there to remain without Bail or Muiuprize; and that the Habeas Corpus, which is the great Security of the Liberties , of the People, will be suspended; and that the Petitioners are deeply affected with what they conceife will be the dangerous Consequence of such a Law, as, from little Motiv es of Kefcntment, and various other Inducements, there may be Persons competent to commit, who may be tempted to exercise that Power in its utmost Latitude and Extent; and that Measures so violent and unconstitutional, so lubverlive of the faored and fundamental Rights of the People, and subjecting them to the most cruel Opprefiion and Bondage, will, in the Judgment of the Petitioners, be introduftive of every Species of Mil’chief and Consulion, and thereby precipitate the impending Ruin of this Country: The Petitioners therefore earnestly beseech the House, That the said Bill may not jKifs into a Law; or at load, to take such Care as in their Wisdom may seem meet, to prevent it from being extended, in its Operation or Construction, to any of His Majesty’s Subjects resident in these Kingdoms.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill to empower His Majesty to feourc and detain Persons charged with, or suspected of, the Crime of High Treason, committed in North America, or on the High Seas, or the Crime

of Piracy, was committed.

A Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, That nothing therein contained shall be construed to be Piracy, but what is committed on the High Seas.

- The House was moved, That an Act, made in the Eighth Year of the Reign of King George the First, intituled, "An Act for the more effectual suppressing " of Piracy," might be read.

And the same being read accordingly;

The said Clause was Twice read; and, upon the Question put therupon, agreed to by the House to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, that no Person shall be secured or detained under this Act, for Treason, or Suspicion of Treason, unless such Person shall be expressly charged to have been locally resident in his Majesty’s Colonies or Plantations in North America, at the Time he shall be charged with, or suspected of, committing such Treason.

The Bill, now ingrossed, to empower His Majesty' to secure and detain Persons charged with, or suspected of, the Crime of High Treason committed in North America, or on the High Seas, or the Crime of Piracy, wa6, according to Order, read the Third Time.

An ingrotled Clause was offered to be added to the Bill by way of Kyder, That nothing therein contained Hi all extend to the same of any other Prisoners than such as shall have been in some or One of the Colonies, or on the High Seas, at the Time of the Offences wherewith they shall be charged; and is as followeth; viz.

Provided also, and it is hereby Declared, That nothing herein contained is intended, or shall be con-llrued, to extend to the same of any other Prisoner or Prisoners than such as shall have been in some or One of the Colonies before mentioned, or on the High Seas, at the Time or Times of the Offence or Offences wherewith he or they shall be charged.

'I'he said Cianfe being read the Second Time;

Several Amendments were proposed to be made thereunto, by leaving out the Words " in some or

One of the Colonies before mentioned, or on the " High Seas," and inserting inliead thereof, the Words out of the Realm;" and at the End of the Clause to add these Words, " or of which he or they shall be " fufjje&ed."

And the said Amendments were, upon the Queliion Severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Then the said Clause, so amended, was read the Third Time; and, upon the Queliion put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill, by way of Ryder; and is as followeth;

Provided also, and it is hereby Declared, That nothing herein contained is intended, or shall be construed, to extend to the same of any other Prisoner or Prisoners than such as shall have been out of the Realm at the "l'ime or Times of the Offence or Offences wherewith he or they shall be charged, or of which he or they shall be suspected.

A Motion was made, and the Queliion being put, That the Bill do pass;

The I louie divided.

The Yeas went forth,

Mr. Alderman Harley reported from the Committee, Hitters;

to whom the Petition of the several Hat Makers, and regulating others concerned in the Hat Manufactory of Fur and die Trade. Wool, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table:

Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Two Acts, One passed in the Eighth Year of Queen -beth, intituled, "An Act for uttering of Caps, and " for true making of Hats and Caps;" and the other passed in the First Year of James the First, intituled,

" An Act for the better Execution of former Laws touching the making of Hats and Felts, and for the " more Rellraint ofunfkilful and deceivable Workmanship there used, ta the Wrong of all the Sorts of

" People in this Realm," were read: And,

Mr. Philip Coxe,a Hatmaker, resident in

being examined, informed your Committee, That there is at present a great Scarcity of Hands in the Hat Trade, which is occasioned by the Restraints laid thereon, with respect to the taking of Apprentices, by the fakl Acts of Parliament: That he had been in Trade Twenty-five Y'ears, in which Time it was much increased, and he had often wanted Hands: That there have lately been Combinations among the Journeymen*

zz which

18° Februarii.

17 Geo. III.

which they cull Congressks; and that they are at this Time all off, or abl'ent from their Work; by which Means the Trade is at a Hand: That formerly the Journeymen were paid according to previous Agreements between the Masters and them; but that in 1772 and 1775 the Men met in Congress, and made Demands of additional Prices, which the Masters were forced, in order to carry on their Trade, to submit to: That the Men have now met in Congress, and demand (exclu-iive of their former Prices for Labour, which was settled at a certain Rate for every Ounce of Materials worked up) Three Shillings a Week for Walking; which the Witness explained to be a Consideration paid by the Journeyman to another Person, for Permission to work in his Shop, in Cafes where his Employer had not Room for him in his own House, and which was understood to be included in the Price paid for manufacturing the Materials at so much Ounce/ and estimated at Six Pence a Day. — And being asked, How much a Journeyman Hatmaker can earn at the present Price? he said. Good ones got from i8x. to £.t. 5.?. per Week, inferior Workmen from i6x. to That Finhhers used to be paid iqs. a Week, and their Small Beer; they left oft’ working, and demanded £.1. ix. a Week, to work Two Hours less in a Day, but returned to Work again on the Masters paying 20X. a Week, and taking oft One Hour of working in a Day.

That the Journeymen, in their present Congress, had made certain Bye Laws: That they have not giyen to the Masters any written Projjofals, as they did formerly (several of which he produced to the Committee) but signifted to them, that they would adhere to the Demands of Increase of Wages that they had made: That the Congress have lately levied a Subscription from the Body of Journeymen of Two Pence a Week each Man; Five out of near Fifty Men whom he employed at that Time refused to pay it; in consequence ef which a large Body of them came to his Shop, and told him, he mult no longer employ those Five Men, as they had refused to comply with the Orders of the Congress; and all his other Men threatening at the same Time to leave him unless he discharged them, he was forced so to do: That One of these Five came to him last January, complained of his Distrefe for want of Employment, and desired to be fumished with Materials, which he would work up, and make a Bill of Parcels of the Goods, by which Means he thought the Congress could not deem him within their Bye Laws: That the Witness’s Partner gave him some Materials as he desired: That as soon as his Journeymen heard of it, they came in a Body, and said, That unless the Man was sent for, and the Materials so delivered to him to manufacture taken back, they would not work a Moment longer: That he was obliged to comply; and that they attended to see that the Man brought back the whole Quantity erf Materials which had been delivered to him; after which they demanded Three Guineas as a Recomi>enfe for their Loss of Time in attending to fee this Act of Justice, as they termed it; and upon the Witness’s abfoLtely refuling to submit to pay it, all left his Service, some of whom have since returned, at the Risque of incurring the Penalties indicted by the Congrets.

Mr. John Frederick Bernard, a Hat Maker, of Christ Church, in Surrey, being examined, confirmed the foregoing Evidence in general; and informed your Committee, That there are in the Hat Trade, a Sort of Masters, called Little Masters, whose Business is to manufacture Materials delivered to them to be worked up by the Master Hat Makers: That the Persons coming under this Description, are considered by the Journeymen as not entitled to take Apprentices; and tliata 11 his Men left him lately in a Body for employing One of the Persons called Little Masters, who had some Apprentices.

Vou 36.

Your Committee then called Mr one of the said Little Mailer Hatters, who being examined, informed your Committee, That about a Fortnight ago a Body of Journeymen Hat Makers came to his House, and asked, if he had any Materials to manufacture for a Matter whom they named; agd upon his acknowledging that he had, forbad him to finish it, and told him he never should have any more Work if he did: That they told his Apprentice that his Time should Hand good as he was already bound, but that if he took any more they would not work with him.

Mr. Coxe, being again called; produced to your Committee, an Account of the Number of Apprentices bound to the Felt Makers Company for the last fifty Years; by which it appeared, that the Number was lately much' diminished. And being asked

What is the Reason of that Diminution ? he said.

There are but about Fifty Masters in London, and the Environs, who work up their own Materials; each of whom taking Two Apprentices makes but One hundred in Seven Years; which number is. greatly di-mi milled by various Events: That, of the Persons called Little Masters, he believed not more than Twenty take Apprentices: That, since the Ad: of the Eighth of Queen Elizabeth, which limits the Number of Apprentices to Two for each Mailer (at that Time perhaps sufficient) the Hat Trade is much increased:

That the Trade has lately decreased in except

for fine Hats, those of a coarser Sort being made at Matichester, where labour is cheaper, and no such Re>* straints laid upon the Little Masters. And being If he considered the Scarcity of Journeymen Hat Makers in London as occasioned by the small Number of Apprentices to the Trade ? he said. He did.

Mr. William Coates, being examined, said. That the moll industrious of the Journeymen have been compelled by the Congresses to quit the Service of such Masters as would not comply with their Demands, and that it had happened to himself.

Your Committee then examined Mr. Thomas Davis, a Hat Maker; who said, That the Journeymen Hat Makers frequently exchange or embezzle a Part of the Materials delivered to them to manufacture; an Instance of which he related to the Committee. And he added, That the Laws against such Offences are very deficient, both with respect to the Conviction. of the Offender, and the Punilliment of the Receiver.

And he concluded his Evidence by saying. That an Act to regulate the Prices of Labour, the Hours of working, and the taking of Apprentices, is absolutely necessary to the well-being of the Hat Trade; which was confirmed by,

Mr. James Olivant,

Mr. George Jackson,

Mr. George Vaughan, and

Mr. John Collinj'on, all Master Hat Makers.

John Spiller, Esquire, being examined, said, That

he employs about Forty Men the Year round, out of which there are not above l'ohr that have served regular Apprenticeiliips: That they can’t find Men of the Trade to do their BuGness, for which Reason he is under the Necelftty of employing such labouring Men, or he could not go on with his Trade: That the Trade does not require that all the Men they employ should he brought up to it, common Labourers are sufficient; for there is a Part of the Trade that good Workmen will not do: That, on account of their employing Men not brought up to the Trade, Prosecutions have been carried on: That about Two Years ago the Witness employed a Man for some Time, who was a Journeyman Baker; and from him he went to work with Mr. Ilopkins, a Dyer — Then,

And an Act made, in the Fourteenth Year of the Reign of his Majesty King George the First, was produced, and read; whereby it appeared, That the said Governor and Company were enabled to purchase of the Commissioners and Trustees appointed by the said Act, Estates in Scotland and England which became forfeited to the Crown; and it appeared by the said Decree, That under the Authority of the said Act, the said Governor and Company did purchase several Estates in Scotland, and also divers Manors, Lands, and Hereditaments, in Northumberland, which had bo-come forfeited to the Crown by the Attainder of Lord Widdrington, for all which the said Governor and Company agreed to pay £.308,093. 14s. 7

And another Act of Parliament, made in the Sixth Year of the Reign of his said Majesty King George the First, was also produced, and read; whereby it appeared. That the said Governor and Company were empowered to fell or encumber the said Estates so purchased,

<0 be purchased, with any Debts or Encumbrances in Law or Equity, as any others might do who had Estates in Fee Simple 3 and also had Power given to them to grant Rent-Charges or Annuities to the Yearly Valoe of foch Estates, and no further; and, to enable the Company to pay for the Use of the Public tlfe Price or Consideration for the Purchase of the said Estates, they were empowered to raise such Supi as should be necessary for that Purpose, by calling in ot directing the same so be paid by their respective Members, according to their respective Interests in the Stock of the said Governor and Company.

And by an Act of the Seventh of George the First; produced, and read. It was Enacted, That, for thfe better enabling the Company to raise and pay the Government the Price or Consideration for the Purchase of the said Estates, the said Company might grant and fell Rent-Charges and Annuities, to the full Extent of such Estates so purchased, by way of Lottery; and that any Persons, Body Politic or Corporate, in that Method might purchase such Annuities of the said Governor and Company.

Mr. Fletcher reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Merchants, Traders, and other principal Inhabitants, of the Town of Workington, in the County of Cumberland, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, of the 25th of 1774, relative to Navigation Bills, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. John Smith, being examined, said, That the Town of Workington is a Place of considerable Trade, ami conveniently situated for Vessels navigating the Sea; that it would be the Means of saving the Lives of many of His Majesty’s Subjects, if the Harbour was made capable of holding Vessels of more considerable Burthen; and if it was properly deepened, enlarged* and secured, it would be of great Benefit to the Trade of the Petitioners, and be a Means of increasing the Revenue, and the Number of Seamen, and also of great public Utility; that several Sums of Money hwl been borrowed for the Security of the Harbour, which had been duly applied; that the Wduel's was -Pier'Mailer, and had collected the Harbour Dues for 20 Years; that in i7168 there was a Debt of £. 1,400, ami that near £.600 now remains due; that if was borrowed at different Times, and some of it had been Handing near Twenty Years.

That, by the Increase of the Trade, the Harbour 4s become too final], and rendered incommodious by high Tides and Land Floods, and is in Danger of being totally Hopped up by a Breach in The Cloffacks, at a Place where it formerly ran, almost 70 Years ago.

And being asked. How the Money was borrowed before 1768 ? he said, By an Agreement between the Owners of Ships and the Trustees; that the Owners engaged to indemnify the Trustees as far as £.2,000, for the Improvement of the Harbour; that they borrowed about £.1,400, which was all laid out on both Sides of the Harbour, as there was Occasion for Additions and Repairs; that the whole Duties collected were meant as a Security for the Money borrowed.

And being asked, Whether, after 1768, when they did not receive Money of Ships on the North Side, they went on with Improvements in the Harbour ? he said. The I Iarbonr was improved, the South Quay was extended, a Pier was built, and the Bed of the South Gut deepened, and that after that Time they only received the Duties on the South Side; that the Interest of the Money was paid from a Tonnage received for Ships loading on the South Side only, that the Quays on the North Side, in 1768, were in good Repair, a great deal of the Work being done in 1767, and was almoftnew; that since 1768, Ships on the North Side have paid the same Tonnage as before to the Agents of Sir James Lorether; that upwards of £.600 of the principal Debt has been paid off.

And being asked. If a Bar should be formed at the Mouth of the Derwent, whether it would not prevent Ships from failing into the Harbour? he said. If a Bar should be formed so high, that the Keels of Ships should touch it, it would; but that he apprehended would he impossible.

And being asked. If he did not think that a heavy Sea, rolling m with the Flood Tide, mull not assist to scour the Channel in its present Direction ? he said. He did not think so; for if there was no Sea at all, the Channel would be Hill deeper than it is.

And being asked. Whether the Stream of the Derwent was not the only Means he relied on to prevent a Bar from being thrown up by the Sea ? he said, It was, and he would not wish for any other Means.

And being asked , If there was no Sea, whether there would be any drifting Gravel or Sand travelling along the Coast ? he said. There would not; but if, by any other Means than the Sea there was, it would still be deeper without a Tide than with; that so far from the Flood Tides assisting the River in scouring the Channel, if the Salt Water was never to come above Low Water Mark, the Channel of the River would wear itself deeper than it is now.

And being asked, Whether the Stream of the Derwent would not be considerably weakened by changing it out of its natural Course from a straight to a curved Line? he laid. He believed in the present Cafe, it could make no sensible Difference.

And being asked. Whether the present Harbonr was not prote6fced from the Force of the Sea by the Beach (marked C in the Plan) which he proposed to remove ? he said, It was, and that the Pier is meant to answer that Purpose; but if it gave way, the Harbour would lie open to the Sea.

And being asked. What Direction the new Channel is to run in from the Jun&ton of the new Pier to the old Frame-work ? he said, Nearly from Eall by South to Well by North.

And being asked. If he did not think Ships coming from the Northward, that could shape a Course into the present Channel of the Harbour, might be prevented from getting in by the proposed Alterations of its Entrance to the Eastward ? he said. He did think in some Cafes they might be prevented, but he thought the Jofing of One Advantage to gain Twenty would be no Loss upon the whole; for he had been informed, that Twenty Ships came from the Southward while One came from the Northward.

And being asked. Whether the Alteration of its Entrance to the Eastward would admit one Vessel more into the Harbour that was coming from the Southward than the present Channel ? he said. He apprehended it would admit many more.

And being asked, Whether he did not conceive the Advantage to arise from Winds which blow from between the North and East ? he said. No, he did not, he meant the Winds from between the South and West, that Vessds will come in with Winds a Point or two more to the Southward than they can at present.

And being asked. Whether the new Channel will not ran nearer the Shore than when it took its ancient Course in that Direction ? he said. It will.

And being asked. Whether the Gravel and Sand which drives along the Coall had gained considerably on the South Shore ? he said. Not very considerably.

The Witness having said, that it was impoffibie such a Bar could be thrown up at the Mouth of the,

as to prevent Ships coming in, he was asked. If, at the Month of a River, which runs over shifting Beds of Gravel, where aconsiderable Quantity of Sand and Gravel

In the present same it is possible to estimate, with all moral Certainty, what it will not do, for at the Mouth of the River Derwent, as above described, there is 33 Feet Depth of Water, when there is only 13 in the Harbour.

And being asked, When a Quantity of Sand, Gravel, or Mud, was carried down by Land Floods in a River into the Sea to High Water Mark, whether that which continued to drive it farther is not the Excess of the Force of the Water of the River in one Direction above that of the Sea in the other? he said. It is.

And being asked, If it is not deposited at or near the Place where those Forces became equal? he said. Yes, but in the present same it did not remain there.

And being asked. By what Cause it is carried from thence ? he mid, By the same Action of the Sea driving it from the South to the North that brings the Gravel and Beach.

And being asked. Whether the Force of the Sea in Storms setting in to the Mouth of the Harbour will not be greater than the Force of the Sea in the Direction from South to North, by which the Gravel and Beach was carried Coastwise ? he said. So long as the Storm remains perhaps it may, but as soon as it is over it loses the Ground it gained while it lalied.

And being asked, Whether that might not produce a temporary Bar during, and for some Time after, great Storms, so as to render it more difficult and dangerous for Ships to take Shelter in the Harbour at the Time when they have moll Occasion ? he said, He believed it was probable that would never be the Cafe.

And being asked, Whether very considerable Quantities of Sand, Gravel, and Mud were not carried down by the River Derwent in Land Floods? he said. He believed there were, but what is carried down by that Means apparently adds no more to the Coail than the River does to the Sea.

And being asked. Whether he had estimated the Place where the Force of the River Derwent loses itself so far as not to exceed that of the Sea ? he said. He had, and believed it to be at or below Low Water Mark.

And being asked. If he spoke of the Force of it in Floods, or of the ordinary Course of the River ? he said. He spoke of the Average, considering both together.

And being asked, Whether the Water, in the present Channel of the Derwent, below High Water Mark, is not deeper than when it ran in its former Channel more to the Southward ? he said. He could not answer, having had no Information.

The Witness having said, that the Water would run obliquely against the Beginning or Eall End of the new rier, at the Point of its Junction to the old, he was asked. Whether that would not lay a Stress upon > that End of the new Pier, tending to undermine, and so carry it away? he answered, It would tend do it, in the same Manner as the River Thames tends to undermine the Foundation of Westminster Bridge.

And being asked. Whether he conceived that it would be possible to fortify the Pier in that Place sufficient to withstand it ? he said, He did not conceive any Difficulty in making a Pier Itrong enough to withstand it.

And being asked. Whether he conceived that the remaining Part of the Pier would be in any Degree saved, by that End of it having received the first Force or Brunt of the Water, and so having diverted the Stream to run nearly in the Direction of the Remainder

of the Pier ?v he said, he did conceive it would be rather an Advantage to the rest, of the Pier.

And being asked. Whether, when he said there would be no Difficulty in fortifying that first Corner, he spoke with that Degree of Certainty which is reasonably to be expected in Works of this Kind ? he said. He did.

And being asked, When it is necessary to run out Piers in any Situation, whether it was not proper that they should cross or thwart some outward Force, from which he expected Danger ? he said. Certainly, otherwise Piers would be useless.

And being asked. If it is not often the moll necessary to interpose Piers and Defences of this Kind, where that Force was the strongell and the Danger the greatest ? he said. It is.

And being asked. If the Stress that laid upon such Pier or Work mull not be proportioned to the Force which it was intended to keep oft ? he said. It mull.

And being asked, "Whether he apprehended that in this particular Situation this Pier could be made sufficiently strong, so as to keep off that outward Force? he said. He apprehended it might be made more than sufficiently strong.

And being asked. Whether it was not often prudent and safe, when he had interposed new Defences against a Danger, to take away old and less effectual ones; although, if the new ones were then to be carried away, he would be in a worse same than before; meaning, when he had a solid Ground of Certainty of the Stability of the new Work, according to the Rules of this Art ? he said. It was.

And being asked. If he had that solid Ground of Certainty here ? he said, He had.

And being asked. If he knew how many Hours before and after High Water there was Water in the Harbour? He said, He never made that Inquiry.

And being asked. Whether the Channel of the River would be narrowed, or more spread, over against The Lantliorn Perch, by the making of the new Work ? he faitk It would most probably be narrowed.

And being asked. Whether the new Work would tend to make the Lantliorn Perch Shore grow more to the Northward ? he said. He believed it would have the contrary Effect.

And being asked. Whether it would tend to make the Shore between The Lantliorn Perch and the South Pier grow more to the Northward? he said. He believed it would have the contrary Effect, because when it came within the Reach of the River it could never after that increase, as the Land Water would carry it off as fail as it came.

And being asked. Whether it would not foonercome to the River Side for the new Work being made ? he said. It was probable it might to the new River Side.

And being asked. Whether the Pier, mentioned by him before, and proposed to run from the Timber Yard Northwards, about Middle-way, between the present South Pier, and the Entrance of the South Gut, would not have the Effect to prevent a further Accumulation of Gravel at the Entrance of the South Gut, which had lately happened, especially if the South Pier was advanced a little nearer to the present Course of the River? he said. It would in some degree' have that Effect.

And being asked. Whether it would not, though the South Pier was not advanced Northwards ? he said, It would still have that Effect, but in a less degree.

And being asked. If the present Harbour was enlarged in the Manner proposed in the Plan, and the Accumulation of Gravel at the Entrance of the South Gut so far prevented, as that it could be easily removed annually, whether the present Harbour would not be in very good Condition ? he said, It would be in a better Condition than at present, but it would still be liable

They would have a better Harbour than now, but not so good as if all the Works were executed as proposed by the Plan.

And being asked, Whether he expected, by those Works, that Ships at The North Hurries would lie quieter and safer than now'? he said. Yes, much quieter and safer.

Without a Pier, but he believed the Seas never came in that Direction.

They would be more exposed than at present, and this would lie the Cafe, whether the new Works were done or not.

appropriated for that particular Purpose; which will be a cruel Burthen on the Petitioners, and all others living at a Distance from Poole, and travelling on the other Parts of the said Roads, especially as by the said Bill die Petitioners, and the Public in general, who may never fee that Town, will be chargeable towards paving, widening, and re pairing/WcStreets, equally at leaftwith the Inhabitants of Poole, which Hardship is greatly increased by the Situation of that Town, which admits of no travelling through it, and from its being a considerable trading Town, and supplied with different Kinds of Merchandises from foreign Parts by Sea, and very few Articles in Trade carried thither by Land Carriage, except Com, so that the Tolls collected at the Turnpike Gates do not very materially affect the Inhabitants of Poole, but the Burthen falls much more heavy on those who live Inland, and are supplied with Coals, Deals, Iron, and other Merchandises, from Poole; and that the said Bill is now prosecuting in a very different Form from one agreed to by the unanimous Resolution of Thirty Trustees, at a Meeting held at Winboum Minster, in November last, where it was agreed, that if Poole Street was to be included in the Bill, a double Toll should be collected at Poole Gate on Sundays, One Half of which should be appropriated for the Purpose of extending the Road through the Town of Poole, and paving the fame, and that Fifty Pounds only, out of the General Stock, should be allowed for the same Purpose; and the Petitioners also conceive, that the said Bill, so far as respects the widening, paving, amending, and repairing Poole Street, appears to be very partial and unreasonable in other Respects, particularly as no Trustees to be therein named, but such as shall reside in Poole, will be empowered to act or intermeddle with the improving, widening, paving, and repairing the fame, notwithstanding the Sum for that Purpose will be raised on the Credit of the Tolls in general, nor will any Persong but such as inhabit and reside in Poole, and assessed to the parochial Rates or Assessments there, have Power to inspect the Account, which is intended to be kept separate from the other Accounts: and that the Petitioners apprehend, the Vot-. 36.

confining the Meetings of the Trustees and the Residence of the Treal’urers to IVinbourn Minster and Poole is unreasonable, for that Hortoti and are equal-

ly or rather more proper Places for the Meeting of the Trustees, as being more centrical, and there are many Places equally as proper for the Residence of the Treasurers as either Winboum or Poole; and the Petitioners likewise apprehend, that the making a separate Division of the Roads Seven Miles North of the Sixteen-Mile Stone at Cranborn, from the other Part of the Roads, will be attended with considerable additional Expences, and not answer any good Purpose, the Toll taken at the Gate not amounting annually to more than Nine or Ten Pounds: And therefore beseechin^ the House, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, or at least to take such Care as in their Wisdom may seem meet, that the said Bill may be altered or amend- ed, so as to bring the Purport of it as near as may be to the former Acts, and by striking out such Parts of the said Bill as relate to the widening, paving, repairing, and cleansing, the Street or Way through the Town of Poole, or by laying on a separate additional Toll at Poole Gate oh Sundays, to be appropriated for that Purpose only, or that the Petitioners may be otherwise relieved in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Sir Thomas Eger ton reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Hatmakers, and others concerned in the Business of Hatmaking, within or near the Town of Manchester, in the County Palatine of

Lancaster, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had di-rested him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Eighth Year of the Reign of Queen Elizabeth, for uttering of Caps, and for true making of Hats and Caps; and also, an Act, passed in the First Year of King James the First, for the better executing of former Laws touching the making of Hats, or Felts, and for other Purposes: and also. Two Acts, passed in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of King George the First, and in the Twenty-second Year of his late Majesty, to prevent unlawful Combinations of Workmen, were read: And,

Mr. Thomas Philips, one of the principal Hatmakers In the said Town of Manchester, being examined, said. That the Prohibitions laid by the Two first-mentioned Acts arc found to be very detrimental to the Trade of Hatmaking, by lessening the Number of Journeymen, of whom no more can be procured than barely furticient to answer the Purposes of the Trade for Home Consumption.

Mr. John Clegg, likewise a principal Hatmaker in the said Town, confirmed the foregoing Evidence; and adder!, that on account of the scarcity of Journeymen, he has been obliged to refuse many foreign Orders for Hats; and he added, that the Two last mentioned Acts have been found in many Parts defective, and that in order to fulfil the good Purposes thereby intended, it is necessary to explain and amend the fame.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Gentlemen, i who are appointed to prepare, and bring in, a Bill, to regulate the Prices of Labour, the Hours of Working, and the taking of Apprentices, in the' Hat Ma-nuiaftory; that they do extend the Provisions of the said Bill, respecting the taking of Apprentices, and preventing unlawful Combinations of Workmen, to that Part of Great Britain called England.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

" County of Nottingham, to the Town of and also the Mortgagees of the Tolls arising and to be taken upon the said Turnpike Road, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Petition is pre* fented, for Leave to bring in a Bill for making a navigable Cut, or Canal, from the Place where the River Trent communicates with the Lordships of Sawley and Long Eaton, in the County of Derby, through Part of the same Lordships, and also through Part of the Lordships of Saniy-acre, Stanton, Little Hallam, llkifone, Shipley, and Eastwood, to or near Langley Bridge, in the Counties of Derby and Nottingham; and that there is £.6,815. 5s already advanced upon the Credit of the Tolls arising from the said Road, which are barely sufficient to pay the Interest thereof, and to keep the Road in Repair; and that, if such intended Bill should pass into a Law, the same would greatly decrease the Tolls arising from the said Road, and the Mortgagees thereof would be thereby greatly injured, as the said Road is chiefly supported, and was Obtained, for the Purpose of conveying Coals to the Town of Nottingham, from the several Collieries which the said intended Cut, or Canal, to be made, lies contiguous to; and that, if the said intended Canal should be made, the said Road would be of very little Use, and the Price of Coals to the Inhabitants of the Town of Nottingham would not be any way reduced thereby, and the Security of such of the Petitioners as have advanced their Money upon the Credit of the said Tolls would be greatly endangered, if not totally abolished: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said intended Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law; and that, if such intended Bill mould pass into a Law, that there may be such Clauses and Provisions contained therein on Belialf of the Petitioners, whereby a reasonable Sa<-tisfaction may be made for the Damage they may so fullain by reason of the said intended Canal.

A Petition of the principal Gentleman, Tradesmen, and others, Inhabitants of the Borough of Derby, in the County of Derby, was also presented to the House, and read; taking Notice of the Application mentioned in the preceding Petition; and setting forth, That the Petitioners apprehend, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, the same will prove highly injurious to them and all others the Inhabitants of the said Borough, and of all the Weltem Part of the said County of Derby; and that, from the Lateness of the Time, and the precipitate Manner in which the said Petition hath been brought into the House, the Petitioners are induced to believe that the Plan and Scheme of the said intended Canal have been only partially considered by a few Individuals, who are manifestly the Promoters and En-couragers thereof, though the same are of such a public Nature and Concern as call for and require the Attention and mature Consideration of the Public, to digefi and approve the same; and that, from the Rea-fons aforesaid, the Petitioners have not the least Doubt but if such Part of the Public, w ho are interested in, and w ill be assessed by, the Event of the said Bill, had been previously acquainted with the Nature of the said Scheme, and had been indulged with sufficient Time to have maturely considered the fame, a Plan of a far more eligible Nature, and of much greater public Utility, might have been contrived and adopted; And therefore praying. That they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Bill, and that the same may not be passed into a Law, and more especially not till after the End of the present Session of Parliament, for the Reasons above alledged.

A Petition and Memorial of the principal Trades-jnen, Shopkeepers, and other Inhabitants, of the Town of Manchester, was presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth. That the Petitioners have, for a long Time past, suffered great Injuries and Inconveniences in the Exercise of their respective Trades, and sustained a considerable Loss in their Property, by the Introduction of large Quantities of Counterfeit Halfpence, which have been circulated in the Town of Manchester and the adjacent Country, in direct Opposition to the lawful Coin of this Realm, and to the manifest Injury and Distress of the fair Trader and the Public; and that the Petitioners, well knowing the fatal Tendency of such illicit Practices, have endeavoured by all lawful Means to suppress the Currency of such Counterfeit Money, and to bring the Offenders to exemplary Punishment, but have, to their great Concern and Disappointment, found all their Attempts fruitless and ineffectual; and have been informed that the Laws, in their present State, are inefficient for that Purpose; and that the Petitioners daily find, that the Introduction of the said Counterfeit Halfpence is a growing Evil, -and loudly calls for Redress, and which, the Petitioners are advised, cannot be obtained without the Intervention of the Legislative Authority: And therefore praying the House to take the above Premises into Consideration, and to provide such Remedies and Relief as they may think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

That several of the Clauses and Provisions of the said Bill are calculated, as the Petitioners conceive, to answer partial Purposes, and will be injurious to them, and others, who travel upon, and contribute to, the Tolls raised upon the said Roads; and that the Petitioners and others have already presented a Petition against: such Parts of the said Bill as affect them, but through Mistake, there was no Prayer contained in the said Petition, that they might be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the same: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, in support of the said former and this present'Petition, against such Parts of the said Bill as affect, and, as they conceive, will be injurious to, them, if the same pafl’es into a Law as it now Hands.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. William Callaway, being examined, said, That the said

Parish of Kensington hath, of late Years, greatly in-

creased in Puddings and Inhabitants, whereby the Poor are become very numerous, and the Poors Rates are daily and gradually encreasing, and the Parish Officers are under great Difficulties in providing Lodgings and proper Accommodations for their Reception; the Alms Houses and Poor Houses belonging to the said Parish being very insufficient for that Purpose.

And the Witness further said, That if a sufficient Workhouse was provided for the Parish, and put under the Care, Management, and Regulation of proper persons, to be from Time to Time annually appointed, the Aged and Infirm, as well as Infants, would be better provided for, and the idle and dissolute might be employed so as to maintain themselves, whereby the Inhabitants and Parishioners would, in that Respect, be greatly eased in the Poor Rates.

That the purchasing of Ground in the said Parish, and building such a W orkhouse, and providing it with proper Accommodations for the Reception of the Poor, would not coll more than £.4,000.

Translation of a Treaty between His Majesty and the Margrave of Brandenburgh Anfpach, concluded and signed at Anfpach the ift of 1777.

Be it known to those whom it may concern. That His Majesty the King of Great Britain having thought proper to accept a Corps of Infantry of the Troops of His Most Serene Highnefe the Reigning Margrave of

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Snifter of State the Baron De Gemmingenwho, after resolve itself into a Committee of the tjje Exchange of their respective full Powers, have whole House, to consider further of Ways and Means, agreed upon the following Articles. for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty. Article 1

, TT . , . The Most Serene Margrave of Brandenburgh yields

And then the House adjourned till Monday Morning jqjs Majesty a Corps of Infantry of One

next, I en of the Clock. thousand Two hundred Men, which shall consist in Two

Regiments, with One Company of Chasseurs, all pro-sessed Soldiers, according to the Lifts annexed to the present Treaty. This Corps shall be at the entire Disposal of the King of Great Britain, provided they be not sent to the East Indies.

Article 2.

The Most Serene Margrave engages to equip this: Corps completely, so that they may be ready to march Vol. 36. gn,

Treaties with the Margrave

Anfpach.

2J2

170 Martiu

A. 1777.

on the 28 th of the present Month at latest, or even sooner if it can be done. The said Corps shall pass in Review before His Britannick Majesty’s Commissary previous to their Departure.

Article 3.

Each Regiment of Infantry of this Corps shall be furnished with Two Pieces of Field Artillery, together with the Officers, Gunners, and other Men, and the Train thereto belonging.

Article 4.

The Most Serene Margrave engages to futnish the Recruits Annually necessary for this Corps, which shall be delivered to his Britannick Majesty’s Commissary, disciplined and completely equipped, at the Place of Embarkation, at such Time as His Majesty shall appoint, in pursuance of the Notice which shall be given thereof Four Months before their Departure.

Article 5.

The King’s Service and the Safety of the Troops equally requiring that the Commanding Officers and Subalterns Should be well skilled, and perfect in the Service, His Most Serene Highnefr will take due Care in the Choice of them.

Article 6.

His Most Serene Highness engages to put this Corps in the best State that shall be possible, and none shall be admitted therein, but Men fit for Campaign Service, and acknowledged as such by His Britannick Majesty’s Commissary.

Article 7.

This Corps shall be provided with Tents, and all the necessary Equipage.

Article 8.

The King grants to this Corps the ordinary and extraordinary Pay, as well as all the Advantages in Forage, Provisions, Xc. Xc. which the Royal Troops enjoy; and the Most Serene Margrave engages, that he will permit this Corps to enjoy all the Emoluments of Pay which His Britannick Majesty allows them. The lick and Wounded of the said Corps shall be taken Care of in the King’s Hospitals, and shall be treated in this respect as the Troops of His Britannick Majesty; and the Wounded, not in a Condition to serve, shall be lent to Europe into their own Country, at the King’s Expence.

Article 9.

There shall be paid to His Most Serene Highness, as Levy Money for each Foot Soldier, Thirty Crowns Banco, the Crown computed at Fifty-three Sols of Holland, and valued at Four Shillings and Nine Pence Three Farthings English Money, as well for the Infantry as for the Chafieurs and Artillery; One Half of this Levy Money shall be paid in Six Weeks after the Signature of the Treaty, and the other Half in Three Months. The Payment of this Levy Money shall be made nevertheless on Condition that Thirty Crowns Banco shall be withheld for each Soldier, who, not on account of Sickness, shall be deficient in the said Corps on the Day of their Embarkation; which Thirty

Crowns Banco shall, however, be paid as soon as the Soldiers, who were deficient, shall afterwards join their respective Corps.

Article 10.

If it should happen that any One of the Battalions or Companies of this Corps should suffer any very extraordinary Damage, whether in a Battle or Siege, or by any uncommon contagious Distemper, or by the Loss of any Transport Vessel in the Passage to,

His Britannick Majesty shall make good, in the most equitable Manner, the Loss of the Officer or Soldier, and defray the Expence of the Recruits necessary for completing the Corps which shall have sustained such extraordinary Damage.

Article 11.

The Most Serene Margrave reserves to himself the Nomination to the vacant Offices, as well as the Administration of Justice. His Britannick Majesty, moreover, will cause Orders to be given to the Commander of the Army in which this Corps shall serve, not to require from this Corps any extraordinary Sendee, or which may exceed their Proportion with the rest of the Army. This Corps shall take the Oath of Fidelity to His Britannick Majesty, without Detriment to that which they have taken to their Sovereign.

Article 12.

The Pay shall commence Seven Days before the March of this Corps of Troops; and from the Time of their being on board the Boats in order to go down The Mayn, all the Transport Charges shall be borne by

His Britannick Majesty.

Article 13.

His Britannick Majesty grants to His Most Serene Highness the Lord Margrave, while this Corps of Troops shall be in His Majesty’s Pay, an Annual Subsidy of Forty-five thousand Crowns Banco, to be computed from the Day of the Ratification of this Treaty; which Subsidy shall be continued Three Months after the Return of the said Corps into the Dominions of His Most Serene Highness: and the Troops shall enjoy the Pay to the End of the Month in which they shall be returned in the Territories of the Lord Margrave.

Article 14.

This Treaty shall be ratified by the HighContra&'ing Parties, and the Ratifications thereof shall be exchanged as soon as possible.

In Testimony whereof We, the undersigned, being furnished with the full Powers of His Majesty the King of Great Britain on the one Part, and of His Most Serene Hjghness the Lord Margrave of Brandenburgh on the other Part, have signed the present Treaty, and have caused the Seals of our Arms to be affixed thereto. 'Done at Anfpach this First Day of February

William FaucitU^^ Charles de Gemmingen.

Transtation of the Ulterior Convention between His Majesty and the Hereditary Prince of HeJJe, concluded and signed at lianau the 10th of

1777*

His Majesty the King of Great Britain having consented that the Troops of the Mott Serene Hereditary Prince of Hcffe, now in His Service iu America, should be augmented with a Corps of ChaiTeurs, and His . Most Serene Highness, in Consequence of that perfect Gratitude, and the respectful and unlimited Attachment with which He is devoted to His Majesty, as well as through Zeal for the Intereils and Service of that Monarch, having with great Alacrity charged himself with the Care of railing and furnishing such a Corps on His Majesty'sSubfidy, His Minister Plenipotentiary Colonel 18

William Faucitt, and the Minister and actual Privy

Councillor of the Most Serene Hereditary Prince of Hesse, Frederick dfMalJbouKg, being furnished with the requisite full Powers of their respective Matters, have agreed upon the following Articles:

t.

The Most Serene Hereditary Prince of Hcjfe engages not only to form a Corps of ChaiTeurs, and to cause them to be properly armed, clothed, disciplined, and put in Readiness to march to the Place of their Defti-nation, but also to cause One Company thereof to march at the Beginning of the next Month at latest; and as His Britunnick Majesty has made known His Desire that this Corps should be extended to a greater Number than that of One Company which was ottered, His Mott Serene Highness, animated with the Desire

of

17 Geo. III.

17® Martii.

275

of conforming himself to His Majesty *s Intentions as far as it depends upon him, promises to use all his Endeavours for such Augmentation, and to increase the Number as much as polfllde: And as the Circum-ilances will not yet allow of the actual settling of the positive Number, it is agreed previOufly to prepare the annexed State, which shall constitute the Balls and ltuie for all the other Companies; of which it is hoped Four at lead may be provided, of One hundred Men each; so that the whole Corps, upon this Supposition, will amount to Four hundred and Twelve Men, the Staff included.

2.

This Corps of Chasseurs (the real Number of which f1ia.ll be fixed and settled at the Time of their March) shall be completely equipped by His Moll Serene Highness, and provided with every Thing necessary to put them in Readiness to march; and His Britannick Majesty promises to take them into His Pay from the Moment of the enliliing of each Man composing the said Corps, and to furnish every Thing necessary when they arrive at the Place of their'Dellination for the Transport of their Equipage, and likewise Provisions, Forage, Ammunition, fife. fife, for their Use, in the same Manner, and upon the same Footing, as shall be furnished to the Ildjian Chasseurs which are on the British Subsidy. And as the Strength of the said Corps cannot be ascertained till they pass in Review before the King’s Commissary, which shall be done as soon as they are complete here at if possible,

or' elsewhere, as the Circilmftance may require, it is agreed, that an exact State shall then be prepared of the Strength of the said Corps, which His Majesty shall take upon Subsidy, whatever may be their Number, without regarding whether they consist of Four Companies, of more, or JeCs, in Conformity to that State which shall be annexed to, and make make Part of, the present Treaty; the Pay, Subsidy, and Levy Money for the said Corps, Ihalfalfo be regulated according to the Number of Men of which it shall then be composed.

3-

The Pay of the Corps of Chasseurs shall be higher than that which His Majesty allows for the Infantry of Hijfe llanau now in His Service; it shall be equal to that of the //f^?a«Cliaffeurs, and consequently in the same Proportion as it was during the last War; and His Majesty promises, moreover, that every Thing already granted, or which shall be hereafter granted, for the said Ihjfian Chasseurs, shall be equally allowed to those which the Moll Serene Hereditary Prince shall furnish by virtue of the present Convention.

4-

The said Pay shall commence forthwith; but as on

the one Hand the Number Of Men is not yet entirely collected, and on the other, those actually provided already receive Pay from the Molt Serene Hereditary Priftcdi it shall be reimbursed to him from the Day of their Engagement, for all those who have entitled into the said Corps since the 19 th of last; and in like

Manner such as are deficient shall not be paid for but as they enlist therein, according to the Returns which shall be made with the utmost Exactness, duly attested and certified.

5*

This Corps shall be composed only of Chasseurs by Profession, or good Fuzileers, all well disciplined, and possessing the requisite Dexterity; and although it is impossible to fix exactly the Time in which this Corps may be entirely completed, it shall not, however, be extended farther than to the End of the Month of April next; and His Most Serene Highness promises that all possible Diligence shall be used in order to assemble them, even before that Period if it can be done, and to cause them to march without Delay for their Destination.

6.

Every Thing that has been agreed upon in the Treaty of the 5th of February in the Year 1776, with regard to the Regiment of HeJJe Hanau, which is now in His Majesty’s Service, shall extend also to this new Augmentation of a Corps of Chasseurs. The Subsidy shall be augmented in proportion from the Day of the Signature of the present Convention; and the Advantages granted by the 7th, 9th, 10th, nth, and 12th Articles of the former Treaty, shall be likewise applied to this Corps. Levy Money at Thirty Crowns Banco ;shall be paid by His Majesty for each Chasseur, the Crown to be computed at Fifty-three' Sols of One Half of which Levy Money shall be paid in One Month, and the other Half in Two Months, after the Signature of the present Convention.

7.

This Ulterior Convention shall be ratified by the High Contracting Parties, and the Ratifications thereof shall be exchanged as soon as possible.

In Testimony whereof. We, the Undersigned, being furnished with the full Powers of His Majesty the King of Great Britain on the one Part, and of His Moll Serene Highness the Hereditary Prince of HeJJe on the other, have ligned the present Convention, and have set thereto the Seals of our Arms.

Done at Hanau, the 10th «f February 1777.

(g) William Faucitt. S)F

Mr. Wilbraham Bootle reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Cojnpany of Proprietors of the Chester Canal Navigation was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, of the 25th of April 1774, relative to Navigation Bills, had been complied with (except that no Lift of Subscribers for carrying the Works into Execution was annexed to the Petition; but that there was annexed to the Petition a Resolution of the said Company of Proprietors to raise f.6o perCent. on the original Subscribers; and also > borrow a further Sum of Money, not exceeding £.30,000, to complete the Navigation); and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table; Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, An Act of Parliament, made in the Twelfth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, intituled, "An Act for making a navigable Cut or Canal' from the River Dee, within the Liberties of the City of Chester, to or near " Middlewich and Nantwich, in the County of Chester f was read. And,

Mr. John Moon, being examined, said. That the Sum of /. 60,000 hath been expended in carrying on the Works directed to be done by the said Act; and that a considerable Part of the said Cut or Canal is finished; but that the Money authorized to be raised by the said Act is not sufficient to complete the same. Then, *

Mr. Thomas Morris,-a. Surveyor, being examined, feid. That it is proposed to vary the Line of Part of the Cut or Canal directed to be made by the said Act, agreeable to the Plan annexed to the Petition; and that he has taken Surveys and Levels of the proposed Variation, and thinks it practicable to make the said Cut or Caned: And he added. That, by making the said Cut or Canal in the Line proposed, will lave an Expence to the Company of Proprietors of upwards of £.7,000. And,

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, An Act, made in the 14th Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for paving, repairing, lighting, and watching, the Streets, and other public Passages and Places, within that Part of the Parish of called Saint James's, and removing Obstructions and Annoyances therein; for widening the Passage from Clerkenwell Green to the Parish Church; and for watching and lighting certain Highways within the said Parish, was read; And,

Mr. Abraham Rhodes, being examined, said. That the Commissioners appointed by the said Act have proceeded in the Execution thereof, but that many Doubts have arisen upon several of the Clauses in the said Act, whereby much Litigation and Expence is likely to ensue thereon; and that the Hates authorized to be raised by the said Ati, are inadequate for the Purposes thereby intended.

And he produced to your Committee an Account of the Annual Amount of Money received and expended by the Commissioners in the Execution of the said Act, whereby it appeared that the Sum of £.1,187 had been received, and £. 1,661 had been expended in one Year.

And the Witness further said, That if the Commissioners were impowered to cleanse the Streets and repair the Highways included in the said Act, it would be of great Benefit to the said Parish; and also that it would be of great Utility to the Inhabitants of the said Parish, if the Way or Passage leading from Clerkenwell Close to Rofoman Street, was widened, by taking down a (mail House and Sheds in the Occupations of John and John Newman, and laying the Ground belonging-thereto into the said Passage; and if the Footway leading from Rofomay Street to John's Street, was

widened, and a Carriage Way made there.

And the Witness added, that it would be very beneficial to the Inhabitants if a Chapel was built near Pen-ton Street; the said Parish being very extensive, and many Parts of it, by reason of the great Increase of Buildings, lie at a great Distance from the Parish Church.

Mr. John Thorpe and Mr. John Severn, Churchwardens of the said Parish, confirmed the Evidence’ of Mr. Rhodes.

An Act, pafl*ed in the Twentieth Year of the same Reign, for the taxing and assessing of the Lands of the Adventurers within the Great Level of the Fens: And also,

A T.aw of Sewers, made at a Session of Sewers, held on the 13th Day of January, in the Sixth Year of King Charles the First, at Norfolk:

And also,

A pretended Act of Parliament, made at Westminster in the Year 1649, for the draining of the Great Level of the Fens: And also,

- An Act, passed in the Twenty-seventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, for discharging the Corporation of the Governor, Bailiffs, and Commonalty, of the Company of Conservators of the Great Level of the Fens, commonly called Bedford Level, from a Debt due to the Duke of Bedford and Earl of Lincoln, and for enabling the Proprietors of Lands in the North Level, Part of the said Great Level, to raise Money to dil’charge the Proportion of the said North Level in the Debts of the said Corporation, and for ascertaining and 14

appropriating the Taxes to be laid on the said North Level, and for the more effectual draining and pre~ serving the North Level, and divers Lands adjoining thereto, in the Manor of CrowlaAnd also. An Exemplification of the St. Ives Law of Sewers* made at St. Ives in the Thirteenth Year of King Charles the Firll; were read: From which it appeared, That the Great Level of the Fens, called Bedford Level, which contains upwards of Three hundred thousand Acres, was, for Ages, overflowed and drowned by the Rain and Spring Waters falling on and issuing out of the Counties of Northampton, Norfolk, Suffolk, Lincoln, Cambridge, and Huntingdon, and Part of Buckingham, Hertford, and E/fe.r,together with the Downfall on the

Plain itself, which have their Course through the said Level to the Outfalls into the Sea at Lynn and Wijbich, so as to render the same of little Value, till Francis Earl of Bedford, in the Sixth Year of King Charles the First, after many fruitless Attempts made by others, undertook to drain the fame; for which the said Earl, and others concerned with him, styling themselves Ad* venturers, were to receive from the Proprietors 95,000 Acres, being nearly One Third of the Whole; of which

95.000 Acres, when drained, 55,000 were to be adjudged to the said Earl and his Adventurers, and the remaining 40,000 were to remain as a Fund, from the Annual Profits of which the Works of Drainage were to be supported: That the said Earl and his Adventurers made such a Progress in draining the fame, at a very great Expence, that the greatest Part of the said

95.000 Acres was divided amongst him and his Adventurers, and their Assigns; and 40,000 Acres, Part of the said 95,000, were set out and specifically allotted for the Maintenance of the Works.

And it further appeared. That by Means of some Interruption the Works fell to Decay, and the Benefit intended to the Public was in great measure prevented, in consequence of which the Son of the said Francis, William Earl of Bedford, applied to the Parliament then fitting at Westminster, who passed an Act, setting forth the great Advantages that would accrue to the Public; and to Individuals, by completely draining the said Level, and giving such Powers to the said Earl and his Participants, as were necessary for the Purpose of completing and continuing the said Work, on the Plan of the Law of Sewers, made at King’s Lynn, in the Sixth Year of King Chathe First, excepting that instead of 40,000 Acres being specifically allotted for the Maintenance of the Works, the whole 95,000 Mere subjected to a Tax for that Purpose: That from, the Time the Land in the said Great Level was adjudged to the Adventurers, the said 95,000 Acres liable to a perpetual Tax for draining, have been known by the Name of Adventure Land, and the Remainder, being double that Quantity, and not liable to be taxed for the general Works of Draiuing, have been called Free Lands.

And it further appeared. That none of tl»e Acts of Parliament nor Laws of Sewers abovementioned, laid any Tax or Toll on the Navigation through the said Great Level, for any Damage done to the Great River Banks, or other Works, by haling thereon, by which Means the Navigation is chiefly carried on; and that both The Adventure Lands and The Free Lands, ly ing intermixed, are equally liable to be overflowed.
