They are, very greatly; that the Horses do not draw in a right Line one behind the other, but obliquely, and so cover a larger Space, and do more Damage than would be done by common Drawing; and that there is not, to his knowledge, any Compensation made to the Bedford Level Corporation for the Damage fe done.

Mr. Cole, the Register, being asked, Whether the Corporation received any Satisfaction for the Damages done by Haling on the Banks ? laid, They do not receive any.

Mr. Golberrte, being further examined, said. That in reckoning the Horses of which he had given the Committee an Account, they counted none but such as came with loaded Boats. — And being asked. Whether the Adventurers have any Banks on the Ouze? he said. They have, 9 Miles being the whole Distance between Denver's Sluice and Littleport, except One Mile which

does not belong to them; that he spoke of the Bank on one Side only; that the major Part of the Banks are 7 or 8 Feet wide at the Top. — And being asked. If the Horses do not tread down and strengthen the Banks ? he said, If they would keep on the Top they. might do feme Service, but that their hind Legs are generally on the Sides, and that they sometimes hale intirely there; and that he has frequently known them throw the Earth into the Rivers.

Mr. Thomas Knowles, being examined, said. He 4s Surveyor of a private District, called Burnt Fen that he is upwards of 60 Years old, and has always lived in the Neighbourhood of the said Fen. — ‘And being asked, he said, The Barges and Lighters employed between Brandon Creek and Ely, on the River Ouze, are greatly increased in Number within his Memory, and are of greater Burthen; and that they are Haled by larger Horses than were formerly used, and more in Number to each Barge. — And being asked. Whether the Banks are trod down by the Haling upon them ? he said. They are very much; that he spoke of a private District, which was so poor as to beaflifled by the Corporation; that there is a Toll paid upon that Bank for the Commissioners of the District, which he receives; and that the Horses in Haling do much Mischief everywhere, thought not equally so on broad Banks and narrow ones, the latter receiving the most Injury; that the general Width of the Top of the Bank of which he speaks, is from 3 to 6 Feet; that if Banks are made 8 Feet wide at the Top, they may be reduced 2 or 3 Feet in a Year’s Time, according to the Wear. — And being asked, Whether when Money is given by the Corporation to artili any particular Diflri6t, it is laid out under the Inspection of the Fen Office ? he said. That so far as relates to the outward Bank it is, but that the interior Works are under the Direction of the Commissionere of that District. — And being asked. If he was particularly acquainted with the Banks from Ely to Brandon Creek ? he said. He was, and that he believed they are still under the Corporation, though repaired of late Years, under Acts of Parliament for

particular Distri6ts. — A fid being asked. What he apprehended to be the Annual Damage to the Banks ? lie said. He really believed it to be very considerable, and that very great Sums are laid out in repairing the Damage done by the Horses haling. — And being asked. What is the Toll on the Bank within the District of which he was speaking ? he said, Six Pence for each HorseHaling; that it is paid to the Proprietors; that the above Toll is taken between Prickivello Bridge and Littleport Bridge, and from Bridge to Bal-

don's Load, which is near Three Miles, Three Pence a Horse. — And being asked. Whether he accounted to the Bedford Level Corporation for the said Tolls ? he said, He did not; and that if no such Tolls were collected, the Corporation mult contribute to repair the Banks, or they would go to ruin; that the Corporation had often allotted Money for the Repair of that Bank. — And being asked. If the Burthen of the Vessels navigating the said Rivers was greater now than formerly ? he said, Yes, but that he could not specify the Particulars; that their Burthen is at present from 5 to 16 Tons; that about 30 Years ago the largest Boat might be of 10 or 12 Tons; that the Water is not deeper now than formerly, nor in his Opinion in many Places so deep, there being but 3 Feet Water now in Parts where once were 7, but that they use more Horses to each Barge; that the Boats were built in the same Manner formerly as they are now, and that they now put Horses enough to each Boat to force her through the Mud. — And being asked. How he apprehended the Water had been diminished ? he said. By the great Floods, Want of a proper Outfall, Stagnation, and the growing of the Weeds. — And being asked. Whether he meant the Outfall at Sea, or the Obstructions in the Rivers ? he laid, He meant the latter, which he attributed to the Definition of the Banks, the Water breaking out, and the consequent Stagnation. — And being asked. Whether the Materials of the Banks are such as would be washed away without their being injured by the Horses haling upon them ? he said, Some of them would, and that wherever there is any bleak Water they would be almost carried away. — And being asked. What Method was taken to prevent it ? he said. They used what is called crwhich is forming Litter Reeds, or what they can get, into Hedges, but that where the Horses go this cannot be done. — And being asked. What Outfall lie alluded to ? he said Denver's Sluice, but that the Water is flopped in the Ouze, between Ely and Littleport, before it reaches that Sluice, and that he did not mean to say the Obstruction.is at the Sluice; that the Haling upon the Banks causes them to moulder into the Rivers, which contributes to the increase of Weeds, the Banks being some only 40 Yards from the Edge of the River, and fomo close to it; that when they are at 40 Yards Distance the Mould from them cannot fall into the River, but that in some Parts the Banks are so near that the Barges ferape against them, for a great way together. — -Ana being asked. Whether, if the Banks were at a proper Distance from the River, they would be damaged by the Haling upon them ? be said. They certainly would, and that the Banks near the River are damaged by the Water working against them; that in same of Floods the Earth trod down from the Banks will be all washed into the Rivers, and that the greater the Distance of the Bank from the River, the greater Injury is done to it by Haling thereon.

Your Committee then called Mr. Philip Cawthorne, who had been Deputy Surveyor to the Bedford Level Corporation, between 6 and 7 Years; and who, being examined, said. He was 70 Years old, 20 of which he had had the Care of the Hundred Foot Bank; that the said Bank is 21 Miles long, and that' the Expence of supporting it for the last 20 Years amounted to about 15,000; that there is very great Commerce on the Hundred Foot River, from Lynn and Ely to -

donshire,

donshire, and other Counties, as far as Bedfordshire. — And being asked, Whether the Haling upon that Bank is attended with any Damage to it? he laid. Yes* very considerable; that it has thereby been endangered in Times of Floods; that he remembered several Breaches in it, particularly a very large one in 1763, the Size of which, as near as he could guess, was 60 Yards long; and 33 Feet deep perpendicular; that it happened in January, and that a great deal of Winter Crop, and Corn in the Stack, was loft, and many Families drowned out. — And being asked. Whether he believed that Breach was in any Degree occasioned by Haling on the Banks? he said, It was believed that the Gang of Lighters which had just passed, and was very heavy, had done it. — And being asked. What Reason he had to suppose so ? he said. That the Drivers suddenly whipping the Horses had occasioned the Lighters to swing against the Bt c. — And being asked. What is the Size of that Bank ? he said. It is about 18 or 20 Feet Batter, 6 Feet high next the River, 7 or 8 on the other Side, and the Top in some Places 6 Feet wide. — And being asked, Whether he had ever seen the Water even with the Top of that Bank ? he said. He had seen it run over it for a Mile together; that even in such Circumstances it is not a very little Matter that will beat it down, but that they generally raise a little Scradge or Hedge at the Top, to keep the Water from running over; that when the Rivers are quite full, the Haling upon the Banks is very dangerous; and that they never permit a Horse to pats at those Times. — And being asked. Whether, if a few Inches being knocked off of the Top of a Bank by any Force or Shock, the Water following it, would occasion a large Breach there? he said. It will cut down the Bank-in a very little Time, and make a very large Hole in the Space of an Hour or two. — And being asked, If he spoke of the Banks in general ? he said. He spoke of those under his own Care. — And being asked, Whether a Breach will at all Times be occasioned by the Water running over the Bank? he said, Yes, if it was not immediately flopped; that when a Barge has passed, and made a Breach, it is not always in their Power to flop it, as they cannot always be upon the Spot. — And being asked. Whether the Expence of repairing the Breach made in the Year 1763 was included in the above-mentioned Sum off. 15,000? he said. It was. — And being asked. If there had been any Breaches since that ? he said. There had, one in May 1773, which he believed was occasioned by the Banks being distressed by the Water; that it was not at the same Place as the former Breach; that it was 04 Yards long and 20 Feet deep perpendicular at the deepest Part; that there was another smaller one the same Year; and that he never heard of any being occasioned by Gangs of Lighters, except that which he had mentioned. — And being asked. Whether the £. 15,000 laid out the last 20 Years would more effectually have secured the Banks, if there had been no Haling upon them ? he said. That if there had not been. any Haling upon them, they would not have been worn down so quick, and con sequently have been more safe. — And being asked, What is the Distance of the Banks from the Hundred Foot River? he laid. He did not think it exceeded 24 Yards in any Part, from the Foot of the Bank to the Edge of the River, and in some Parts was not Yards. — And being asked. How much Slope these Banks have ? he said. Eighteen Feet to the River Side, meaning the diagonal, the Bank being Six Feet high. — And being asked, How they Haled on this Bank? he described it in the same Manner as a former Witness had done, with respect to other Banks; and added, that by suddenly whipping the Horses, or driving them on the Side of the Bunk, the Flag or Facing of it is much tom down. — And being asked. Whether all the Injuries he had specified occasioned a general Increase of the Expence to the Corporation on account of keeping Vot. 36.

them in Repair ? he said, tt did, and was very considerable; as they were obliged to employ Men immediately to repair all Damages. — And being asked. For what yearly Sum he would undertake to make good the Damages done to the Banks under his Care, by Haling upon them ? he should nOt be willing to undertake it for £. 10 a Year per Mile; saying, he mea, nt the Hundred Foot Bank. — And being asked. Whether any Compensation had been made to the Corporation for the Damages done those Banks by Haling upon them? he said, None that he knew of — And being asked.

Whether Carts, Chaises, Persons on Horseback, and Droves of Cattle, travel on those Banks? he said. That sometimes in dry Weather there are; but that there have been Hr ift Orders for 6 or 7 Years, that Carriages should not pass; and now none go. — And being asked. What is the Burthen of the Barges now navigating the Hundred Foot River? he said. From to 14 Chaldron of Coals; that they have been of that Burthen for 20 Years; that the said River has been made more than 100 Years. —

And being asked. Whether the Droves that go from Norfolk to St. Ives Market travel along that Bank ? he said, They do at ail Times, except when the River is full of Water. — And being asked. Whether any Toll is paid for them? he said. They pay for going over Denver's Sluice, but he did not know what $ that they also pay . something at Oxload, but he did not know what; and at no other Place. — And being asked. If those Cattle do not trample down the Banks? he said. They are driven at the Top of the Bank as much as possible,. and that they certainly mull do some Damage; that the Toll at Denver's Sluice is paid, whether they go along the Bank or not. — And being asked, To whom the Toll at Oxload is paid ? he said. He believes a Person receives it for the Bedford Level Corporation; that the Man who receives it is notan Officer under the Corporation, but he believes Farms the Tolls of them. — And being asked. Whether the Cattle pass in considerable DroVes? he' said, 40, 50, or 100 Black Cattle at a Time, once a Week, for 3 Months in the Year. — And being asked. Whether there are always Cattle feeding on the Banks ? he said. Yes, except in High Water Times; and that he believed the Corporation let the Feeding upon them. — And being asked. Whether the Horses haling paid any Toll at Oxload? he said, They do not. Then,

Mr. Thomas Hogard, an Engineer, being examined, informed your Committee, That he had been conversant in the Management of Low Lands liable to be drowned near 40 Years; that he had lately viewed the several Rivers and Banks within the Middle and South Levels of the Bedford Level; that the Extent of the Banks within those Two Districts, under the Jurisdiction of the Corporation, is upwards of 170 Miles; that he had measured them, and that he had observed the Haling upon them, and the Cattle passing; that all the Banks are haled upon, more or less; that Horses passing along the Banks, not drawing, do not do as much Damage as when Hading; that Haling upon the Banks does them much Injury, and necessarily increases the Expence of the Corporation in repairing them, which is very considerable; that if he was asked to undertake the Repair of them by the Mile, he should not chuse tat do it; that taking them altogether, which he had considered when he made the Estimate, he was of Opinion they could not be repaired, with respect to the Damage done by Haling only, under £.% per Annum a Mile* on an Average, of the whole 170 Miles; that he apprehends the Damage sustained for some Years past has amounted to that; and that if the Banks were nOt to be repaired they would go down, and of Course there could be no Haling upon them; that the Haling would be in a great Measure the Cause of their Deltruction, if not constantly repaired; that Horses not drawing do as much mischief in passing the Banks as an equal Number of Cattle would do; that to his Knowledge the Corporation are at a very considerable Expence in flagging the

Then, Mr. Thomas Knowles, being further examined, said. There have, been many Mills erected within the last 30 Years for throwing Water into the Rivers, which have thrown also great Quantities of Moor mixed with Water, by which Means the Beds of the Rivers have 20

in many Parts been greatly filled up, and the Depth of Water thereby deCreased; that he has sometimes teen the Mills, Seven of which he has under his Care, throw up little else than Dirt; that the Mud so thrown damages the Navigation also, and makes it necessary to use a greater Number of Horses in Haling; that where he is concerned the Mills were erected by the Commissioners of the Burnt Fen District. — And being atked, Whether they could have eroded those Mills without Leave of the Corporation ? he said. He believed not; that the intention of erecting them was to drain the Fen; that the Mills of which he spoke drain only the particular District, some Part of which is free Land, and some Corporation Land.

Mr. Cole, being further examined, said, That the Mills have been the Cause of almost the Dellrudion of the Country; that in 1711 they.were determined by the Court of Exchequer to be a Nuisance; that in the Course of about 30 Years the Beds of the Rivers being much grown up, and there being no fall out of the Fens into the Rivers, the Water stagnated within the Fen, and Mills were introduced to lift it up into the Rivers, the Beds of which were above the Level of the Fens.- — And being asked. Whether it was his Opi* nion that every kind of Mills are detrimental to a proper Plan of Drainage ? he said, That he thought where the Level of the Country is so much lower than the adjacent Drains which are to carry off the Water, and those Drains cannot be made lower than the Level, as is the same in many Parts of the Water mutt

be lifted up by Engines: but where the adjacent Drains can be made lower than the Lands to be drained, Mills, besides the Expence of them, are totally uleless. — And being asked. Whether the Country of which he spoke drained itfejf formerly without Mills, and would do so again, if the Rivers were properly scoured or deepened ? he said. He spoke with regard to the South Level, which is in the worst Situation for draining; and which he remembers about 45 Years ago without one Mill in it, since when he had not seen it in so fine a Situation as it was then.

Mr. Thomas Ilogard, being again examined, said. That after heavy Rains, and in wet Seasons, the Great Level of the Fens is always liable to be overflowed; that the Rivers in general want deepening, and the Banks repairing, heightening, and strengthening, and will from time to time require great Sums for the continuing them in a proper State, to preserve the Great Level from being overflowed; that it will also require great Sums to furnish proper Haling Ways for the Navigators through the said Rivers; and that considerable Works are wanting for the Preservation of the Navigation; that the present Banks are inadequate to the Purpose of Haling upon them, being too weak, and liable to be broke down by the Horses belonging to every Gang that passes; that the Bank of Morton's Tea me, though not so liable to be broke down as some others, is in Danger of it in high Floods; that the Hundred, Foot Bank is not in Danger of being broke down but in Times of Floods, nor the Ten Mile Bank. — And being asked. If any of them are liable to be broke down except in Flood-Time? he said. Some are; particularly the Banks of The Stoke River, The the Brandon, and the Grant, from to Harri-

viter; and that he did not look upon any Bank as in a State of Security, which is liable to be broke down in Time of Flood. — And being asked. Whether the Forty Foot Bank is liable to be broke down, except in Times of Floods? he said. It is, by Haling upon it; that without being absolutely broken down, the Banks fufier conllant Damage from Haling upon them, by being weakened and mouldered down; that the Banks of the Brandon River had in several Places been so broken and trod down, by the Horses Haling upon them, that the W ater ran over the Banks. — And being asked, Wrhether those Banks are not greatly damaged by Cattle feeding and going on them? he said, At that Time Ire saw no Cattle in the Country; that he was going up the River in a Boat, and being (lopped by the Ice was obliged to walk from the Outfall of Brandon River to Wilton, which is about Ten Miles. — And being

Your Committee then called Charles Naljim Esquire, again; who being examined, said. He had been Regiller and Auditor to The Bedford Level Corporation 20 Years; that he has constantly attended the Meetings of the Corporation at Ely, and the Fen Office in London, where their Bufinefe is transacted, except Once. — And being asked. What he had observed in the Conduct of the Gentlemen who compose The Bedford Level Corporation, in Discharge of their Duty as Trustees for that Level ? he said. It is a Trust of a great deal of Business, and eonfequently great Trouble; that the Execution of it is attended with Expence to the Trustees, and from the Time he had known any Thing of the Matter they have discharged it with the greatest Fidelity, Justice and Attention; that they have, by every Means in their Power, enereased their Revenue, and in the Dil'position of it, have, to the belt of their Judgment, applied it to the Execution of the Trust, which, at the Time of their Election, they are sworn to perform; that when he went to the April Meeting in 1773, he passed through a Country almoll overflowed from Cambridge to Ely, and found in general, from the Conversation he had with People who came from the latter Place to attend the Business of that Meeting, that nothing could equal the general Distrel’s of the Country; that there had been a Breach in the South Bank of the Bedford River, the Hopping of which had colt a very large Sum; that there had been a Breach also in the North Bank; that the Water had ran over most of the great Banks, and that tl.e Expence in Breaches and Flood Bills alone had that Year amounted to .3,590; that he found the Receiver General had exhaulled all the Revenues in his 1 lands, and that there were considerable outstand-ingl )ebf.s unprovided for; that the Streets were crowded with Labourers, Ibliciting the Payment of their Wages for the Maintenance of their Wives and Families; and that to Satisfy and relieve them, Mr Gould, Mr. Grave*, Mr. If did bore, Mr. Sir Thomas

ton, Mr. Partridge, Mr. Drage, and Mr. Dixon, advanced £. 1,800 on the Spot for that Purpose; that the Corporation have always given every Aliiftance in their Power to private Districts; that The Burnt Fen Dilirict has been assisted to the Amount of 4,000 at Jeaft; The Middle Fen District to the Amount of £. 2,000, and The Swaffiham District very considerably; that, from the Accounts at present in the Possession of the Corporation, it is not possible to discover the Amount of the Expence of the original Adventurers in the first draining of the Level; but lie had been told by People, wi.o, from their Age, were more likely to know than himself, that it was the general Opinion of the Country, that from the First of the Undertaking, to the Fifteenth Year of King Charles the Second, not leis than £. 400,000 was expended; and the late Sir Francis St. John, of Thorpe,\\ear Peterborough, said. He had Papers in his Custody which would shew it; that from the Fifteenth of Charles the Second, to the Year 1776, the Expences of the Corporation on all the 3 Levels had amounted to at least £,500,000, besides which they have contracted Debts, on account of the Middle and South Levels, to the Amount of £.38,500; that all the Revenues have been applied, and the Debt incurred, in the Execution of their Trust; that there has hardly been a Meeting of the Corporation in the Country at which Applications for Aliiftance have not been made, which they were obliged, from the Deficiency of their Revenues, to refuse complying with; and that such Refusals of Assistance, had their Funds been competent, would have been a Breach of their Trust; that the Adventure. Lands have been so high taxed, as to induce the Holders thereof to throw up, from Time to Time,- considerable Quantities thereof. — And being asked. Whether, upon the Whole, he VOL. 36.

What Interest the Corporation pay for Money borrowed ? he said,

£. 4 per Cent. — And being asked. Whether all the Adventure Lands are not answerable to their full Value for the Expence of the Drainage ? he said. The Corporation have, by the Act of the Fifteenth of Charles the Second, a Power of taxing them without Limb tat ion for the Support and Maintenance of the Great

Level; that the highell Tax ever imposed was in 1776, which was a Tax and an Half, and the lowest has been a Angle Tax; that for the last Century there have been 13 Years, in which a Tax and an Half was laid, 55 Years a Tax and a Quarter, and 33 Years a Angle Tax, and this from the Year 1673 to 1774 inclusive. — And being asked. Whether those Lands have not been taxed as high as they would bear ? he said,

He believed there was a Period, about the Year 1750* in which, if they had laid a Tax and an Half Year after Year for 3 Years, and the Country could have had no assurances that at the End of that Time it would have been reduced, he believed they would have abandoned more than a Quarter of -it, and that in the present State of Circumftauces, if greater Taxes were laid, he conceived less Money would be raised; that an Advertisement had been inserted in a public Paper, for a Meeting at Ely, to take into Consideration the distressed State of the Country, in.Consequence of which. Meetings were held, at which it was deemed necessary that Application should be made to Parliament for the Purposes mentioned in the Petition.

— And being asked. Whether all the Persons who have signed the Petition are Owners of Free Land ? he said. He could not speak to all, but that many- of them were, and that he does not know of their Consent to the Application being Signified in any other Way than by their signing the Petition.

A Petition of the Mailers and Journeymen Felt regulating Makers, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, resideut c Trade. jn an(j the City of Bristol, was presented to the

House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners are Persons employed in the Art and Myliery of Felt-making, having lawfully served their Apprenticeship thereto, and, by a close Application and lndullry, have been enabled comfortably to support themselves and Families for many Years pall; and that by Two Acts of Parliament, passed in the Eighth Year of Queen Elizabeth, and the First Year of King James the First, it is En-nacted, " That no Mailer Manufacturer shall have but " Two Apprentices, besides their own Sons, at one " Time, nor those for lefsTime than Seven Years;" And that the Petitioners have been informed. Application has been made to the House, for a Bill to repeal fitch Parts of the said Acts as relate to the Mailers Manufacturers taking more than Two Apprentices at one Time; and that, by reason of the great Number of Journeymen in the said Trade, many of them are at present wholly unempleyed therein, and are obliged to work in Coal Pits, and to serve as Labourers in other Employments; and that, since the Year 1774, there have been 1,325 Men relieved in the City of Bristol, and County of Gloucester, seeking for Employ; and if the said Acts should be repealed, and the Felt Makers be at Liberty to take what Number of Apprentices they shall think proper, a much greater Number of Journeymen will be unavoidably out of Employ, to the great Prejudice of the Petitioners and their Families, and the respective Parishes whereunto they belong: And therefore praying the House, to take their same into Consideration, and to grant them such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet,

Bhtc. A Petition of the Journeymen Hat and Felt Makers VoL. 3b.

and until the said "Works are finished, the Estate of the Petitioner and others, within the said Dales, Fep, and inclosed Low Lands, mull remain in their present unimproved State; and there is great Reason to believe the said Commissioners do not intend to complete the said Works within any reasonable Time; and that the said Dales are now chargeable with a Tax of Eight Pence an Acre, and the said Common Fen with a Tax of Four Pence an Acre, by virtue of the said Act; and that, When the same are inclosed and used in Severalty, the Whole will be chargeable with a Tax of One Shilling ah Acre, being the same Tax that is now paid for all the melofed Low Lands within the said Parish; which said additional Tax will produce an annual Increase to the Income of the said Commissioners of £. 110, or thereabouts, to be applied towards the general Works of Drainage; which said Sutn, together with the Rates now payable upon the Lands within the Lordship of ' Billinghay, will amount to the annual Sum of £. 260, or thereabouts; and that, in order to forward the general Works of Drainage, and to drain and improve the said Dales, Fen, and inclosed Low Lands, the Petitioner is desirous that he and the other Owners of the said Dales, Fen, and inclosed Low Lands, may be enabled !o make and complete the Banks and Works aforesaid; and that the Money they thall expend in completing the same may be repaid to them by the said Commissioners within a reasonable Time after the same shall be completed: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that Provision may be made in the said Bill, for draining and improving the said Dales, Fen, and inclosed Low Lands, by such Ways and Means, and in such Manner, as the House shall think just and reasonable.

A Petition of Andrew Robinson Bowes, Esquire, N*wc*flle was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, "P00 Tvn* That, at the last Election of a Member to serve in £lea, on* Parliament for the Town of Newcastle upon Tyne, in the room of Sir Walter Blackett, Baronet, deceased.

Sir John Trevelyan, Baronet, and the Petitioner were Candidates; and that the said Sir John Trevelyan, and divers other Persons, on his Behalf, and by his Direction, did, by giving Money and other Rewards, by Promises of Money and other Rewards, and by Threats and other unwarrantable Proceedings, prevail upon several Persons to give their Votes at the said Election, for the said Sir John Trevelyan, who otherwise would have voted for the Petitioner; and did thereby also prevail upon several Persons to withhold their Votes at the said Election, who otherwise would have voted for the Petitioner; and that, in the Course of the said Election, James Thomas Loraine, Esquire, then Sheriff of the said Town, the Returning Officer, admitted several Persons, not qualified to vote at the said Election, to poll for the said Sir John Trevelyan; and refilled the Votes of several Persons, who had an undoubted Right to vote, and offered to poll for the Petitioner; and that, by those and other illegal Practices, the said Sir John Trevelyan hath been unduly elected and returned, to the manifest Injury of the Petitioner, and in Violation of the Freedom of Election: And therefore praying the House will take his same into Consideration, and grant him such Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Tuesday the 22d Day of April next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

Memorandum,

In pursuance of Two Acts, made in the lothand 1 ith Years of His present Majesty’s Reign, to regulate the Trials of controverted Elections, , or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament, the like Notices, as in the former Cafes, were sent to the Parties; accompanied with Orders for their Attendance, by themselves, their Coun-fel, or Agents, at the Time on which the said Petition was ordered to be taken into Consideration.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do ifiite his Warrant, or Warrants, for such Persons,' Papers, and Records, as shall be thought necessary by the several Parties, on the Hearing of the Matter of the said Petition.

A Petition of the Owners and Occupiers of Lands

on the Maifemore Side of the River Severn, and other Persons trading with, and resorting to, the City of Gloucester, across the said River, w’hose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That it appears to the Petitioners, that the same will be attendea with manifest Hardship and Inconvenience, if passed into a Law; and that, in respect to Maifemore Bridge, in which the Petitioners are chiefly concerned, the same lies upon a great and public Highway, leading through the County of Gloucester, is of great Utility, and has been constantly used by the Public ever since the First Erection thereof; and therefore the Petitioners conceive, that the County of Gloucester is liable by Law to re-build the said Bridge, and keep the same in Repair, as a County Bridge; and that the said Bridge is also comprized in, and is a Part of, certain Turnpike Roads, for the repairing w hereof an Act was passed in the Ninth Year of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act to enlarge the Term and Powers of an Act, made in the Thirty-third Year of the Reign of King George the Second, for repairing and widening the Road leading from Gloucester to- wards Hereford, and other Roads therein mentioned,

44 and for amending several other Roads near or ad- joining to some of the said Roadsand that the Commissioners acting under the said Act ought, as the Petitioners apprehend, to contribute to rebuild the fame, as being a Part of the Road included within the said Act; and that the said Commissioners appeared to be satisfied thereof, by taking under their Care the Erection of a temporary Bridge, although, as the Petitioners apprehend, they acted illegally in authorizing any additional Toll to be taken, further than what was allowed by the said Act, and have taken into their own Hands certain Grounds that were appropriated for repairing the said Bridge and Causeway leading thereto; and that the Petitioners apprehend, it would be a great Hardship to burthen Passengers upon the said Road with such additional Tolls as would be of themselves alone sufficient to rebuild, the said Bridge, and to keep the same in Repair, in total Exoneration of the said County and Turnpike; and that a Drawbridge at the West Gate of Gloucester, is by no Means necessary to, nor desired by, Persons uling the Navigation of the said River, and will be of infinite Inconvenience and Obstruction to Passengers by Land: And therefore praying. That they may be at Liberty to be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law.

And the Order of the House, made the First Day of November last, requiring all Persons that will question any Returns to do it within Fourteen Days next; and so within Fourteen Days next after any new Return shall be brought in, was also read.

But the House having been adjourned from the 27th Day of March last, to this Day;

And the House being informed, that the said Petitioners would have petitioned this House within Fourteen Days next after the said Return was brought in, if the 1 Ioufe had not been so adjourned;

And the Entry in the Journal of the House of the 1 qth Day of January 1762, containing the Proceedings of the House, in relation to the Petition of Major General John Lambtonj and also to the Petition of the Freemen of the City of Durham, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the said City, which Petitions were not presented in due Time, because of the Adjournment of the House, being read;

Ordered, That the said Petition, now offered to be presented to the House, be admitted to be received; the same not being presented in due Time, because of the last Adjournment of the House.

Then the said Petition was delivered in, and read: Setting forth, That, at the last Election of Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the said Town of upon

Tyne, Andrew Robinson Bones, Esquire, and Sir John Trevelyan, Baronet, were Candidates; and that the Petitioners and others, making a Majority of the lawful Electors, attended, and gave their Votes at the said Election for the said Andreio Robinson Boioes, Esquire;

notwithstanding which, the said Sir John Trevelyan procured himself to be returned as a Member to serve in Parliament for the said Town, as having a Majority of ‘Votes at the said Election; and that the said Sir John Trevelyan, by his Agents and Managers, corrupted divers of the Voters for the said Town, by Money and Proiniles of Money, and other Rewards, in order to give their Votes at the said Election, and, by these and

>7

other illegal Methods, obtained a colourable Majority on the Poll; and that James Thomas Lor nine, Esquire, Sheriff and Returning Officer of the said Town, admitted several Persons to vote for the said Sir John Trevelyan, who ought not to have been admitted on the said Poll; and rejected some, who ought to have been admitted, and offered to poll for the said Andrew Robinson Bowes, Esquire; and that the said Sir John Trevelyan and his Agents and Managers did, after the Vacancy, and after the Telle of the Writ, give to divers of the Voters, and Persons claiming to vote, Meat, Drink, and other Entertainment, in o,rder to procure their Votes at the said Election; and that in Consequence of the said illegal Proceedings, the said Majority of Votes were unfairly obtained, in Favour of the said Sir John Trevelyan, whereby the Petitioners

and many other Burgesses of the said Town have been deprived of the due Benefit of their Franchises; and that the Person so returned is not in Truth the Repre-fentative of the said Town of Newcastle; but that the said Return is wholly illegal, and great Injustice to the Petitioners, an high Violation of the Freedom of Election, and the Rights and Authority of Parliament: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, to restore the Petitioners to the due Exercise or Benefit of their Franchises, and to inflict such Punishment on the Offenders, as in their Justice and Wisdom shall l'eem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Tuejilaythe 22d Day of this Instant April, at the same Time that the Petition of Andreio Robinson Bowes, Esquire, is ordered to be taken into Consideration.

The Lord North acquainted the I Ionfe, That he had a Message from His Majesty to this House, signed by His Majesty; and he presented the same to the House, and it was read by Mr. Speaker (all the Members of the House being uncovered), and is as followeth;

GEORGE R.

It gives 11 is Majesty much Concern, to find Himself obliged to acquaint the House of Commons with the Difficulties He labours under, by reason of Debts incurred by the Expences of His Household and of His Civil Government; which, being computed on the Fifth Day of January last, do amount to more than Six Hundred Thousand Pounds. His Majesty relies on the Loyalty and Afteftion of His faithful Commons, of which he has received so many lignal Proofs, for enabling Him to discharge this Debt; and that they will, at the same Time, make some further Provision, for the better Support of His Majesty’s Household, and of the Honour and Dignity of the Crown.

R.

Hatter*; A Petition of the Mailers and Journeymen Felt regulating Makers, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, resident their 1 rade. jn an(] about the Borough of Derby, was presented to the House, $nd read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are Persons employed in the Art and Mystery of Felt-making, having lawfully served their Apprenticeship thereto, and, by a elofe Application and Industry, have been enabled comfortably to support themselves and Families for many Years pail; and that by Two Acts of Parliament, passed in the Eighth Year of Queen and the First Year of King James the First, it is En-nafted, " That no Mailer Manufacturer shall have but " Two Apprentices, besides their own Sons, at one " Time, nor those for lefsTime than Seven Years;" And that the Petitioners have been informed. Application has been made to the House, for a Bill to repeal such Parts of the said Acts as relate to the Mailers Manufacturers taking more than Two Apprentices at one Time; and that, by reason of the great Number of Journeymen in the said Trade, many of them are at present wholly unemployed therein, and are obliged to work in Coal Pits, and to serve as Labourers in other Employments; and that, within these few Years pall, there have been a great Number of Men relieved in the Borough of Derby, feekingfor Employ; and if the said Acts should be repealed, and the Felt Makers be at Liberty to take what Number of Apprentices they shall think proper, a much greater Number of Journeymen will be unavoidably out of Employ, to the great Prejudice of the Petitioners and their Families, and the respective Parishes whereunto they belong: And therefore praying the House to take their same into Consideration, and to grant them such Belief in the Premises as tolhe House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Cousideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill to regulate the Prices of Labour, the Hours of Working, and the taking of Apprentices, in the Hat Manufactory, is committed.

A Petition of the Merchants, Traders, Manufac- Severn turers, of the Town of Wolverhampton, in the County of Stafford, was presented to the House, and read; Setting qj oucelUr forth, That the Petitioners are much alarmed at a Bill’ 8trteu< which is now depending in Parliament, from the May of and Burgesses of the City of Gloucester, so far as relates to laying a Tax upon aH Vessels -passing under a Bridge* contiguous to the said City, called West Gate Bridge ‘ ansi that the Petitioners cannot view this ‘Attempt without the great eft Surprise, either in regard to the Reasons assigned for'demanding such Tax on the one Hand, or, on the other, from the bad Consequencei and dangerous Precedent of laying fneh a Tax on tllC River Severn, which has ever been a' free Navigation; and that they cannot fee the Shadow of a Reason why aVeflei on the Water, and in Tides Way, should pay towards the Reparation of Streets, Lanes,* Causeways, fife, on the Land, or even towards repairing or improving of Bridges, which can in no wife be supposed a Convenience to such Vessels; nor can they fail of being apprehensive of bad Consequences from the Imposition of a Tax which not only would fall on their Martufactures, btrt also on the raw Material? consumed therein, as well as on other Foreign Merchandize coming that Way, which is very considerable for the Supply of that populous Neighbourhood; and tltat the dangerous Precedent is but too apparent at first View* for should this new and unprecedented Tax be fub-rnitted tq in one Instance, thqy cannot fee where it might terminate: And therefore.praying the House to take their Petition into Considerfttion, and prevent any Duties being laid on the Navigation of the Rivpr Severn.

dom, from which there is a Communication with the said River by means of navigable Canals, are supplied with great Quantities of Goods, Wares, and Merchandize, from the City of Bristol, and other Places below the said Bridge, by means of Vessels navigating on the said River, which ure unavoidably obliged to pais under the (hid Bridge; and great Quantities of Goods, Wares, Merchandize, and Coals, are daily conveyed to the said City of Bristol, as well as to Stroud and other Parts of the Clothing Country, from several Parts of the Kingdom, without paying any Tonnage or Toll whatsoever, on passing under any Bridge upon the said River, which is a free navigable River; and that the Petitioners apprehend a Drawbridge will be a real Obstruction to Land Carriage, as a Number of Vessels usually pals through the Bridge, when the Tide flows, so soon after each other,-that the Bridge, for a considerable Time, together, must be kept up, which will neoeflarily put a Stop to all Carriages and Passengers for the Time; and that the Petitioners are informed, the said Corporation of Gloucester are seised of divers Manors, Messuages,

Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, of a very considerable Annual Value, which were given tb them for the express Purpose of keeping the said Bridge and Causeways in Repair; and that the Revenues arising therefrom are amply sufficient for the Repairs of the said Bridge and Causeways; and that it will be a great Hard-ship upon Persons navigating on the said River to be obliged to contribute to the building and repairing a Bridge and Causeway, from which they are not, neither can they be, in any wise benefited; and the Petitioners, apprehend, that the granting a Tonnage, or Toll, to the said Corporation, to be paid by Vessels navigating on the said River, will be a very great Discouragement and Injury to the Trade, and be of public Mischief: And therefore praying. That the same Bill may not pals into a Law, with any Provision therein, whereby the Trade carried on upon the said River may be burthened or discouraged; and that the Petitioners may have all such other Relief as to the House may seem meet.

In Obedience to the Orders of the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury, dated the 19th of October

1766,1 proceeded to examine the Accounts of the Foreign Hospitals in Germany, which remained unpaid

4 at the End of the lait War.

H.

The greatest Part of these Accounts I had transi&itted to the Commissioners for the German Demands, who returned them to me in 1765, with such other Hospital Demands as had been laid before them by the respective Claimants.

These, with my Accounts of the Monies received and expended by me in this Department, I delivered to the Auditor of the Imprefts, in Obedience to the Commands of the Lords of the Treasury, signified to me on the 7th o (June 17 65. The Delay of the Auditors report on my own Accounts, which is now before your Lord-

flnps, and the Difficulty of determining, with proper Certainty, how far the Demands of the Landgrave of Htjfe, for the Hospitals eiiablithed for the Sick and Wounded of his Troops, were duly vouched, and what Part of them ought to be allowed, have hitherto prevented me from making a final Report of those Demands; the Hejfian Hospitals were not so immediately under my Inspection as those of all the Foreign Troops of the combined Army; the Landgrave having, by his Officers, demanded of me a Reimbursement of the Sums which he had advanced for the Hospitals, to his proper Directors, fending me such Accounts as had been usually £ prepared by such Directors, and claiming a Right, by Treaty, to the Privilege of having the Hospitals conducted under the Management of his own People.

These Demands and Claims of the Landgrave, and his Officers, occasioned much Altercation during the Course of the Expenditure, and in the Uncertainty how far they were well-founded, Colonel PeirJ’on, on the atft of June 1761, then at the Head of the Commissariat, granted a Warrant for Eleven Thousand Pistoles to be paid to the Hospital Officers of the Landgrave on Account.

1 he First Physician, First Surgeon, and principal Directors, make a Board in the Hessian Hospitals, for conducting the Business of them, and they have ligned all these Accounts; and, as they alledge, observed such Forms as it had been the Practice in such Hospitals to observe in former Wars, and on similar Occasions; and 1 think myself obliged in Justice to declare, that whenever 1 had an Opportunity of examining and comparing the Number of Sick actually maintained in the Hospitals, with these specified in the Reports, which the Directors periodically sent me, I never found the Number of Sick were miftated in any such Reports, nor does it appear to me that the Amount of the Expences of these Hospitals is, upon the Whole, greater than they would have been if they had been more immediately under the Direction of the British Commissariat.

The Accounts of the Landgrave of Hejfe Hand as follows:

In Obedience to the Commands of the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury, I have examined an Account of Expences of an Hospital at Freburg, for the Sick of a Corps of the Allied Army, when in Saxony, under the Command of his Serene Highness the Hereditary Prince of Brunswic, in February, March, April, and May 1760, amounting to 768 Rx. 5 M. 1 j P.

The Hereditary Prince of Brunswic was, at the Time above mentioned, detached into Saxony, with an Army confiding of Three Hanoverian, Two Hessian, and Four Brunfioic Regiments; and the above Claim is in Consequence of Expences incurred by the eliablishing an Hospital Depot at Freburg.

Commissary Wolff', in his Answer to my former Remarks, lays, the Hessian Cashier paid 170 Rx. 14 4 P.

for the Hessian Regiments; and, if there tliould be no Possibility of getting Payment for the Sick, the

proportion* ’ Share due for the Hanoverians ought to be paid, being a Third of the Whole, from which 1 have deducted Two Charges, being Regimental, and not Hospital Disbursements.

This Account issigned by the Officers who had the Direction of the Hospital; and I think the Peculiarity of the Situation of those Troops, in that Expedition, might-excuse the Want-of proper Vouchers for each separate Disbursement, and induce tl eir Lordships to allow them the Hanoverian Part of the above Expence, which, after the aforesaid Deductions, amounts to 116 Rx. 9 M.8 which makes in Pounds Sterling 41. is.

March a8th 1777.

This Account was delivered to me when I was in Germany.

The establishing of an Hospital for a Angle Regiment while there were at that Time regular Hospitals in the Neighbourhood of Severn, was one of my principal Objections to the Account. I apprehended the permission to do it was procured by some indirect Means, but his Serene Highness declared it was by his express Orders. The reigning Duke gave the above Declaration to establish that Fact, and in all the Applications I have had Cnee from the Brunjivic Agents, they seem to rely much upon that Declaration.

If Characters of such high Rank and great Consideration had not solicited the Repayment of it I should have rejected it, as I have done many others, which, except their wanting the Support of the Commander in Chief, were exactly similar. The Account is made up as most of these Accounts are usually done, with One or. Two Men giving Receipts for the Whole, and mull rest on their Testimony, and the Declaration of the reigning Duke.

If their Lordships admit of this Claim, under these peculiar Circumstances, there will be due to the Military Chest of Brunswic 1366 Rx. 16 Mr. 7 JP. which reduced into Pounds Sterling makes £.160. gd.

March 28th 1777.

Tho' Bishop.

and Inconvenience, or be totally Iolt, as they apprehend no Remittance under £.5 -can be made in negotiable Bills by Poll, every Drawer of-such Bill (though for Goods fold in Trade) being subject to the Penalty of £. zo, which will " be found to -be-the greatest Dif-couragement and Difficulty ever laid upon Trade in general by the Legislature of this Kingdom, therefore a public Loss; besides, the Consequence will be a Diminution of the Revenue of the Post Office: And therefore praying, That such Part of the said- Bill as relates to Bills of Exchange, or Draughts, may not pass into a Law, in the present Plan, but, provided all such Bills of Exchange and Draughts were only to be made payable at such Dates as the House shall think proper, the Petitioners hope the Evil complained of would in a good degree be remedied.

Lord Broicnlmo Bertie reported from the~Committee, Billinghajf-to whom the Petition of the Right honourable William Drainage, Earl Fi/zwilliam, Owner and Proprietor of Lands, in &c* the Parish of Billinghay, in the County of Lincoln, on

Behalf of himself and other Owners and Proprietors of Lands, within the same Parish, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the feme, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

John Louden, being examined, informed your Committee, That he knows the Dales, Common Fen, and inclosed Low Lands, in the Parish of Billinghay, in the County of Lincoln; and that Part of the Banks of the River Witham, Kyme Eau, and Billinghay Skirths, ad-

join to or against the said Lands, which Lands are subject to be overflowed; and unless such Parts of the said Banks are made and completed, the said Lands cannot be drained and improved.

Then An Act of Parliament, made in the Second Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for draining and preserving certain Low Lands,

" called The Fens, lying on both Sides of the River " Witham, in the County of Lincoln, and for restoring " and maintaining the Navigation of the said River,

" from The High Bridge, in the City of Lincoln, through " the Borough of Boson, to the Sea," was read, whereby it appeared, that such Parts of the Banks of the said *

River Witham, Kyme Eau, and Billinghay Skirths, as adjoin to the said Dales, Common Fen, and inclosed Low Lands, in the said Parish of Billinghay, are Part of the Works directed to be done by the Commissioners appointed to put the said Act in execution; and that the said Dales, and Common Fen, and inclosed Low Lands, are subjectto certain Rates and Taxes mentioned in the said Act, to be applied towards the general Works of Drainage.

And Mr. Landen further said. That, feme Years ago, the Commissioners begun to make such Parts of the said Banks as adjoin to or are against the said Lands; and that the greatest Part of the Bank of the River Witham, which adjoins to the said Dales, Common Fen, and inclosed Low Lands, and also Part of the Banks of Kyme Eau and Billinghay Skirths, were made, but those Works have been discontinued for several Years, , and are daily going to decay.

Then Mr. Thomas Hogard, an Engineer, informed your Committee, That he had surveyed such Parts of the Banks of the said River Witham, Kyme Eau, and Billinghay Skirths, as adjoin to or against the said Dales,

Common Fen, and inclosed Low Lands; and said.

That unless such Parts of the said Banks as adjoin to or against the said Lands are made and completed those Lands cannot be properly drained and improved: And the Witness further said. That almost the Whole of such Part of the Bank of the said River Witham, and also Part of so much of the Banks of Kyme Eau and Billinghay Skirths, as adjoin to or against the said Dales, Common Fen, and inclosed Low Lands, have been already made by the Commissioners for putting the said recited Act in execution: but those Works are going to decay; and if the same are not completed the Money already expended therein will be loft: And he added, That those Works, in their present unfinished State, are detrimental to the Landsproposed to be drained. — And being asked. What he thought would be the Expence of finishing and completing those Works ? he said, He bad computed the Expence so amount to £. 2,029. 7s. 6 — And being asked. If he was conversant in W’orks of this fort? he said. He was; and that in his Opinion, the Expence of making and completing those Works Would not exceed the Sum he had mentioned. Then

Mr. Whitworth, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to eoulider of allowing Lumber to be carried, irt British Ships, to the West India Blands, for a Time

to he limited, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as fjlloweth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Planters in the West India Blands are in great Want of Staves, and other Lumber, lor the Cultiia-tion of their Plantations.

Resolved, I’hat it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That it is expedient to authorize British Ships to carry Lumber from the Baltic to the North Sea and the Mediterranean, for a limited Time, under certain Restrictions.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That it may be expedient, to grant a Bounty upon Staves, and other Lumber, imported from Canada,

F.ajl and WeJl Florida's, Nova Scotia, and the Bland of Saint Johfi's, to the West Indies and the Shore.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That it may he also expedient to enable His Majesty’s Commissioners in North America, and Governor to grant Licences to the Commanders of British Ships to export Lumber to the West Indies, from the Port of New York, for a limited Time.

The First Resolution of the Committee being read a Second Time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The Second Ilesolution of the Committee being read a Second Time;

And the Question being put, that the House do agree with the Committee in the said Rel'olution;

It passed in the Negative.

The Third Resolution of the Committee being read a Second Time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made thereto, by inserting after the Words " John's," the

Words, " and from the MufquiloShore."

And the Question being put. That those Words be there in ferted;

It passed in the Negative.

Another Amendment was proposed to be made to the said Resolution, by leaving out the Words, " and " the Mufquilo Shore."

And the Question being put, That the YVprds, " and " the Mufquilo Shore," Itand Part of the said Resolution;

It palfed in the Negative.

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution so amended. That it may be expedient to grant a Bounty upon Staves, and other Lumber, imported from Canada, East and West Florida's, Nova Scotia, and the Island of Saint John's, to the West Indies.

The subsequent Resolution of the Committee being read a Second Time;

And the Question being put. That the House do agree with the Committee in the said Kefolutiou;

It passed in the Negative.

whom the Petition of His Majesty’s Justices of the Peace for the County of Warwick, in General Quarter Session assembled, was referred; That the Commitee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place j and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read, and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, John Lloyd, Esquire, being examined, said. That the Common Gaol of the said County, situate in the Borough of Warwick, is too small for the Reception and Confinement of Prisoners, and that the Justices of the Peace have, upon that Account, been obliged to commit many Offenders to the House of Correction for the said County, who ought to have been committed to the Common Gaol, if there had been Room to receive them.

That the House of Correction was presented by the Grand Jury, at the Assizes held fcfr the said County on the 23d of March 1776* by reason of the Insufficiency and Small ness thereof.

That the Justices being' of Opinion, That certain Premisses adjoining to the said House of Correction, (and which also adjoin to the said Common Gaol) should be purchased for enlarging the said House of Correction, the same were accordingly purchased, and conveyed, upon Trust, to be made Use of as Part of the House of Correction.

That since the Purchjife it hath been found, that it will be much more convenient and useful for the County, if the Whole, or the greatest Part of the said Premisses were made Use of for enlarging the said County Gaol, as in that same it will become unnecessary to enlarge the said House of Correction, or at least to apply the Whole of the said Premisses for such Enlargement. — And the Witness further said. That he apprehends the said Purposes cannot be effected without the Aid of Parliament, the said Premisses being wholly veiled in Trustees for the Purpose of enlarging the said House of Correction.

A Member present informed Your Committee, That he apprehended it would be of Benefit to the County, if the Justices were empowered to appropriate, for such Time as they shall think proper. Part of the Premisses aforesaid, as a Place for depositing and keeping the Public Rolls and Records of the County.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Common Gaol of the County of Warwick, and for other Purposes therein mentioned: And that Mr. Skipioithand Sir Charles Uolte do prepare and bring iu, the fame.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

The Bill, which it is now my Duty to present to Your Majesty, is intituled, "An Act for the better " Support of I lis Majesty’w Houl'ehold, and of the 1 lonour and Dignity of the Crown of Great Britain to which your Commons humbly beg Your Royal Assent.

By this Bill, Sir, and the rofpeftful CircumstanceJ which preceded and accompanied it, Y’our Common* have given the fullcft and cleared Proof of their Zeal and Afleftion for Y’our Majesty. For, in a Time of public Distress, full of Difficulty and Danger, their Constilucnts labouring under Burthens almost too heavy to be borne, Your'faithful Commons postponed all other Business; and with as much Dil'patch as the Nature of their Proceedings W'ould admit, have not only granted to Ybnr Majesty a large present Supply,

Mr. Taylor informed the Committee, That in valuing Lives upon Estates it was usual to take the Value of Vox. 36.

the Life -according to the most approved Tables; and that Intenest was only taken at £. 4 per Cent.: That he never remembers any Life valued so low as Six Years Purchase in any Transaction for the Purchase of Estates; and that he has been very conversant in the Buying and Selling Estates: That undoubtedly there is great Difference in the real Value of Lives between the Ages of 20 and 50.

The Committee were satisfied, from general Information,

Laws

concerning

Usury

and

Annuities,

49a Mail. 1777.

mation. That before the Period to which the Evidence upon the First Branch of their Enquiry relates, being about Twelve Years, Annuities for the Life of the Grantor were purchased at a Price much nearer their real Value than they have been since. Ten Years Purchase, upon good Security, has been given for a Life of 50; nor was there One general Price for all Ages; but the Value varied according to the Estimate of the Life on which the Annuity was granted; whereas, in the present Mode of granting Annuities, there is but One Price taken for all Ages between 20 and 50.

The Fasts submitted to the Consideration of the House will enable them to judge how far the Committee are warranted in the Observations they have made,*and the Resolutions formed upon them.

Six Years Purchase is. allowed to be the current Price of an Annuity upon a Life from the Age of 21 to the Age of 50.

If the Transaction was intended to be a real Sale, Things so different in their Value could not yield the same Price.

The Persons advancing their Money upon Annuities at this Rate, have a reasonable Expectation that the Principal will be returned; and the Persons to whom it is advanced have a Confidence that they may repay it when they can.

The Transaction then is formally a Sale, but in Sub fiance it is a Loan of Money upon a perishable Security, w'here the Advantage taken bears no Proportion to the Hazard, though that Hazard may be estimated, and in other Transactions, where there is a real Sale of a Life Interest, or a Reversion expectant upon it, is estimated with reasonable Certainty.

The exorbitant Profit gained by this Mode of advancing Money, is contrary to the Intention of the Law that regulates Interest upon Loans; it is a Restraint upon all those who have Occasion to borrow upon a Life Estate for any prudent Purpose; and it is a Public Mischief in respect both of the Gain and of the Ruin which such Bargains produce.

The Excess of this Profit may be corrected by limiting the Gain of such Bargains to legal Interest, and a reasonable Compensation for that Risk, which in Cafes under no peculiar Hazard attends the Security.

The Value of the different Classes of Lives appears not only by Calculations, upon which Men daily aft in the Purchase of Estates, but by the Rate at which Lives of different ages are insured with Profit.

The Compensation for the Risk of the Life ought to be taken upon a larger Allowance not only than its real Value, but even than the Rate at which such Risk may be insured; and the Reduction of the Price to a lower Sum may be left to the Competition that mull arise in Transactions which will no longer be disgraceful.

All Adyantage beyond the Rate prescribed ought to be deemed Usurious, and made subject to the Penalties provided against Usury; with an Exception only of the Lives of those, who, from the Nature of their Employment, are exposed to peculiar Hazards: And all Annuities ought to be redeemable; because, if a fair Consideration is paid, the Redemption never can be a Lois to the Person possessed of an Interest which k daily diminishing.

Upon the Whole, your Committee came to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Purchase of Annuities for the Life of the Grantor, being generally intended as a Loan of Money, ought to be regulated accordingly.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, 1 That £. 4 per Cent, is a sufficient Compensation for the

Rifle of a Life above 21 Years, and unaer 25 Years.

That £. 5 per Cent, is a sufficient Compensation for the Rilk of a Life above 30 Years, and under 35 Years.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That to take any larger annual Sum than the legal Interest; of each £. 100 advanced in the Purchase of an Annuity for the Life of the Grantor, together with the Sums above specified, being the Values of the re-speeiive Rilks attending such Annuities, ought to be made Usury.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That all Annuities for the Life of the Grantor, ought to be redeemable on Payment of the Sum advanced, with the Arrears of the Annuity to the Time of Payment.

Ri/olved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

Sir Charles Whitmortk, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to^rhon it

was referred to cdnfider of the Eleventh Rule in the Book of Rates, so far as the same relates to the making any Allowance upon the Importation of damaged Currants, Raiiins, Figs, and Prunes, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table 1 Where the fume were read; and'are as followeth;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Eleventh Rule annexed to the Book of Rates, so far as the same relates to the Allowances to be made for damaged Currants, Raiiins, Figs, and Prunes, be repealed* ,

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Abatement of Eight Pounds per Centum, of the Net Amount of the Duties payable upon the Importation of Currants, be made to the Importer thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Abatement of One Pound per Centum, of the Net Amount of the Duties payable upon the Importation of Raiiins Solis, be made to the Importer thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee* That an Abatement of Six Pounds per Centum, of the Net Amount of the Duties payable upon the Importation of Smyrna Raiiins, be made to the Importer thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee1* That an Abatement of 'Fen Pounds per Centum, of the Net Amount of the Duties payable upon the Importation of Li pari. Faro, and Great or

Lexia Raiiins, be made, to the Importer thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Abatement of Eight Pounds per Centum, of the Net Amount of the Duties payable upon the Importation of Denia Raisins, be made to the Importer thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Abatement of Twenty-five Pounds per Centum, of the Net Amount of the Duties payable upon the Importation of Faro Figs, be made to the Importer thereof

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Abatement of Ten Pounds per Centum, of the Net Amount of the Duties payable upon the Importation of Smyrna Figs, be made to the Importer thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Abatement of Six Pounds per Centum, of the Net Amount of the Duties payable upon the Importation of Prunes, be made to the Importer thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said several Abatements shall be taken to be in lieu of all former Allowances such Goods were intitled to, in consideration of any Damage whatsoever.

The Five First Resolutious of the Committee being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The Sixth Kesolution of the Committee being read a Second Time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made thereunto, by leaving out the Word " Eight" and inserting the Word "Twenty" inlicad thereof.

And the Question being put. That the Word "Eight’* stand Part of the said Hei’olution;

It palTerl in the Negative.

And the Question being put. That the Word " Twenty" be inserted instead thereof;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Refolded, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, so amended, That an Abatement of Twenty Pounds per Centum, of the Net Amount of the Duties payable upon the Importation of Denia Raiiins, be made to the Importer thereof.

A Petition of John Bourke and John Barnes, Members of the Committee of the Company of Merchants trading to Africa, was presented to the House, and read: Setting forth. That the Petitioners are Committee Men for the Direction and Management of the Affairs of the African Company, under the Authority, and according to the Provisions of an Act, passed in t lie Twenty-third Year of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act for extending and " improving the Trade to Africa and that the present Committee doth annually receive from Parliament considerable Sums of Public Money, for the faithful Application of which they are responsible; this Public Money they would be most unworthy to hold, and it would be highly improper for the House to entrust it in their Hands, if they stood justly chargeable with any Abuse whatsoever; and that the Petitioners, having a legal Tenure in their said Corporate Office, during the Term, and under the Conditions, appointed by the said Act, are, by the Law of this Land, entitled to Protection for their Corporate Character, without which Protection they will be unable to perform their Duty; they have also a Property equally to be protested, by the same Law in their honest Fame and Reputation as private Citizens and Merchants; their private Credit, they humbly represent to thel louse, must be assessed to their extreme Detriment, lliouH any Mif-conductor Unfaithfulness, particularly in a Pecuniary and Commercial Trull, be publicly imputed to them, and not publicly disproved; and that the Petitioners observe, with the utmost Concern, a Paper laid before the House, and ordered by its Authority to he printed, purporting to he " A Return from the Commissioners " for Trade and Plantations, relating to the General " State of the Trade to Aand ligned "

" Germain, Soame Jcnyns, R1 Spencer, Bamber Gas-

" coyne, WhUshed Keene, C.Fand and that in the said Return, the following heavy Charge against the Committee for conducting the said Trade is made, and pretended to be supported by Evidence. viz. " It appears, so far from this Trade (meaning " that Part of the African Trade under the l)ire6tion " of the Committee) having been carried on in a free " and open Manner for the Benefit of the Public, ao " cording to the Intention of this honourable House,

" and agreeable to the Spirit and Tenor of the Act " which constitutes the present Committee, that a " private Trade, directly tending to a Monopoly hath " been set. up and established by the Governors and " Chiefs of the Forts in Africa; and that this private " Trade, so injurious to the Interests of the Public,

" hath been carried on by them in Conjunction with " Persons at Home, some One or more of whom have " at the same Time been Members of the Committee " abovementioned and that the Petitioners, Members of the present Committee, deliberately weighing and considering all the Particulars and Circu alliances of the said Charge, do affirm to this honourable House, that the same (so far as the Petitioners are or may be comprehended therein, by Participation, Connivance, or Neglect) is absolutely false; and that the Petitioners, in Justice to the Character of Daniel Esquire,

Commissary General in America, a Member of this Committee, and now Abroad on His Majesty’s Service in a most important Trust, do affine this honourable House, that they have abundant Reason to be persuaded, that the said Charges with Regard to him, are equally groundless and injurious; and if any other Committee Man has acted contrary to his Duty, and contrary to the true Intent and Meaning of the said Act, the Petitioners are not acquainted with or privy to the fame; and that the Petitioners, with the Feelings of injured and the Confidence of innocent Men, do supplicate from the House a full and strict Enquiry into their Conduct, offering themselves to the lieavieft Punishment which the just Indignation of this House can inflict, if any Part of the said Charge, so far as regards them, can be made good by the said Commissioners of Trade, or by any other Persons, and most humbly re-quell, that they may be confronted, as the Rules of Justice require, with their Accusers; and the Petitioners in order to facilitate the Enquiry oft his honourable House, do wave the Privilege of all accused Persons, in not being compellable to answer such Questions as may criminate themselves, and are ready most chearfully, to give full and satisfactory Answers to all Interrogatories, without Exception, which this House, or any Committee thereof, shall think proper to propose to them; and that the Petitioners represent to this honourable House, that the said Commissioners of Trade are appointed by the African Act aforesaid, supreme Judges and Comptrollers in all Cases of Abuse or Misbehaviour in the African Trade, with the fullest Powers over the Committee and all the Servants of the Company, without exception, and are authorized by the said Act, " to remove any of the said Committee Men or " any Servant appointed by them, who shall be guilty " of any Misbehvaiour contrary to the true Intent and " Meaning of the said Act;" and, in order to enable the said Commissioners of Trade to execute with Effect the said Trulls and Powers, the Petitioners, as Members of that Committee, are also directed, by the Act aforesaid, to give to the said Commissioners, "a just " and perleft Account of all their Transactions, Once a " Year, or oftener if thereunto required by the said " Commissioners, or any Three or more of them, in " which shall be contained an Account of all the Monies received and disbursed by the said Committee, or " their Order; and also an Account of all the Orders " and Instructionsgiven by the said Committee, as well to their Officers and Servants in Great Britain, as on
