and the Petitioners humbly conceive, that it is a noft unwarrantable Proceeding in the said Commissioners, who are authorized by Act of Parliament to judge the Committee Men, and to punish them if Delinquents, to ooait the Performance of this Duty, and to charge those whom tiiey liad Power to order and controul, with the Consequences of their own Neglect; and that the Po-niiliment and Remedy, appointed by Act of Parliament for such Misbehaviour as is ftuted in the said Return, is to remove the Committee Men charged therewith from their Employments; and the Mode of Proceeding prescribed by the Act is, that " whenever any Committee Man shall be charged with Misbehaviour in his Employment, the Commissioners foe Trade and Plantatio is ilia.Il summon such Committee " Man to appear before them, and shall, in same he at- tends, hear the said Committee Man, and upon his " Attendance or Default examine into the Truth of the said Charge before they shall remove him from his " Employment as aforesaid-," but the Petitioners represent to this honourable House, that the Commissioners of Trade, instead of summoning and hearing the Petitioners, and removing or acquitting them according to their D» forts, did, contrary to the true Intent and Meaning of the said Act, and to all the Rulesof Equity and Justice, intlitute of their own Authority afeeret Inquisition, and lid privately examine Secretary to the said Committee, and did, without any M arram from Law, as the Petitioners conceive, enjoin him to keep secret the Matters on which he had been examined; which Inja. nation the [mid Richard Camplin did comply with, ami refused to give the Petitioners any Information thereof, although by his Duty, as the confidential Servant of the African Company, he was bound to inform them of any Acoufation or Proceedings again!! them; and when the Petitioners did repeatedly desire of the Commissioners of Trade that they might have a Copy of the said Report, or the Heads thereof, the said Commissioners did absolutely re-lufe to comply with the said just and reasonable Re-queli; and that this Method of Proceeding is not only injurious to the Petitioners, but tends to niifinforui and misguide this House; the Order of this honourable House is, to lav before them a general State of the Trade to Africa: the Return is a partial State, relating only to that particular Distrfet which is under the Management of the African Committee, which the Pe>-titioners assert, must tend to produce a fallacious and dclulive State of the said Branch of Commerce; and the Petitioners most humbly conceive, that even supposing this Return did not contain Matter tending to criminate any Persons in a public Trull, yet, as a mere State of the Trade, it ought to have been formed on some Sort of Examination or Enquiry of the Committee Men, who are chiefly concerned in the Management of that Trade; by declining to make this natural, obvious, and necetlury Enquiry, and by proceeding in a secretandfurreptitious Manner, the Petitioners assert, and engage to prove, that a moll erroneous as well as imperfect State of the African Commerce, is laid before this House; for the Petitioners affirm, that the said Trade, until the Troubles in America had come to their Height, was in a most flourjlfiing and growing Condition; and that, therefore, all Causes assigned for Vot. 36.

its Decay must, as such,. be improperly assigned, the African Effect itself not existing; and that the Petitioners do Company, not assert that in such a remote and complex Object as the Trade and Settlements under the Management of the African Committee, no Abuses or Errors whatsoever do now, or have at any Time prevailed; but they do insist, that no Abuses have ever been complained of, and proved to them, to which they have not given such Remedy as the same required, or their legal Authority did admit; and they most humbly submit to the \Vifidom and Justice of this House, the mif-chievous Consequence inevitable to every Administration of public A flairs, from the higbell to the lowed,

if Persons shall be encouraged to pase over the proper Department fop Complaint and Redress of Grievances, and then to criminate, for a Defect of such Redress, that Office to which Application has never been made; and the Petitioners cannot avoid observing to this Hoafe, that, in the vast Multiplicity of Abuses, Grievances, and Mismanagements, with which the said Return is filled, scarce One Date, Place or Person is specified, so as ta enable the Petitioners to discover the Delinquents (if any Delinquents there be) or to remove the Abuse (if any Abuse exists) nor have the Commissioners of Trade thought proper to communicate to the Committee the Names of the Accusers, or the particular Circumstances of the Accusations, by which alone the Nature of the Charges could he ascertained, or their Credibility established; the Petitioners therefore do most humbly and earneftiy implore the Justice of this honourable House, that, for their present Defence and future Direction, the Whole of the Evidence on which the said Return has been founded, together with the Names of those who have wdtnefl'ed the said several Fasts, be laid before this honourable House, or be made otherwise accessible to the Petitioners, as they find themselves much injured, and the Trade under their Management greatly misrepre-fented by the said loose and general Charges; and the Petitioners lastly beg Leave to represent to this honourable House, that, in the confused Body of Matter contained in the said Return, several Things are alledged as Grievances, which the Petitioners have always ap-

prehended, and do ltill conceive, to be ftriflly legal; 4

and oilier Matters and Practices are complained of, as A

detrimental to Commerce, which the Petitioners apprehend to be extremely useful, if not necessary, to it; these last Matters the Petitioners do request Leave to state at the Bar of this honourable House, most humbly desiring the Opinion of this House on the Merits of the fame, being determined to proceed in all Things in the most exact Conformity to the Sense of this House;.

The Petitioners, therefore humbly pray. To be heard, by themselves and their Counsel, against all Charges di-refUy or indirectly made against them, or against the general Administration of the African Company, in the said Return, as also to the State of the said Trade, and to all other Matters and Things Hated in the said Return or the Papers thereto annexed, in order to obtain thereby the Exculpation of their injured Character, and such other Relief as this honourable House in its Wisdom shall think fit to give.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider of the Return from the Commissioners for Trade and Plantations, to the honourable House of Commons, in Consequence of the Address of the said House to His Majesty, of the 29th Day of January last, relating to the general State of the Trade to Africa, the Condition of the Forts and Settlements there, belonging to the African Company, 0 and in what Manner the several Sums of Money granted by Parliament for maintaining and supporting the fame, have been applied; and that the Petitioners be heard by themselves or Counsel before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

After which, His Majesty was pleased to make a moil Gracious Speech from the Throne, to both Houses of Parliament, as followeth; viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

The Conclusion of the Public Business, and the Confederation of the Inconvenience which I fear you must have suffered by so long an Attendance, call upon Me to put an End to this Session of Parliament; but I cannot let you go into your several Counties without ‘ expressing My entire Approbation of your Conduct, and without thanking you for the unquestionable Proofs „ you have given to Me, and to all the World, of the Continuance of your Attacliment to My Person and Government, of your clear Dilbernment of the true Interests of your Country, and of your Heady Perseverance in maintaining the Rights of the Legiuature.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I cannot sufficiently thank you for the Zeal and public Spirit with which you have granted the large and extraordinary Supplies, which I have found Myself under the Necessity of asking of My faithful Commons, for the Service of the current Year; and I must at the same Time acknowledge the particular Marks of your Attention to Me, as well in enabling Me to discharge the Debts contrafted on Account of My Civil Government, as in making so considerable an Augmentation to the Civil List Revenue during My Life.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I trust in the Divine Providence, that by a well-concerted and vigorous Exertion of the great Force you have put into My Hands, the Operations of this Campaign by Sea and Land will be blessed with such Success as may most effectually tend to the Suppression of the Rebellion in America, and to the Re-establish merit of that Constitutional Obedience which all the Subjects of a free State owe to the Authority of Law.

Vot,. 36.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

It is a great Satisfaction to Me, that I can have Recourse to the Wisdom and Support of My Parliament, in this Conjuncture, when the Continuance of the Rebellion in North America demands Our most serious Attention. The Powers, which you have in-trusted Me with for the Suppression of this Revolt, have been faithfully exerted; and I have a just Confidence, that the Conduct and Courage of My Officers, and the Spirit and Intrepidity of My Forces, both by Sea and Land, will, under the Blessing of Divine Providence, be attended with important Succcfs: But as I am persuaded, that you will fee the Necessity of preparing for such further Operations, as the Contingencies of the War, and the Obllinacy of the Rebels, may render expedient, I am, for that Purpose, purluing the proper Measures for keeping My Land Forces compleat to their present Establishment; and if I should have Occasion to increase them, by contrafting any new Engagements, I rely on your Zeal and public Spirit, to enable Me to make them good.

I receive repeated Assurances from Foreign Powers, of their pacific Dispositions. My own cannot be doubted: But, at this Time, when the Armaments in the Ports of France and Spain continue, I have thought it advisable to make a considerable Augmentation to My Naval Force, as well to keep My Kingdoms in a respectable State of Security, as to provide an adequate Protection for the extensive Commerce of My Subjects; and as, on the one Hand, I am determined that the Peace of Europe shall not be disturbed by Me, so, on the other, I will always be a faithful Guardian of the Honour of the Crown of Great Britain.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I have ordered the Ellimates for theenfuing Year to be laid before you. The various Services which I have mentioned to you will unavoidably require large Supplies; and nothing could relieve My Mind front

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I will steadily pursue the Measures in which we are engaged for the Re-establishment of that Coniiitutional Subordination, which, with the Blessing of God, I will maintain through the several Parts of My Dominions: But I shall ever be watchful for an Opportunity of putting a Stop to the Effulion of the Blood of My Subjects, and the Calamities which are inseparable from a State of War. And I dill hope, that the deluded and unhappy Multitude will return to their Allegiance; and that the Remembrance of what they once enjoyed, the Regret for what they have loft, and the Feelings of what they now suffer under the arbitrary Tyranny of their Leaders, will re-kindle in their Hearts a Spirit of Loyalty to their Sovereign, and of Attachment to their Mother Country; and that they will enable Me, with the Concurrence and Support of My Parliament, to accomplish, what I shall consider as the greatest Happiness of My Life, and the greatest Glory of My Reign, the Restoration of Peace, Order, and Confidence to My American Colonies.

A Motion was made, and the Question bein proposed. Than an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, to return His Majesty the Thanks of this House, for His most Gracious Speech from the Throne.

With Hearts deeply interested in every Event, which tends to increase His Majesty’s domeftie Felicity, and imprelTed with the liveliest Sentiments of Duty and Attachment to the Queen, to offer to His Majesty the Congratulations of His faithful Commons, on the Birth of another Princess, and on Her Majesty’s happy Recovery.

To assure His Majesty, that we take a sincere Part in the Confidence which His Majesty expresses, that the Conduct and Courage of His Officers, and the Spirit and Intrepidity of His Forces, both by Sea and I.and, will, under the Divine Providence, be attended with important Success; but at the same Time we entirely concur with His Majesty, in thinking that it is necessary to prepare for such further Operations, as future Events, and the Contingencies of the War, may render expedient; and that we learn, with much Satisfaction, that His Majesty is for that Purpol'e pursuing the proper Measures, for keeping His Land Forces compleat to their present Establishment; and that, whenever His Majesty shall be pleased to communicate to this House any new Engagements, which He may have entered into for increasing His Military Force, we will take the same into our Consideration j and we trust His Majesty will not be disappointed in the gracious Sentiments which He entertains of the Zeal and public Spirit of His faithful Commons.

To declare, that we are truly sensible, that His Majesty’s constant Care for the Welfare of His People, and His generous Concern for the Happiness of Mankind, dispose His Majesty to desire, that the Peace of Europe may not be diliurbed; but that we acknowledge, with equal Gratitude, His Majesty’s Attention to the Security of His Kingdoms, and the Protection of the ex-tenlive Commerce of His Subjects, in His having made a considerable Augmentation to His Naval Force, on which the Reputation and Importance of this Nation mult ever principally depend; and we hear, with the highest Satisfaction, and rely with perfect Confidence on His Royal Declaration, that He will always be the faithful Guardian of the Honour of the Crown.

Usual Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right Order*, to give his V'otc in the Election of any Member to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That where this House shall jadge any Petition touching Elections to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath procured himself to be elected or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence, the same is declared to be a high Crime and Mifilemeanor; and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath given false Evidence, in any Case, before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is a high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, Your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, iti Parliament assembled, beg Leave to return Your Majesty the humble Thanks of this House, for Your most gracious Speech from the Throne.

Deeply intereded in every Event which tends to increase Your Majesty’s domedic Felicity, and impressed with the liveliest Sentiments of Duty and Attachment to the Queen , we beg Leave to offer to Your Majesty our Congratulations on the Birth of another Princess, and on Her Majesty’s happy Recovery.

We assure Your Majesty, that we take a sincere Part in the Confidence which Your Majesty expresses, that the Conduct and Courage of Your Officers, and the Spirit and Intrepidity of Your Forces, both by Sea and Land, will, under the Divine Providence, be attended with important Success. But at the same Time, we entirety concur with Your Majesty in thinking, that it is necessary to prepare for such further Operations, as future Events, and the Contingencies of the War, may render expedient. And we learn, with much Satisfaction, that Your Majesty is, for that Purpose, pursuing the proper Measures for keeping Your Land Forces compleat to their present Establishment. And whenever Your Majesty shall be pleased to communicate to us any new Engagements which You may have entered into for increasing Your Military Force, we will take the same into our Consideration: And we trufi Your Majesty will not be dilappointed in the gra-21

cious Sentiments which You entertain of the Zeal and Public Spirit of Your faithful Commons.

We are truly sensible, that Your Majesty’s condant Care for the Welfare of Your People, and Your generous Concern for the Happiness of Mankind, dif-pole Your Majesty to desire, that the Peace of Europe may not be disturbed; but we acknowledge, with equal Gratitude, Your Majesty’s Attention to the Security of Your Kingdoms, and the Protection of the extensive Commerce of Your Subjects, in having made a considerable Augmentation to Your Naval Force, on which the Reputation and Importance of this Nation mud ever principally depend; and wc hear with the highed Satisfaction, and rely with perfect Confidence on Your Royal Declaration, that Your Majesty will always be the faithful Guardian of the Honour of the British Crown.

We beg Leave to assure Your Majesty, that we will, without Delay, enter into the Consideration of the Supplies for the ensuing Year; and that we will chcar-fully and efi'edtually provide for all such Expences as shall be found necessary for the Welliire and essential Intereds of these Kingdoms, and for the vigorous Pro-lecution of the Measures in which we are engaged for the Re-edablishment of that Constitutional Subordination, which, we trud, with the Blessing of God, Your Majesty will be able to maintain through the several Parts of Your Dominions.

We acknowledge, with equal Gratitude and Admiration, Your Majesty’s paternal Declaration, that You will be ever watchful for an Opportunity of putting a Stop to the Efiufion of the Blood of Your Subjects, and the Calamities of AVar.

Permit us to assure Your Majesty, that we cannot but dill entertain a Hope, that the Discernment of their true Intereds, the Remembrance of the Blessings they once enjoyed, and the Sense of their present Sufferings under the arbitrary Tyranny of their Leaders, will induce the deluded and unhappy Multitude to return to their Allegiance, and will re-animate their Hearts with a Spirit of Loyalty to their Sovereign, and of Attachment to their Mother Country.

The gracious and condescending Manner in which Your Majesty expresses Your Desire, that You may be enabled to restore' Peace, Order, and Confidence, to Your American Colonies, cannot fail of endearing Your Majesty to the Hearts of all Aonr Subjects; and we assure Your Ma jedy, that when this great AVork can be accomplished, and settled on the true Principles of the Conditution, Your Majesty may depend on the most zealous Concurrence and Support of Y'our faithful Commons.

City of Worcester, and County of the City of Glou* cefier, and in the River Verniew, with improper Nets, and other unwarrantable Engines, to the great Prejudice of the Petitioners, and all Persons residing near the said River; and that, if the said Act was amended* and some further Powers given for the Preservation of the Salmon and other Fish in the River Severn, and the Provisions thereof extended to that Part of the River Severn that lies in the Counties of Montgomery and Stafford, and County of the City of Worcester, and County of the City of Gloucester, and to the River

Vernieio, it would be of great Benefit to the Petitioners, and to all Persons having Estates, or residing near the said' Rivers: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for more, effectually preserv-ing the Salmon and other Fish, within the said Rivers Severn and Vernieio, in such Manner as the House shall think fit.

llie House resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the Supply granted to His Majesty;

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Sir Charles Whitworth took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker re famed the Chair.

Sir Charles Whitworth reported from the Committee,

That they had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be received Tomorrow Morning.

Sir Charles Whitworth also acquainted the House, that he was directed by the Committee to move, that they may have Leave to fit again.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Friday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Acts Were read: And,

Mr. Joseph Ellis, the Surveyor of the.Roads, being,

examined, said. That the Trustees have proceeded in the execution of the said Acts, and have borrowed a considerable Sum of Money upon the Credit of the Tolls thereby granted, which, together with the Tolls, has been laid out in the Repair of the said Roads; and that the said Sum so borrowed is now owing upon the.

Credit of the said Acts.

That by reason of the great Number of very heavy Carriages passing the said Roads, some of which are subject only to Half Tolls, and others not subject to any Toll, the Expences of the Repairs of the Roads are so greatly increased that the present Tolls are not sufficient to keep the same in Repair; and that, unless the Terms of the said Acts are further continued, the Tolls increased, and tfte Powers altered and enlarged, the Money now owing cannot be repaid, nor the Roads kept in proper Repair for the future.

THE Lord Cranborne acquainted the House, that the Gentlemen appointed to attend Her Majesty with the congratulatory Message of this House, had attended Her Majesty accordingly; and that Her Majesty was pleased to say.

Gentlemen,

No One can feel, more strongly than I do, every Instance of the dutiful Attachment of the House of Commons tb the King, and Attention for Me.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that, a Petition has been presented, for Leave to bring in a Bill to enable His Majesty to license aTheatre in Birmingham; and that the Peti tioners apprehend, that the licensing of a Theatre in the Town of Birmingham will be disagreeable to the major Part of the Inhabitants, and prejudicial to the Interest and Trade of the said Town: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and permit them to be heard, by their Counsel, at the Bar, against the Bill, and to grant to the Petitioners such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the several Owners and Proprietors of, or otherwise interested in the Open and Common Fields, and other Commonable Lands and Grounds, of and within the Parish and Liberties of North Marston, in the County of Bucks, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Lands and Grounds of the Petitioners, in the said Open and Common Fields, and other Commonable Lands and Grounds, lie intermixed and dispersed, and in their present Situation are incapable of any considerable Improvement; and it would be very advantageous to the several Persons interested therein, if the said Fields, Lands, and Grounds, were divided and inclosed, and specific Shares

thereof allotted to the several Proprietors, according to their respective Rights and Interests: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to briitg in ;? Bill for dividing and inclosing the said Open and Common Fields, and other Commonable Lands and Grounds, in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, put-suant. to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Grenville and Mr. Hopkins do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Mr. Bartow reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Proprietors of, or Persons interested in, the Fisheries in the River Severn below. Gloucester Bridge, on Behalf of themselves, and others and also the Petition of the Mpft noble Henry Duke of Beaufort, being a Proprietor of considerable Fitlieries in the River Severn below Gloucester f were several ly referred; That the Committee had examined the Matters of the said Petitions; and had directed him to report the fame, as tfiey appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petitions, an Act, passed in the First Year of the Reign of Queen Elizabeth, for Prfefervation of Spawn and Fry of sith; was read; which enacts. That no Person tliall sith, or take Fish, with any Net or Engine, but only with Net or Tramel, whereof every Meih or Math shall be Two Inches and an Half broad (Angling excepted): And an Act, passed in the Thirtieth Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, for Prefer vat ion of Fishing in the River Severn, was also read; which confirms the Size of the Meshes as declared in the said Act of Queen Elizabeth, and lays a Penalty on all Persons who thall sith, below Gloucester Bridge, with any Net for taking the Sorts of Fish therein mentioned, which shall be above Sixty Yards in Length; or with more than One of those Nets at a Time. And,

Mr. Richard Mafhfteld, who has been a Esther man all his Life-time on the River Severn below Gloucester Bridge, and who is 67 Years of Age, being examined; said. That great Inconveniences have arisen to the Fisheries, owing to the restrictive Mode of fithing preferred by the above Acts, the Methes of the Nets being too large, and the Nets too tliort; that the Methes of the Nets being so large, they will not take several Sorts of Fith, namely. Lampreys, which are in feafop in February and continue till May, also another Sort of Fith called Shads, in season the tame Months, and are much esteemed as Delicacies; and also another Sort of Fith called Thwaites, which are in season, and come in great Shoals and Quantities about the latter End of April, and continue till June, and are a boney coarse Fish, but chiefly supply the Poor of the several adjacent Parishes, and many other Places; that there is also another Species of Fith about the same Month o i June, after the larger Salmon are gone up to spawn, called Botchers (of the Salmon Kind) which are ftipted in their Growth by not being tpawned in due Season.

Mr. Daniel Ellis and Mr. James Darke, Fithernjep,

confirmed the above Evidence.

Mr. Mai/hfield further said. That, the Length of the Nets, allowed by the said Acts, are not sufficient, owing to the Weirs being taken out of the River for the Benefit of the Navigation; and that formerly they could only sith between the Weirs and the Shore.

The Witnesses declared, That the ltatiitgble Nets are too short, the River in fopie Places being from 150 to 500 Y'ards broad: And,- ....

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, that He will be graciously pleased to give Directions, that there be laid before this House an Account of the Number of Troops ordered to be raised during the late Adjournment of Parliament; specifying the different Corps, and the Names of the Officers appointed to command them, and also the Names of all the Officers appointed to serve in each Rank in the different Corps, and the Time each Officer had served in any other Corps in the Army, previous to such Appointment, and the Rank he held.

The Amendments following were severally proposed to be made to the Question; To leave out the Words " of the Number of Troops ordered to be " raised during the late Adjournment of Parliament," and alter " Corps" to insert " which have been ordered to be raised during the late Adjournment of this House;" and to leave out " them" and insert " those " Corps" instead thereof; and at the end of the Question to add, " and the Terms on which such Corps " are to be raised."

And the Question being put. That the Words " of " the Number of Troops ordered to be raised duri ng

19

" the late Adjournment of Parliament," Hand Part of the Question;

It passed in the Negative.

And the Question being put, That the Words" which " have been ordered to be raised during the late Adjournment of this House," be inserted after the Word " Corps;"

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

And the Question being put. That the Word " them" Hand Part of the Question;

It passed in the Negative.

And the Quest ion being put, That the Words " those " Corps" be inserted instead thereof;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

And the Question being put, That the Words " and " the Terms on which such Corps are to be raised," be added at the end of the Question;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Then the main Question, so amended, being put;

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, that He will be graciously pleased to give Directions that there be laid before this House an Account, specifying the different Corps which have been ordered to be raised during the late Adjournment of this House, with the Names of the Officers appointed to command those Corps; and also the Names of all the Officers appointed to serve in each Rank in the different Corps, and the Time each Officer had served in any other Corps in the Army, previous to such Appointment, and the Rank he held; and the Terms on which such Corps are to be raised.

COPY of a Letter from the Secretary at War to Sir Thomas , Baronet, dated 16th December 1777-

SIR, War-Offrce, 16th December 1777.

I AM commanded by the King to acquaint you, that His Majesty approves of the very handsome Offer made by the Town of Manchester, through you, for raising a Regiment of Foot at their own Expence; the Regiment to consist of Eight Battalion Companies, One Company of Grenadiers, and One'of Light Infantry. The Battalion Companies to consist each of 1 Cftptairt, Lieutenants, 1 Ensign, .,. Serjeants, ... Corporals; 2 Duimmers, and 100 private Men; the Grenadier Company of 1 Captain, 3 Lieutenants, ... Serjeants, ... Corporals, a Drummers, 2 Fifers, and 100 Men; tli’e Light Infantry Company of 1 Captain, 3 Lieutenants,

Serjeants, Corporals, 2 Drummers, and 100 Private, with the usual Staff Officers. The Regiment to have 1 Colonel Commandant, 1 Lieutenant Colonel, and 1 Major, each having also a Company.

The Non-cominillioned Officers and private Men are to receive Pay from the Days of their respective Attestations.

No more than Three Guineas Bounty Money will be allowed to be givdrt to each Recruit.

None are to be en lifted under Five Fbfet Four Inches, nor under Eighteeh Years, or above Thirty.

It is required, that the Regiment shall be actually raised and approved (after bfeing reviewed by a General Officer) within Four Months from the Date hereof. I have represented to His Majesty, that Commissions are not desired for the Officers until the Regiment shall be so reviewed and approved, except for Captain,

of the 23d, and RogerAy faun, Esquire, late of the nth DrSgOOfis, the intended Major and eldest Captain.

The Lift of the other Gentlemen, recommended through you, for Commissions, has been laid before the King, and honoured with His Royal Approbation; and they may be affuied that they shall have Commissions as soon as ever the Regiment is raised and approved.

I am likewise authorized by His Majesty to acquaint you, that the Officers wilt bfe entitted to Half Pay irt case the Regiment shall be reduced after it has been once established.

I have the Honour to be,

Slit, Kc.

Sir Thomas Egerton, Baronet,

Heaton, Lancashire.

COPY of a Letter from the Secretary at War to Lieutenant Colonel John Campbell, dated 19th December 1777.

SIR, War-Office, 19 th 1777;

I AM commanded by the King to acquaint you, that His Majesty approves of your Proposal for raising a Regiment of Foot in the Highlands of Scotland; to consist of Eight Battalion Companies, One Company of Grenadiers, and One of Light Infantry. The Battalion Companies to consist ekeh of 1 Captain, 2 Lieutenants, 1 Ensign, 5 Serjeants, 5 Corporals, 2 Drummers, and 100 private Men; the Grenadier Company of 1 Captain, 3 Lieutenants, 5 Serjeants, 5 Corporals, 2 Drummers, 2 Pipers, and 100 private Men; the Light Infantry Company of 1 Captain, 3 Lieutenants, 5 Serjeants, 5 Corporals, 2 Drummers, and 100 Private, with the usual Staff Officers. The Regiment to have 2 Majors, each having also a Company; and to be under your Command, as Lieutenant Colonel Commandant, with the Command of a Company.

I am to inform you, that Levy Money will be issued to you, at the Rate of £. 3 per Man, for 1,082 Men; and that His Majesty has been pleased to direct, that the Pay of the Regiment shall take place from the Date of your Beating Order, and shall be allowed you in Aid of Recruiting, on Condition that you do render an exact Account of the said Levy Money, and Pay, that shall be issued to you, charging against it Five Guineas for each Man reviewed and approved, together with the Subsistence of the Non-commissioned Officers and private Men, from the Day of their respective Attestations; and if there should be any Balance remaining it is to be considered as a Saving to the Public, to be hereafter disposed of as shall be thought proper.

No more than Three Guineas will be allowed to be given to each Recruit.

None are to be enlisted under Five Feet Four Inches, nor under Eighteen Years, or above Thirty.

It is required, that the Regiment shall be actually raised and approved (after being reviewed by a General Officer) within Four Months from the Date hereof.

1 have represented to His Majesty, that you humbly hope you shall be indulged in recommending the Officers, being such as are well affected to His Majesty, and most likely, by their Interest and Connections, to assist iu railing the Corps without Delay; but that you do not desire any Commissions for them until the Regiment shall have been raised and approved.

You will therefore be pleased to send to me, for His Majesty’s Consideration, a List of such Persons as you propose for Officers, who, if they meet with His Royal Approbation, may be assured that they shall have Commissions as soon as ever the Regiment is completed. And I am to acquaint you, it is His Majesty’s Intention, that the Companies which shall be first raised shall entitle their Captains and Subalterns to Seniority in the Regiment, according to their respective Ranks, and the different Periods at which the said Companies shall be completed.

I am to inform you, that in case the Persons approved by the King for the Rank of Major should be of less than Five Years Handing in the Army as Captains, they are to pay £. 300 each for their Commissions; which Sums are to be carried in Aid of the Charge brought on the Public for Levy Money, and credited to the General Account.

I am likewise authorized by His Majesty to acquaint you, the Officers will be entitled to Half Pay in case the Regiment shall be reduced after it has been once established.

I have the King’s Commands to add, that as Orders are given for several other Highland Corps, it is His Majesty’s Intention that their Seniority in the Army shall be determined by the Periods at which they shall be respectively completed.

I have the Honour to be,

SIR, Sic.

Lieutenant Colonel John Campbell, Barrington.

A Petition of severalof the Free Fiihcfs and Dredgers belonging to the Oyster Fishery within the Manor and Koyaii v of /i1 tillable, in the County of Kent, in Behalf of themlVlves and all other Free Fishers and Dredgers there, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, for Time out of Mind, there hath been an Oyster Fishery w ithin the said Manor and Royalty, limited by well-known Marks and Bounds, wherein all Persons, who have been regularly admitted Freemen of the said Fishery at a Court of Dredging, and none others, have a Right to fish for or catch Oysters, or the Brood thereof; and that the Petitioners whole Dependence for themselves and Families is in the said Fishery; which is greatly annoyed and prejudiced by Strangers and other Persons, fithing and dredging for, and carrying off, the Oysters, by which Meaus the Free Fishermen are deprived of their immediate Property, and the Brood destroyed by fishing in improper Seasons; and that, if the said Fishery was protected from such Practices, the same would be of great Advantage and Convenience to the Inhabitants of the Fall Part of the said County of , especially to the poorer Sort; and the said Fishery hath been a great Nursery for Seairten- for the Royal Navy: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for eficftually securing the said Fishery, by such Means as the House shall think proper.

A Petition of the High Sheriff, Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freeholders of the County of Cormcall, assembled at the General Quarter Sessions of the Peace, holden at Bodmin, the 9th Day of October 1777, in and for the said County, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Common Gaol of the said County, for Criminals, is within the Calile of Launcejton, which is at present in a very bad Condition, the Repairs whereof have hitherto been borne out of the Revenues of the Duke of Cormcall for the Time being; and that the said

Gaol, and the Town of Launcejton, being situated near the Ealtem Extremity of the said County, the Ease ami Convenience of the Public would be best failed by an additional Gaol for Criminals being provided nearer the Centie of the said County; and that the Borough of Bodmin, belt answering the Description aforesaid, and besides being favoured with healthy Air, a good Soil, and Plenty of wholesome Water, is eltecmed the most proper Situation for placing the said new Gaol; and it will be necessary that a Parcel of Ground, called Berrycoombe, otherwise Burcom, within VOL. 36.

the said Borough, Part of the Possessions of the Mayor and Burgesses of the said Borough, and also a small Portion of Ground, the Property of private Persons, should be taken, and used as the Site of the said new Gaol, and for conveying, by a higher Level, a certain Stream of Water, from a Place called Wash,

to the said intended Gaol; and that His Majesty hath been graciously pleased to order to be advanced, but of the Revenues of the Duke of CoYnxoall, a certain Stun, to be applied in repairing the said Gabl in the Calile of Launceston, and also a further Slim, tb be employed towards erecting a new Gaol, at or near Bodmin aforesaid, upon Condition that the Duke of Cornwall for the Time being, may be for ever exonerated from all Charges which may attend the future Repairs, not only of the said present Gaol at Launceston, but of the said new Gaol to be built at or near Bodmin aforesaid; Which Sums have been advanced and accepted upon the said Condition; and that the said Mayor and Burgesses are freely disposed, without any pecuniary Consideration to divelt themselves of the said Parcel of Ground, Part of their Possessions; and the said other Owners of the Lands necessary to be taken for the Purposes aforesaid are consenting to give up their Property in the said Lands, upon a reasonable Satisfaction being made to them for the fame; and that, besides the said Gaols, a Ward or Prison for the secure keeping of Debtors, and a House of Correction or Bridewell, are greatly wanted in the said County, the erecting and finishing whereof, will necessarily occasion a considerable additional Expence beyond the Sum already advanced by His Majesty as aforesaid: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for indemnifying the Duke of Cornwall, for the Time being, from all Repairs of the said Gaols for Felons; and for the appropriating, and properly veiling* the said Parcels of Ground; anti for raising not only a' competent Sum for the Purpose of erecting, completing, and finishing, the said new Gaol for Criminals, House of Correction, and Sheriffs Ward or Prison, and making Satisfaction to the respective Owners of the Grounds, to be taken and used for the Purposes aforesaid, but also, from Time to Time, for ever, as Need or Occasion shall require, sufficient Sums of Money for paying the Salaries of proper Keepers and Officers, to be appointed by the Justices of the said County, for the said new Gaol for Felons, and Bridewell or House of Correction; and for sustaining the Expences necessarily incident to, and which may attend, the said new Gaol and House of Correction; for supporting and keeping in sufficient Repair, as well the said Gaol at Launcejton, when l'o repaired, as the said new Gaol and House of Correction at Bodmin, and other the Conveniences which may belong thereto; and for making all such further and other Provisions as may be necessary, and as the same shall require, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as to the House shall seem moll meet and expedient.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

in the County of Lincoln, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, in the said Soke and Wapentake, there is an extensive Tract of Country,

Hamlets, and Places, besides the Three Market Towns of Spilsby, Burgh, and Waiirfleet, several of which are

rendered very populous, as Well by the Vicinity of several considerable Tracts of Commonable Lands and Waste Grounds therein, containing in the Whole 40,000 Acres, and upwards, called The Fens (whereon several Thousands of People, by Fillring, Fowling, cutting of Fewel, Reed, and other Thatch, entirely subsist and maintain themselves and Families,) as of the Sea-port Town of Boston, and by that Means carry on a considerable Trade with the Inhabitants of the said Parishes,

Villages, Hamlets, and Places; to a great Number of whom they are obliged to give Credit for finall Sums of Money, amounting in the Whole to a large Sum of Money Yearly,' who frequently refuse, although well able, to pay the same, presuming on the Discouragement with Creditors lie under, from the great Expences they are unavoidably put unto in firing for such Debts in the County Court, which is upwards of Thirty Miles distant from any of the said Parishes, Villages, Hamlets, and Places; and that, if there was an easy and speedy Method of recovering small Debts within the said Soke and Wapentake, the same would greatly contribute to promote Industry, and encourage Trade and Credit therein: And therefore praying, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the more easy and speedy Recovery of small Debts in the Parishes, Villages, I lam-lets and Places, within the said Soke and Wapentake, under such Regulations and Restrictions as to the House shall appear just and reasonable.

and that great Crops of Oats, the only Com fit to be sown thereon, are annually produced from the same; and that the said Oats are very fit for the London and other Markets, and are of great Benefit to the Consumers of Oats; and that, by the Regulation of the said Act of the Thirteenth of His present Majesty, the Ports in this Kingdom are frequently opened for the Importation of Oats, at a Time when great Quantities of Oats, grown on the said Low Lands, are at Market, and ready to be sold at or under the Price as fixed by the said last mentioned Act for opening the said Ports, by which means Foreigners are enabled to import great Quantities, to the great Distress of the Markets for these Low-Land Oats, by which the same are so reduced in Price as to give no Encouragement to the Owuers and Occupiers of the said Low Lands to improve and cultivate the fame, which, if they are encouraged to do, the London apd other Markets may always depend upon a conllant Supply from the said Countries; and that, if the Importation of Foreign Oats, upon the Payment of Two Pence per Quarter, was not allowed, unless Oats were at a higher Price per Quarter than what is settled by the said Act of the Thirteenth Year of His present Majesty, and if the Weight of what is to be deemed middling British Oats was fixed, it would be more beneficial to the Petitioners, and particularly so to such of them as are Occupiers of Low Lands employed in the Cultivation of Oats, who now give much higher Rents for the said Lands, and a greater Price for Labour, than at the Time of passing the said Act of the Twenty-second of Charles the Second, and be a Means of saving them from utter Ruin, giving them Encouragement to cultivate the said Lands, and secure a Permanency of Supply to the several Markets for the fame, and a proportionable Return for the Expence and Pains incurred in draining and preserving a Tract of Country so valuable and beneficial to the Community in general; . And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to give such Relief as to the House shall leem meet.

particularly with respect to the1 Putt Fisheries; for m the Months of March and Aprils the young Fry 6f Salmon return from the fresh Water, where they are spawned, down the River Severn towards the Sea; and that the Putts'being placed on the Sides of the River, the Months. of which are Twenty-one ‘Feet round and about Seven Feet high, great Quantities of the said Fry are taken in the said Putts, and an Engine called a Diddle, being plaeed with-in the Putt, they cannot pass through, but are de-'stroyed in those Months; but that if the Diddle was removed, -and the Bottom or lower End of the Putt was only cross-fprowed, there would be sufficient Room for the said Fry to pass through the same unhurt, and -which-would be the Means-of preserving the Spawn and! Fry of Fish.

That the said Town is very large and populous, and a great Number of Persons of considerable Property reside therein, and many of the Nobility and Persons of Distin6tion live in the Neighbourhood thereof; and that several considerable Manufactures are carried on within and near the said Town, which occasions a great Resort thereto of Persons of Rank and Fortune, particularly in the Summer Season; and that the Petitioners apprehend, if a public Theatre was legally established, for performing Plays and other Entertainments of the Stage, in Birmingham, during the Months of June, July, Augajl, and September, in every Year, it would be agreeable to the Nobility and other Persons resorting to the said Town, and very beneficial to the Inhabitants; and that the Petitioners have, at a very considerable Expence, erected a large and commodious Building in New-Street aforesaid, which has been made CJfe of as a Theatre for some Years, and which they apprehend is the most convenient Situation for that Purpose: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, to enable His Majesty to grant Letters Patent for licensing the said Theatre, for such Time, and under such Regulations, as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Thirtieth Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, for Preservation of Fishing in the River Severn, was read: And,

Mr. John Owens, being examined, laid, That the Salmon, and other Fish, and the Fry, are very much destroyed in the said River, in the County of Montgomery, and in the River by Means of im-

proper Nets, and other Engines; that there are Nets used, the Mellies of which are only Two Inches in Circumference, though by Law they ought to be . Ten, and that, by the above Practices, the Fishery is greatly injured. Aud,

Mr. John Bradney, being examined, gave your Committee ttie like Evidence with respect to that Part of the Severn running through the Counties of Salop, Stafford, Worcester, and Gbu and the Counties of

the Cities of Gbucester and Worcester, and added, that he has known Nets used with Melhes only One inch and an Half in the Circumference.

and the Counties of the Cities of Worcester and Gbucester; that, if the Powers thereof were explained and enlarged, and the Provisions of it extended to the above Counties, it would tend to the Preservation of the Fry of Fish, and he, in many respects, beneficial *0 the Fishery in general.

Then the said Report was delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Resolutions of the Committee were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Rifolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Two hundred Eighty-six thousand Six hundred Thirty-two Pounds Fourteen Shillings and Six Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge of several Augmentations to His Majesty’s Forces, from their respective Commence* ments, to the Twenty-fourth Day of December One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-eight.

Rrfolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Ninety thousand Nine hundred and Thirty-nine Pounds and Fifteen Shillings, be granted to His Majesty, upon Account of the Reduced Officers of His Majesty’s Land Forces and Marines, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-eight.

Rrfolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Seven hundred and Twelve Pounds and Five Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge for Allowances to the several Officers, and Private Gentlemen, of the Two Troops of Horse Guards reduced, and to the Superannuated Gentlemen of the Four Troops of Horse Guards, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-eight.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred Five thousand Four hundred and Thirty-one Pounds Fifteen Shillings and Five Pence, be granted to His Majesty, upon Account, towards defraying the Charge of the Out-Pensioners of Che feu Hospital, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-eight.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Two hundred and Thirty-eight Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, for the paying of Pensions to the Widows of such Reduced Officers of His Majesty’s Land Forces, and Marines, as died upon the Establishment of Half Pay in Great Britain, and were married to them before the Twenty-fifth Day of December One thousand Seven hundred and Sixteen, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-eight.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That there be laid before this House, an Account of such Ships, or Vessels, as have been purchased, to be employed in His Majesty’s Royal Navy since the Commencement of the present Hostilities in North America, together with the Tonnage and former Name (if altered) and State and Condition of such Ships or Vessels, respectively, at the Time of such Purchase; also the Price paid, the Time when, the Person or Persons from whom the Ship or Vessel was bought, and by whom the Purchase was made.

Charles Eyles, Deputy Cleric of the Pence for the County of Middlesex, produced Letters Patent, under tile Great Seal of England, dated the 7th Day of Jane, in the Seventh Yeat of the Reign of his Majesty King James the Pirft (r6to) whereby all that Piece of Ground situate in Saint John Street, in the County of containing in Breadth, from Eall to West, 32 Feet of Assize, and in Length, from South to North, 120 Feet, was- granted to Sir Thomas , Knight, and divers other Persons, then Justices of the Peace for the County of Middlesex, and their Heirs, for ever, to the Intent that the fame, and all Buildings thereupon to be erected, should for ever be used as a Session House for the Justices of the Peace for the said County, and for keeping a Prison or Correction House, to be holden of the King, his Heirs and Successors, in Fealty only, and Free and Common Soccage.

That in 1612, being soon after the Date of the said Letters Patent, the said Session House for the County of MiddlrJ'cx, known by the Name of Jlicks Hall, was built on the said Piece of Ground so granted by the said Letters Patent, and the then Justices purchased another Piece of Ground, in the Parish of in the said County, and thereon erected a Prison and House of Correction.

The Witness also produced Letters Patent, under the Great Seal, dated the 10th Day of August, in the 17th Year of the Reign of King^om^r the First, whereby the having the Prison and House of Correction in Clerkenwellwas approved of.

And the Witness said, That Hicks Hall, aforesaid, has ever since been used as a Session House for the County of Middlesex-, and that the said Building is very incommodious, and unfit for the public Business; and there is not proper Room or Accommodation for the Justices, Officers of the Court, Juries, or Suitors.

Mr. Robert Taylor, Architect, being examined, said, That he had surveyed Hicks Hall, and found the whole Building in so ruinous ja State, that he is clearly of Opinion it is not worth repairing.

Mr. Kenton Couse, Architect, surveyed the Building along with the lad Witness, and is of the same Opinion.

The said Mr. Eyles produced a Presentment of the Grand Jury of the County of Middlesex, sworn and charged to inquire for the Body of the said County, at the General Session of the Peace holden for the said County at Hicks Hall, in Saint John Street, on the 19th Day of February 1777, whereby it appears, that upon their View and Examination of the said Building, they found the External Walls much bulged, and the Foundations very rotten; the internal, Walls greatly decayed, and much cracked; the principal Timbers very rotten; and, from the ruinous State of the Whole, the same is very dangerous, and unsafe, and ought forthwith to be taken down.

And he said. That the Justices have no public Fund for defraying the Expence of repairing the said House, or for rebuilding the fame.

lie also produced a Book, containing several Resolutions of the Noblemen and Gentlemen, named in the Commission of the Peace for the County of Middlesex, and, among!! other Things, as follows: "That Hicks " Hall, the present Session House for the County of

" Middlesex, is very old, too small, and in many Re-

" spects inconvenient."

" That a new Session House ought to be built for " the Use of the County, when a proper Spot of " Ground can be procured, convenient as to Size and " Situation, for that Purpose."

" That the present Spot of Ground belonging to " Hicks Hull is in many Respects inconvenient, and " not iiillioiently large for the building a new Session " House for the County of Middlesex."

" That 1 Piece of Freehold Ground, situate at the " West End of Clerkemcell Green, in the Parish of Saint

" James Clerkemcell, within the said County, was the

" most convenient and proper Spot for the Purpose of " building a new Session I loiife lor this County."

And Mr. Eyles produced Plans of the said Ground, and said. That the said Piece of Ground can be purchased for £.2,000.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to authorize the Justices of the Peace for the County of Middlesex, to fell the present Session House for the said County, together with the Scite thereof, and to build another Session House in a more convenient Situation: And that Mr. Alderman Wilkes, Sir Mackworth,

Mr. Pulteney, Mr. Brett, Mr. and Mr. Byng,

do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Sir Charles Whitworth, according to Order, reported

from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read, and are as followeth, viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Three hundred Eighty-nine thousand Two hundred Pounds, and Sixteen Shillings, be granted to His Majesty, for the Ordinary of the Navy, including Half Pay to Sea and Marine Officers, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-eight.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Four hundred Eighty-eight thousand Six hundred and Ninety-five Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, towards the Buildings, Rebuildings, and Repairs, of Ships of War in His Majesty’s Yards, and other Extra Works, over and above what are proposed to be done upon the Heads of Wear and Tear, and Ordinary, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-eight.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Four thousand Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, upon Account, to be applied by the Commissioners or Governors of the Royal Hospital for Seamen at Greenwich, for the Support and Relief of Seamen, worn out and become decrepit in the Service of their Country, who shall not be provided for within the said Hospital, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-eight.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

A Petition of several of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, and others, of the County of Norfolk, and of the City of Norwich, was presented to the House, and read: Setting forth. That your Petitioners observe, with the utmost Concern and Surprise, that extraordinary En-

deavours are used in this County and in many other; Parts of the Kingdom, to raise Men and Money for His Majesty’s Service by free Gifts and Contributions, not given and granted in a Parliamentary Gourse, which. unusual and strained Efforts (concerning the very Le-. gality of which they conceive Doubts may jullly be. entertained) while Parliament actually fits, and at a- Time when His Majesty is in apparent Peaee with all"

... f

18 Geo. III. 170 Februarii. 711

the Powers in Europe, strongly indicate some violent Distemper in the State, to which its ordinary Powers and Means of Supply are not sufficient. We most humbly apprehend, that if a War with any of the neighbouring Nations threatens to break out, nothing can give more Encouragement to it than the taking such Measures as tend to prove this Kingdom to be as much exluiuftrd in its Strength at the very Commencement of Foreign Hostilities, as it has been at the Close of the longed and rood wasteful Wars. Your Petitioners have been also called upon, in a Manner equally alarming, by IYrfons of great Power and Rank in His Majesty’s Service, to raise Men and 9 Money for supporting the Constitiitional Authority of Great Britain. We hope and trull, that Constitutional Authority is safe,-and well supported in the affections, of a loyal and a free People; we know of no Attack upon, or Rirfiftance to, the Operation of the Laws in this County, or in this Kingdom; impaired, as we may be, in Power or Reputation Abroad, we have how-c\er Peace at Home; hut in the Thirteen once-dou-rishing, and obedient Colonies of Great Britain, His Majesty has no Authority or other Government to be supported. A Misrepresentation of our unhappy Situation would be a Mockery of our Distress. An Empire is loft. A great Continent in Arms is to be conquered or abandoned. One whole Britishi Army of veteran Troops has surrendered Prisoners of War to the Hidden Levies of a new Nation; another, abandoning a Province which had been overrun in the laftCampaign, and after two Engagements in the Field successful without Advantage, having marched out to take a View of an Enemy ported in one of those Places of inacceinble Strength with which America abounds, has been compelled, by, Necessity, to march buck to an open Town, which they are obliged to fortify for Winter Quarters at an enormous Expence; the Continent of America is, it feenss, to be conquered by defeated and defeiifive Armies. It is a Project we cannot comprehend. Sixty thousand Soldiers, a Force of Artillery (if we are to judge by the Charge) such as never has been sent out of this Kingdom, Sixty thou-latid Seamen voted, more than an Hundred armed ( Ships employed in this special Service, an unheard-of Expence in every Sort of Military Supply, have* after Three Years Struggle, brought Things to such a Mate, that, inftend of quieting our Civil Troubles, we are threatened with a Foreign War, lor which, after such an Abundance (for we cannot call it Profusion) of Parliamentary Grants, increasing daily', and wrth the . most exuberant recruiting Funds, we are called upon . to piece out the Deficiency of public Wealth by pri-. rate Contribution; a Nation of such Power as this reduced to such a State must lole its Reason and its Feelings, together with its Glory, if it could acquiefee in its Condition. It is not in our Choice to suppose ..that it can have happened-without a Fault somewhere: In the Generals and Armies tin? Fault cannot be; if their known and tried Characters did not iorbid all Suspicions of them, yet His Majesty’s most gracious Speeches from the Throne make it improper fonts to entertain the least Doubt of their Courage and Conduct; but His Majesty has not forbid os to entertain Doubts of the Wisdom, Care, and Prudence of those who conduct His Affairs; and we trust, that the House of Commons, whose Duty calls, and whose Competence and Coustitution enables, them rocome to the Bottom of those Evils, will ferioully inquire into the Cause of ourpresent calamitous Situation, for we greatly fear that we, with the rest of your Constituents, have been hitherto greatly deceived and deluded, with regard to the Nature, the Cause. and the Importance, of the American Troubles, as well as concerning the Means of quieting them, both legal and coercive, else we tliould not have the Misfortune to fee Acts of Par-Vox.. 36.

liament made only to be sent back to be repealed;

Armies sent out to enforce them only to be returned to us as Prisoners under Capitulation: and, to speak with the filial Confidence of free Subjects, we plainly declare ourselves unwilling to commit any more of our Natiorial Glory to Attaint, and the Persons of more of our Countrymen to Foreign Hardships and Perils, without any common human Security that they shall not, by the same Errors, be exposed to the same Ca- ' larnities and Disgraces which many of those have fallen into who have already been sent forth. Without -wife Council at Home we cannot have Empire or Reputation Abroad; it is our Duty to our Sovereign, to whose Person and illustrious House we have ever borne the most distinguiilied and zealous Attachment, which compels us to lay before this Honourable House this Representation of His Affairs; we shall ever be fore-most in prov iding for every reasonable and useful Supply for the Public Service; but we cannot make ourselves the Instruments of any Faction, or grant Money as a Tell of our Support of it; if the Colonies can be brought to Obedience, we are convinced, by, fad. Experience, it must be by wife and lenient Councils, and by those in whom they have no Experience of Ill-will, or Incapacity, the one producing Hatred,-the other Contempt: for our domestic Protection, we riioft humbly conceive, that our Coiiftitutional Militia, which His Majesty has been enabled to call out, is the most effective and least invidious Delence: Twelve entirely new Corps, confiding of Fifteen thousand Highlanders of the Northern Part of the United Kingdom, and of the Towns of M anchester and Liverpoole, appointed during the Sitting, without the previous Approbation of Parliament, and which can hardly be ready in Tinye for A meric an Service, are not, yvemolt humbly submit it to superior Wisdom, the Defence in which we can or ought, for obvious reasons, to trust In'preference: to that Vnore numerous and equally well-trained and well affected Body the National Militia; nor have we been givep to understand at a Time when {lie War Establilliment Hands at comparatively Tow Numbers, arid those Nuro-. her far from complete, and -at a Time when the public Burthens are i’o oppfeilive, for what reason new Corps ‘ should" be raised; or on what Grounds; if Compliment was1 meant: (at, the Expence*oT our. Finances, aild what We conceive the most Jfery.iceabje Military Arrangement) that Compliment has been confined to the above rrientioned Parts" of this) Kingdom.

*We do therefore, with all Earnestness and Humility, pray an Inquiry' into the true Grounds and.Conduct of this unhappy Civil War; that the heft Means may be found for bringing it to a speedy Termination, for facilitating the Reftbration of Concord and Confidence to all the Citizens of the British Empire, to avert, if possible, a Foreign WUr, or, if that be not poffihle, to take duO Care'that rational, effectual, and becoming Provision, in an' orderly and parliamentary Way, be madeTor otir Defence and Safety; under the accumulated Distress of Foreign arid Civil Hostility, we throw ourselves with the moll perfect Reliance on the Care and-’ Wisdom (never more called for than in the present Exigency) of a BratiOi House of Commons; on them we rest the last Hdpes of a deserving, but,

vvie fear, an injured, deceived and endangered People.

Ordered, That the said.Petition do lie upon the Table. ~V: '

viz.

To prove the Allegations of the fold Petition; Mr.

Thomas Gaun, being examined, said, That there has been. Time out of Mind, an Oyster Fishery within the Manor and Royalty of Whitstable, in the County of Kent, wherein all Persons who are regularly admitted Freemen of the said Fishery, at a Court called a Court of Dredging, have a Right to fish or catch Oysters, or the Brood thereof — That he has known the Fishery upwards of Forty-two Years — That it is marked out by.

Buoys and Beacons, at the Expence of the Fishermen — Inat a Court is held every Year for the Regulation of it — That the Fishery has suffered greatly of late, and particularly within this last Year, by Means of Strangers and Intruders fishing and dredging within the Limits thereof, to the great Prejudice of the Person&.entitled to it, as Freemen of the said Fishery, notwithstanding the y do, at a great Expence, keep a Watch, in order to protect the same — That the said Fishery, on former Occasions, and lately, has iurnished many useful Seamen for the Service of the Public — That great Numbers of the People of the Country are employed in the Fishery, and that the said Freemen generally have between 50 and 60 Apprentices employed in it — That if the Fishery was protected from the lntrufion of Strangers, and properly secured to the Persons entitled to it as Freemen, whose Livelihood almost wholly depends thereupon, the same would not only be of great Advantage to them, but also to Numbers of the Inhabitants of the Fast

Mr. William Hodgkmfon, a Surveyor, confirmed the Evidence given by Mr. Parker, as to the Practicability of making the said Canal; and being asked, W hat Number of Locks were proposed to be made, and how much each Lock would coll; he said, He was of Opinion, it . would, be proper to make 40 Five Feet Locks, and that the Expence of each Lock would be about £.350. Then,

who, fipd, That the Price in the Carriage of Timber, Corn, and all other heavy Goods, between Hampshire and London, will be reduced Two-thirds, which will be a great Saving in the Price of the Carriage of Timber used in ;His Majesty’s Yards at Deptford, and

That the Corn grown in Hampshire, is in general sent to die London Markets, some by Reading, and some by Chertsey, but that some is sent Wellward, to Winchester and Newbury Markets.

Mr. Thomas May, being examined, was asked his Opinion with respect to the Utility of the ,proposed Canal; he said. He thought it would be of great Utility to all the Counties through which it is to pass, and for many Miles round; and also of public Utility.

Being asked, If he thought it would be of Advantage to Winchester? he said, It w ould certainly be pre-

judicial to the Canal from Winchester to Southampton, because they would not then bring so many Goods to Bafngstoke as they now do, because at many Seasons of the Year, and in particular Months, Coals are Cheaper at London than at Winclief er, and are of a much superior Quality.

That the Witness thinks, when the proposed Canal is made, the Price of Coals in the Neighbourhood of Bafngstoke, will be reduced 2d. or 3d. a Bushel; that the common Price of Coal, in the Neighbourhood of Bafngstoke, is at present about 1 s. a Bushel; that upon an Average, they are about a Bushel more at Bafngstoke than at Winchefie

Being asked, Whether he did not think that Reading would be injured by this Canal i he said. He did not think the Canal would be any Advantage to Reading.

Being asked, What is the Price of the Carriage of a Load of Meal from Bafngstoke to Reading he said,

12 s.6 d. — that the intended Price between Queenhithe and Bafngstoke will be 11 s. 6rf.

And being asked, Whether he did not think, that from the Facility of the Carriage from Bafngstoke to Queenhithe, when the proposed Canal is made, it would not encrease the Value of Corn in the Neighbourhood of Bafngstoke ? he said. He thought it would make it rather dearer; but that it would depend upon the Markets; — that he thought the making the Canal would make Oats rather cheaper in the Neighbourhood of Bafngstoke.

The Witness was then asked, If London, was not their chief Market at present for Meal and Malt, and how those Commodities are conveyed at present? he said, London was their Chief Market for Meal and^Malt, and that they are sent in Waggons to Reading, Staines, ChcrtJ'ey, and Aldermafon, and from thence conveyed

by Water Carriage to London -, and that the major Part of the Timber sent out of the Neighbourhood of Bafngstoke was sent down the Thames.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for making a navigable Canal from the Town of Bafngstoke, in the County of Southampton, to communicate with the River Wey, in the Parish of Chertsey, in the County of Surrey: And that Sir Simeon Stuart and Sir Henry St.John, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Two Acts, made in the Seventh Year of King George the First, and the Eighth Year of His present Majesty, for regulating the Journeymen Taylors within the Weekly Bills of Mortality, were produced to your Committee, whereby it appeared that several Penalties and Punish-wents are inflated upon Matter Taylors for giving, and upon Journeymen for receiving, any more or greater Wages than by the said Acts are directed. And,

Mr. George Johnstone, a Matter Taylor, being examined, said,. That in pursuance of the said Act of the Eighth Year of* His present Majesty, the Justices of the Peace at the Quarter Sessions for the City of London have fixed the Wages of Journeymen Taylors indiscriminately upon all Sorts, from whence great In* conveniences have arisen to the Matters; for tfaofe Men being very unequal in their Capacities, it has prevented that Emulation which ought to be encouraged amongii them, and also prevents the Matters from rewarding Men of Merit according to their Deserts j that, on this Account, great Combinations have been formed, amongii the Journeymen, to fix their own Wages; and, if their Demands are not immediately complied with, to leave their Work, which prevents |he Matters from executing their Orders, and occasions Difiippointment to their Customers.

And the Witness added. That the Powers and Re- gelations authorized by the 1 aft-mentioned Act, are You 36.

found to be ineffectual, and are attended with great Inconveniences.

Mr. James Pearce and Mr. John Shell confirmed the above Evidence.

AMerfgate Mr. yohnes. Junior, reported from the Committee, Paviag. whom the Petition of several Inhabitants and Owners of Eliates in and near1 the High Street or Road leading from Aldersgate Bars, in the Parish of Saint Botolph,

without Aldersgate, London, to the Turnpike near the

End of Goswell Street, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. George Wyatt, a Surveyor, being examined, said, That the Pavement of the Street or Road from Aldersgate Bars to the Turnpike, near the End of Goswell Street, is in a ruinous Condition, and very dangerous to Passengers; and that he finds the Expence of paving it will be £.6,000, including the old Materials, and allowing for Incidents. Then,

Mr. George Dale, being examined, said. That the said Street has been much deserted since the other Avenues to London have been improved, and the Trade there greatly decayed in consequence thereof;, that of Five Inns, there are Three shut up, on Account of the Badness of the Passage through the Street, and the Rents are much reduced; that if the said Street was properly paved, it would be of great public Utility; but the Inhabitants are not able to do it of themselves.

Mr. Peter Clugh and Mr. James confirmed

the Evidence of Mr. Dale.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider of the Report which was made from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, in Common Council assembled, was referred.

' to allow the Petitioners to be heard* by their Counsel, why the said intended Bill should not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie tipon the Table* until the Bill for repairing the Highways and Bridges in the County of Stirling, be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at' the same Time, ia Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

A Petition of Jacob Earl of Radnor, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioner is Lord of the Hundred of PuckUchurch, in

in the County of Gloucester, and as such entitled to hold a Court of Pleas, every Three Weeks, in all Personal Actions arising within the said Hundred for Debt or Damages under Forty Shillings, which Court the Petitioner, his Ancellors and Predecessors, Lords of the said Hundred, have constantly, or as often as was requisite, to the present Time, actually held; and that the Petitioner observes, by the Votes, that an Application has been made, for a Bill to establish a new Court, of similar Form, Power, and Jurisdiction, in certain Parts of the said County, including the said Hundred; and that the Petitioner has never heard or received, and believes there is not, any Complaint of any Proceeding in his said Court; and therefore presumes to think, that the Establishment of a new Court of Pleas in the said District would be an unnecessary and unjust Infringement upon his private Right and Property; And therefore praying the House, That, if they shall lie pleased to order in a Bill to establish a Court, in Compliance with the said Application, such Court may have no Jurisdiction within the said Hundred of Packlechurch.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Freeholders, Tradesmen, Manufacturers, Farmers, and other principal Inhabitants, residing within the Hundreds of Grumbalds Ash and Pucklechurch, and in the several Parishes, Precincts, and Hamlets, of Marfiifield, Iron A don, Raingworthy, Yale Bitton, Doynton, Frampton CottereU., Hanham, Oldland, and in the County of Gloucester, and in the several Parishes of Bathford, Batheafion, Cat/terine, and Swavfioicke, in the County of Somerset, is referred: And that they do examine the Matter of this Petition, and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

Pair is a Week’s Work — That the Deductions are as above — That the Prices of these have not altered lately — That it is real Necessity has drove the Journeymen to this Application, but no ill Will to the Masters — That this Work is for Exportation and Home Consumption, a great Quantity of both — That Complaints were made Twenty Years ago to the Matters, but they would not alter the Price — That the Matters oblige the Workmen to make 24 Gauge as good as 26, which reduces the Maker’s Profit — That the Journeymen wish to have their Wages raised about id. in is. in Worsted, Thread, and Cotton, and about
