(id. or is. a Week, and they would be very well contented with that Advance — That they don’t desire any Advance upon figured Work, that is to say, Lappet* and Ruffles, Mr. s Patent, or

Lace.

Your Committee then called Mr. William;

who being examined, said, That he was a Framework-knitter at Leicester, and is acquainted with some Branches

of the Worsted Mit and Glove Business — That they make them by the Dozen — That the medium Price is about 4$. or 5 s.a Dozen — That a middling Workman can make Two Dozen, at 4*. a Dozen — That the Outgoings are, for the Frame is. a Week, 8 a Week Seaming, 6d. a Week Fire and Candle, upon an Average, all the Year round, Needles about id. a Week, Winding about id. a. Week — That, in general, in this Article the Workmen have 5.s'. 6d. a Week clear to maintain themselves and Family — That, in some Articles, the Workman’s Profit is more, but less in more than it is greater — That very few Women can Work at this Business — That Children begin to work at this about the Age of Eleven, but mutt work Three or Four Years before they are Proficients — That no Profit arises from them for Two or Three Years — That they earn 5 s.6d. a Week — That some Children work Overwork for themselves, and that sometimes the Matters take some of it from them — That the clear Profit to the Matter is 4.s'. — That the Matters find them in Clothes, but when they take full Task, they find themselves in Clothes — That this Work does not require bodily Strength — That Women very seldom work, but those who do work make nearly as much as Men — That the Work lies upon the Eye, and the Activity of the Fingers — That he never remembers the Wages ever being lower than they are now — That they were higher about Ten or Twelve Years ago — That they were above One-third better in some Articles than others — That it has been gradually declining since the Year 1756 or 1757 — That he remembers the Time when lie could get One-third more than he can now — That lie believes in general they are made for Exportation and Home Consumption — That a Man who earns 5s. 6d. a Week, mutt work Fifteen Hours in the Day — That the Day he goes to fetch the Work in, he cannot get so much — That this Application to Parliament was not made on Account of any Quarrel betw een the Matters VoL. 36.

and the Journeymen, but the Difficulty of subsisting Framework- — That the Number of Manufactures in Mits and knatm; Gloves decrease every Day. tSrW««.

Mr. William llallam, being again examined, said.

That he has been employed in making Silk Mits —

That he had a great Trade for about Seven Years —

That they reckon them by the Pair — That Journeymen’s Wages are about 13 or i\d. a Pair, the middling Sort — That they can make Seven Pair a Week — That they pay out of that is. a Week for Frame Rent, 3a.

Standing, 3 d.Needles, 6d. Fire and Candle — That a Man mutt work Fifteen or Sixteen Hours in a Day, for Five Days, to earn this — That they cannot work One Half Day in a Week, on Account of putting the Goods into the Warehouse — That Women can earn nearly as much as Men — That Apprentices are put to this about the Age of Eleven or Twelve — That when they have served about Four Years, they can do as much as Men — That a good Workman can make Three Gloves in a Day, if he works an Hour extraordinary — That the worst Sort of Workmen cannot make more than One Pair a Day — That the clear Profit of One Pair a Day is about 5 s.6d. a Week — That the Glove and Mit Trade has decreased lately, that is since Mr. Morris's Patent has been in Fashion, and since the Troubles ip America — That the Glove Trade is a good deal for Exportation — That the Wagesare lower now than they were formerly, but that some Matters, who are ho nett, keep up the IPrice, but others do not.

A Petition of James Lai/man and William Stone, on behalf of themselves anti others. Proprietors of the Antigallican Private Ship of AVar, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Proprietors fitted out the said Ship, at an Expence of £.10,453, and on the 26th of December 1757, the made a lawful Capture of the Due de Penthicvre, a French Ship from China, valued £. 335,000, which Prize was, m confluence of voluntary Evidence from the French Pr ifoners, condemned at Gibraltar, the 2 ‘th of February follow ing; and that, on the 2d of March 1758, the Antigallican and her Prize, being in the Port of Cadiz, the Spaniards with Force and Violence seized the said Prize, without any real’onable Ground for such Procedure; and that, after various Applications-to the Spanish Mimfters for Redress, they, in-field of relieving the Petitioners, ordered the Ship Antigallican to be also seized, which was accordingly done on the 11th of August following, and the Petitioners have never received the least Satisfaction for the Injury; and that His Majesty gave the Proprietors His Royal Word, that the Petitioners should he relieved, by an Article in the late Peace, and that Orders were given for that Purpose, which were by feme fatal Delay or Neglect never complied with; and the Petitioners are well assured, that Copies of such Orders, and other material Papers relative to this Business, are now in the late Lord- Egremont's Office; that to relate all the Difficulties which the Petitioners have undergone, and the Delays and ill Treatment they have received in the Prosecution of this Business, would shock narrative Faith; and the Petitioners apprehend, that the Proprietors, being Englishmen, have a Claim of Protection, both m their Liberty and Property, from that Government which they contribute to support, particularly as their same is a public insult to the whole Nation; that the House hath relieved Petitioners, whose Claims do not appear to be supported in a more ample Manner; the Faith reposed in National Protection, which every civilized Country affords to its Inhabitants, the Honour of the Crown, and the unparalleled Hardships of the Petitioners Cafe, all tend to support their Petition: And therefore intreating the House, That they may be relieved in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

the Petition of feversd Gentlemen and others, of the Counties of Hereford and Radnor, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, of the 25th of April 1774, relative to Turnpike Bills, had not been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followethj viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, made in the Twenty-ninth Year of the Reign of 21

aforesaid, by The Maidenhead, to Wooferton, in the County of Salop, was read; whereby it appeared, that the Term thereof will expire at the End of this present Session of Parliament: And,

Mr. John Perry informed ypur Committee, That a considerable Sum of Money is due to him, and several other Persons, upon the Credit of the Tolls authorized by the said Act; and that, if the said Act is suffered to expire, himself, and the rest of the Creditors, will be injured thereby, as the Money owing cannot be paid oft:

And he added. That the said Roads have been repaired at great Expence, and Hill want further Repair, which cannot be done, unless the Term of the said Act be further continued, and some Amendments made thereto. Then,

Thomas Evans was examined, who informed your Committee, That he knew the Three different Branches of Road described in the Petition; one leading from the Turnpike Road at Lingen to Wigmore; another from the Turnpike Road near Prefeigne, by Rodhurjt, to Titley; and the other from Naish Lime Kilns, by Rodhurf aforesaid, to Broadford; that the First Branch of those Roads is about Two Miles in Length, and the other Two Branches about One Mile each; that the said Roads communicate with the Roads directed to be repaired by the said Act, and are in a ruinous Condition, and narrow, and cannot be properly amended and kept in Repair by the ordinary Course of Law; and' that the repairing the said Roads will be of great Convenience to all Persons residing near the fame.

And the Witness added. That no additional TolUf are intended to be taken for repairing the said Roads* nor any Money borrowed for that Purpose.

Several Members present confirmed the foregoing Evidence.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That, in Consideration of the particular Circumstances megitioped in the said Report, Leave be granted that Norrces may be given at the ensuing Easier Quarter Sessions of the Peace to be held for the Counties of Herefordand Radnor, and by Advertise-

ments in the public Newspapers, published within the same Counties, in the Months of March and April next, or one of them, of the Application to Parliament for a Continuation of the Term of the said Act, and for repairing the Roads described in thlfsaid Petition, in such and the like Manner as are required to be given by the Standing Orders of the House, of the 25th of April 1774, of Application's intended to be made relative to Turnpike Bills.

the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Fisheries in the River Severn below Gloucester Bridge, quite down " from the Coal. Wharfs, within the City of Gloucester, to the Mouth of the said River into the Sea, an Extent of 40 or 50 Miles, are private Property, and as . such have been immemorially held and enjoyed by the . Proprietors and Owners thereof, and their Tenants; and that great Quantities of Fifti come up the said River, and afford a great Supply to the Inhabitants of

the adjacent Places, and the Public in general 5 and that, by Two Acts, passed in the First Year of Queen Elizabeth, and the Thirtieth of King Charles the Second, the Length of Nets to be used for ftihing in the River Severn below Gloucester Bridge is limited to 60 Y ards, and above Gloucester Bridge, where there is no private Property, to 50 Yards, and the Size of the Melhes is limited to 10 Inches round, or 2 Inches and an Half from Knot to Knot; and that, at the Time of passing the said Acts, there were many Weirs in the said River below Gloucester Bridge (the Remains whereof Hill appear) from which Fishermen were enabled to take Fish with Nets of that Length, which Weirs being destroyed, and the Width of the River consider-abty increased, that Regulation with respect to the Length of Nets has never since been observed, but Nets of several Lengths have been used, in Proportion to the Breadth of the River at the several Fishing Draughts, which Breadth at the Time of Tides, is, in the narrowell Parts, about as wide again as the Length, of 60 Yards, and, in many Places, Four Times as wide; and that Nets cannot be put in directly ncross the River, but are drove by the Current obliquely down, and thrown out of Boats rowed with Oars, which cannot reach within a considerable Distance of the opposite Bank; and that for Three or Four Days, upon the Height of the Spring Tides, Fishermen are prevented from fishing, at lean Three Hours, during the Flow and Return of the Tides, and in Times of Floods, which happen frequently every Year, they cannot fish at all, and, in general, for Four Days or more in the Neap Tide in the Spring of the Year they lish only in the Night; and that the Tides do not flow with any considerable Head but very little higher up than Tewkesbury, about 10 Miles above Gloucester, and the Fishing is therefore interrupted (if at all) but for a very short Time above that Place, and the Breadth of the River in general is much narrower and more confined above than below Gloucester Bridge, and besides, in the broader Parts above are many Shoals and Sand Banks on the Sides or in the Middle of the Rivers, which operate as natural Weirs, and have the like Efleft to oonfine the Current to a narrow Paflitge; and that, in the Months of January, February, March, April, and May, there are Lampreys and Shads, and a great Quantity of Twaits, come up the said River, Which cannot be taken by Nets with Melhes of the Dimensions limited by the said Acts; and that, by Two Acts, passed in the First Year of King George the First, and the Thirty-third of King George the Second, for the Preservation of Salmon, and of the Spawn and Fry of Fish, proper Penalties and Modes of Conviction for setting up any Bank, Dam, Hedge, or Net, across any River, or any Part thereof and for destroying, having ip Possession, or exposing to Sale, any unfizeable or unseasonable Fish, or any Spawn or Fry of Fish, are difiefted and appointed; and further fettingibrth, that a Bill is depending in the House, for preserving the Salmon and other Fish within the Rivers Severn and Verniew, by which Bill so much of the said Act of King Charles the Second, as relates to the Punishment of Pterions unlawfully destroying Fish, or the Spawn or Fry of Fish, in the said River Severn, within the Limits of the said Act, is intended to be repealed, and a great Destruction of the Fry of Salmon is intended to be allowed, which Fry, if permitted to go down to Salt Water, would, in Three Months, return of a considerable Siae, but the Length of Net and Size of the Melhes . are avowedly intended to be restrained, as by the Acts of the First of Queen Elizabeth, and the Thirtieth of King Charles the Second, although the Weirs below Gloucester Bridge are destroyed and the River widened, and although no Lampreys, nor any Shad or Twait,

but of the largest Size, can (during the said Months, when only they come up the River be taken

'by Melhes of that Dimepfion, and fishing by Night ,18

is also thereby intended to be totally reftrafeed, although the Tide flows at different Times Twice in every 24 Hours; and that, by the said Bill, new Offences are intended to be created, new Regulations and Restrictions made, and new unreasonable and oppressive Powers and Penalties unnecessarily given; the Whole therefore of the said Bill, if it should pass into a Law, would be highly injurious, and indeed almost totally destructive, to the Fisheries of many of the Proprietors, from the Mouth of the River Severn up to Gloucester Bridge, who would thereby be deprived of great Part of their private Property, without any Compensation for the fame, or any public Utility; and the Inhabitants of the Cities of Bristol, Bath, and Gloucester, and the neighbouring Counties of Gloucester, Somer-J'et, Hereford, and Monmouth, and the Public in general, would lose a great Supply of Fish in the higbeft and bell Perfection, as being nearest to the Sear And therefore praying, That the said Bill, intituled, w A " Bill for preserving the Salmon and other Fish, within " the Rivers Severn and Ve," may not pals into a Law, and that the Petitioners may be heard by their Counsel against the said Bill.

A Petition of the Malter, Wardens, and Commonalty, of the Society of Merchants Venturers, of the City of Bristol, under their Common Seal, was presented to the House, and read; taking Notice of the Bill to enable the Corporation of Trinity House of Deptford Stroud, to establish and maintain a Lighthouse on the Rocks called 11 ic Smalls, in S George’s Channel; and

letting forth. That the Petitioners, in the Year 1775, expressed to the House their Doubt, and Experience

since increases that Doubt, whether a Lighthouse can be supported on the said Rocks; but if the said Corporation can prove, to the Satisf.dion of the House, that they can support such a Light, the Petitioners apprehend it may prove ufoful to Ships and Vessels passing between ttye Port of and Ireland, or to

the Northward of the said Rocks; but they conceive, that nothing less than lhcwing Three Lights will be sufficient to distinguish such Light from other Lights; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that the Proof to be laid before the House, of the Practicability of maintaining such Light, ought to be very strong and substantial, as a temporary Exhibition of a Light is delusive, and worse than no Light, and may prove fatal to the Lives and Property -of 11 is Majesty’s Subjects; and that the Tract of Ships and YelK ts, coming from the Well ward, Southward, or Eafi.yard; to thdPort of Bristol, dogs not lie within View of the said Light, for which lleafon the Pet itioners conceive, that such Ships ought not to be subject to any Duty; And therefore praying, That, if it shall appear reaion-able to the House to grant the Petition of the Corporation of Trinity House, that no Ships or Vessels coming to, or going from, t|iis Port, except fuel) as go to, or come from, Ireland, and such as go to the Northward of the said Light, may be charged with the Duties to be imposed for the Maintenance thereof; that such Duties may be reasonable, and chargeable only whillt the said Lights are well maintained; and that the same may not be made perpetual, but be totally annihilated, in case the Lighthouse iliould be destroyed.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the said Bill be read a Second Time.

Gener*l Mr. Frederick Montagu reported from the Comtnit-I^u tee, who were appointed to inspect the Progress made ihsJuUfM by the several Persons appointed to make a General Index to the Journals of this House; and to report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House; That the Committee had inspectedthe some accordingly, and had come to several Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; a^d afterwards delivered it in.at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

In order to inform themselves what Steps had been taken, and Proceedings formerly had, upon this Sub-Jett, your Committee read over the Two Reports, which were made to the House on the 13 th and 22d of May: 1776, from " the Committee who were appointed to inspect the Progress that had been made " by the several Persons appointed, by Mr. Speaker, " to make a General Index to the Journals of this House, and to report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the iloule;" and from" the Committee " who were appointed to consider of a Method of com-* pleting the General Index to the Journals of this " House, and to appoint proner Persons for executing " the fame, and who were inliructed to consider what " further Recompence should be made to the Persons " who have been employed to make the said General " Index, over and above what they have already re- ( " ceived, and to report the fame, with their Opinion " thereupon, to the House;" and which are entered in the Journals of the House.

Your Committeethen called before them Mr. Edward Moore, the Reverend Mr. the Reverend Dr.

Flexman, and Mr. Cunninghame, being the several Persons who have been employed in making the said Index; and Mr. Moore informed your Committee, That his Part of the Index (which comprehends the Period from ill George the Firli to 14th George the Third, and is contained in 17 Volumes of the printed Journals) is completely ready for the" Press; that he has been employed in it from May 1765 to this Time, and that he has received £.1,700 on Account. — Mr. Moore then delivered in a Paper, in which he dated, that if he were to be paid by the Year, he supposed he should be entitled to £.6,250, over and above the £.1,700 be had already received; but, if it should be thought more proper that he should be paid by the Volume, it would then come to £.6,400, over and above the Ibid.£.1,700; which he underilands to be in full of all Demands.

The Reverend Mr. Forjler also informed your Committee, That his Part of the Index (which comprehends a Period from the 9th of William the Third to the 13th of Anne, and is contained in 6 Volumes of the printed Journals) is ready for the press; that he had been engaged in that Employment ever since July 177 x to this Time, and has received £.740 upon Account; and that he experts £.2,860, over and above the said £.740; which he underilands to be in full Discharge for what he has done, and for his Labour for One Year to come. Mr. Forjler also mentioned several Circumstances to your Committee, why his Labour should not be merely rated by the Number of printed Volumes on which he had been employed.

Dr. Flexman being then examined, informed your Committee, That his Part (comprehending a Period from the 12th Charles the Second to 9th William the Third, contained in Volumes of the printed Journals) is ready for the Press; that he has been employed in this Work from the First Week in May 1770 to this Time; and he delivered in a Paper, in which he expressed his Hopes, that he might be allowed at the Rate of £.300 per Annum for the 8 Years You 36.

Attendance he has given, and the Pains he has1 taken in this Work.

And it appeared to your Committee, on the Inspec* ♦ion of the several Parts that had been assigned to Mr. Moore, Mr. Forjler, and Dr. Flexman, that their Indexes for those Periods were finished, and ready for the Press.

Mr. Cunninghame being then called, said, He has made a great Progress in the Part which was assigned to him (which is the Period from the ill Edward the Sixth to the 10th Charles the Second, and is contained in 7 Volumes of the printed Journals) but that it is not yet ready for the Press, owing to the greater Quantity of Matter contained in his Part of the Work, when compared with the like Number of Volumes in any other Period; that he has been employed since July 1771, has received £.700 on Account; that he should expert for his whole Work, when completed, £.7,900, including the laid£.700. And being asked, in what Time he would undertake to complete his Part ? he said, In One Year and an Half.

As your Committee supposed it will be thought proper, by the House, to direct those Indexes which are already completed and ready foT the Ppefsto be printed, that is, Mr. Moore's, Mr. Forjland Dr. Flexman's, in order to form some Judgment of the Expence that will attend this Work, they called in and examined Mr. Hughs, the printer to the House, and who has for several Years been employed in printing the Journals, and the' Indexes to the Journals; and he informed your Committee, That he imagined the Printing of the said Index will coll a Sum not exceeding £.4 a Sheet, if 1,500 Copies are printed; and that he thought the Printing those Parts which are ready for the Press, could be finished by the Beginning of the Year 1779.

And Mr. Strahan, Junior, Printer, who was also examined, informed your Committee, That the Print-' ing such a Number of Copies would, in his Opinion, coli between Four and Five Pounds a Sheet; and he thought it might be printed by January next.

Upon the whole Matter, your Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Mr. Moore is deserving^over and above £1.700, which he has already received, of a further Sum of £.6,400, as a final Compensation for his Pains, Trouble, and Expence, in having, compiled a General Index to the Journals of the House of Commons, from 1765 to January 1779.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee That Mr. Forjler is deferring, over and above £.740, which he has already received, of a further Sum of £.3,000, as a final Compensation for his Pains, Trouble, and Expence, in having compiled a General Index to the Journals of the House of Commons, from; July 1771 to ill January 1779.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Dr.. Flexman is deserving of, over and above £.850, which he has already received, the further Sum of £.3,000, as a final Compensation for his Pains,. Trouble, and Expence, in having compiled a General Index to the Journals of the House of Commons, from 1770 to 1779.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Mr. Cunninghame is deferring of £.500 on Account.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the General Indexes to the Journals of this House, compiled by Mr. Edward Moore, the Reverend Mr. Forjler, and the Reverend Dr. , be-

printed by the Person usually employed in printing the Journals of this House, under the Care and Inspection of the several Persons who have compiled the fame.

A Petition of the Merchant s, Traders, and Inhabitants, w-ithin the Hundred of Kirton, in the Parts of Holland, in the County of Lincoln, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; taking.

Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That the said Act has been found to be of the greatest Utility to the several Par ilhes therein mentioned, by enablingmany industrious labouring People to obtain Credit for the Necessaries of Life, which , before they wrere unable to do, from the Difficulty Creditors lay under in recovering firiall Sums of Money due to them; and that the Commissioners, appointed by the said Act, have Power and Authority to ofder and decree the Debts sued for-by Creditors to be paid to them by the respective Debtors, either altogether, or at several Payments, as they lha.ll judge necessary, for the Ease and Convenience of such Debtors; and that the Petitioners are informed, that the Commissioners have, pursuant to the aforesaid Power, ordered and decreed a great Number of Credit tors to be paid their Debts at future Days, and; in case the said Act is repealed, that such Creditors will be then debarred from receiving the fame; and that the Petitioners are informed, that filing for Small Debts in die Court of Pleas claimed by the Earl of Exeter is attended frequently with great Delay and Expence; and that the said Court of Pleas hath not of late Years been, held so frequently as the Petitioners conceive to be necessary for the Recovery of such Debts as are provided for by the said Act; and that Application w’as made to the House, to obtain the said Act, in the Year 1776; and that, in the last Session of Parliament, the Petition for the said Act was presented to the House on the 1 oth of February, and the Act did not pass both Houses until the 27th of May following, and the Petition was of public Notoriety to the Inhabitants of the several Parishes included in the said Act; and the said Act has been attended with many salutary Effects, and will, as the Petitioners apprehend, be of general Utility to the several Parishes therein mentioned: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the Repeal of the said Act, and have such Relief in the Premisee as to the House shall appear proper and expedient.

A Petition of several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Proprietors, on Behalf of themselves and other Proprietors of, and Persons interfiled in, the Fisheries in the River Severn, below Gloucester Bridge, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by Two Acts, passed in the First Year of Quetn Elizabeth, and the Thirtieth of King Charles the Second, the Length of Nets to be used for Fishing in the River Severn, below Bridge, is

limited to Sixty Yards, and above Bridge to

Fifty Yards, and the Size of the Melhes to be Ten Inches round, or Two Inches and an Half, from Knot to Knot; and that, at the Time of passing the said Acts, there were many Weirs in the said River below Gloucester Bridge (the Remains whereof ltill appear) from which Fiibermen were enabled to take Fish with Nets of that Length, which Weirs beingdestroyed, the Regulation with respect to the Length of the Nets has never since been observed, but Nets of several Lengths have been used, in Proportion to the Breadth of the River at the several Fishing Draughts, which Breadth, at the Time of Tides (which flow Twice a Day) is, in the narrowed Parts, about as wide again as the Length of Sixty Yards, and, in many Places, Four Times as wide; and that Nets cannot be put in directly across the River, but are drove by the Current obliquely down, and throvyn out of Boats rowed with Oars, which cannot reach within Six or Seven Yards of the opposite Bank; and that for Three or Four Days, upon the Height of the Spring Tides, Fiibermen are prevented from Fishing, for at lead Three Hours, during the Flow and Return of the Tide, and in Times of Floods, which happen frequently every Year, they cannot fish at all, and in general, for Four Days or more in the Neap Tides in the Spring of the Year, they fish only in the Night; and that the Tides do not flow with any considerable Head but very little higher up than bury, about Ten Miles above Gloucester, and the Fishing is therefore interrupted but for a very short Time, and the Breadth of the River, in general, is much narrower and confined above than below Gloucester Bridge, and, besides, in the broader Parts above, there are many Shoals and Sand Banks on the Sides, or in the Middle of the River, which operate as natural Weirs, and have the like Effect to confine the Current to a narrow Pass; and that, in the Months of January, Februan/, March, April, and May, there are Lampreys and Shads, and a great Quantity of Twaits, come- up the said River, which cannot be taken by Nets with Melhes of the Dimensions limited by the said Acts; and that, by Two Acts, passed in the First Year of Kin the

First, and the Thirty third of King George the Second, Vol. 36.

for the PreferVation of Salmon, and of the {spawn and Fry of Fish, proper Penalties and Modes of Com ic* tion, for setting up any Bank, Dam, Hedge, or Net; across any River, or any Part (hereof, and for destroy* ing, having in Possession, or ex poling to Sale, any un-sizeable or unseasonable Fish, or any Spawn or Fry of Fill), are directed and appointed; and further setting forth; That a Bill is depending in the HoUfe, for preserving the Salmon and other Fish within the Rivers Severn and VemiezC, by which Bill, so much of the Act of the Thirtieth of King Charles the Second, as relates! to the Punishment of Persons unlawfully destroying Fish, or the Spawn or Fry of Fish, in the said River Severn, within the Limits of the said Act, is intended to be repealed, and a great Destruction of the try of Salmon is intended to be allowed, which, if permitted to go down into the Salt Water, would, in Three Months, return of a considerable Size; but the Length of the Net, and the Size of the Melhes, are avowedl/ intended to be restrained, as by the Acts of the First of Queen Elizabeth, and the Thirtieth of King Charles the Second, although the Weirs below Gloucester Bridge are destroyed, and although no Lampreys, nor any Shad or Twaits, but of the largest Size, can (during the said Months, when they only come up the Rivet* Severn)be taken by Melhes of that Dimension, and fithing by Night isalfo thereby intended to be totally restrained, although the Tide flows at different Times Twice in every Twenty-four Hours; and that, by the said Bill, new Offences are intended to be created, new Regulations made, and newunreasonable and oppressive Powers and Penalties unnecessarily given; the Whole; therefore, of the said Bill, if it should pass into a Law, would be highly injurious, and indeed almost totally destructive to some of the Fisheries of some of the Proprietors, from the Mouth of the River Severn to Gloucester Bridge (an Extent of Forty Miles or up4 wards) who would thereby be deprived of great Part of their private Property, and the Cities of Bristol and Gloucester, and the Public in general, would lol'e a great Supply of Fish in the highest Perfection, as being nearer the Sea; and therefore a Petition hath been presented to the House by several Persons being Proprietors of, or Persons interested in, the Fisheries in tl)e River Severn, below. Gloucester Bridge, on behalf of themselves and others, for Leave to bring in a Bill for repealing so much of the said Acts of Queen,

and of the Thirtieth of King Charles the Second, as relates to the Length of the Nets, and Size of the Melhes, to be used below Gloucester, which Bill hath been since presented for that Purpose, and for allowing a further reasonable Length of Net, and a Temporary Diminution of the Melhes: And therefore praying, That the said Bill, intituled, " A Bill for preferring the " Salmon and other Fill), w ithin the Rivers Severn and " Vernieio," may not pass into a Law, and that the Petitioners may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for more effectually preferring the Salmon, and other Fish, within the Rivers Severn and Fernievo, be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard by their Counsel against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

A Petition of the Governor, Bailiffs, and Commonalty, of the Company of Conservators of the Great Level of the Fens, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are Owners of a considerable Tra6t of Low Lands, containing upwards of 80,000 Acres, lying within lho Limits of the Bedford Level, as described by an Act of the Fifteenth of Charles the Second, for settling the Draining of the Great Level of the Fens, called Bedford Level-, and that the same were, together with 190,000 Acres contiguous thereto, and lying intermixed with the fame, recovered from a drowned Stale by the Petitioners Predecessors, by their adventuring ;uid laying out large Sums thereon, and have beenfinee preserved, as. effectually as the Situation thereof would permit, by a constant Annual Expence, the Fund for which are Taxes laid on the Petitioners Lands; and that the said Lands are, from their Nature, particularly fit for the Culture of Oats, and large Quantities are annually produced therefrom, every Check to which, is a tna-nifeft Injury to the Petitioners* as thereby the Value of the said Land is decreased, the Charges arising for the Preservation and Culture still remaining the same; and that, by the Provisions in the several Acts of Parliament now in Force, by which the opening the Ports for the Importation of Oats of Foreign Growth is regulated, the Interests of the Petitioners are much aft* feefed, inso much that, when their Tenants have great Quantities of Oats to fell, towards the Supply of the London and other Markets, at reasonable Rates, the Ports are opened for the Importation of Oats of Foreign Growth, whereby the Price of Oats grown in the Low Lands herein set forth is, from the Markets being overstocked, so reduced, that their Tenants are thereby greatly distressed, their Landed Interest much affected; and which Mischiefs, if some Remedy be not found therefore, may, in a Course of Time, put an End to the Culture of so necessary and valuable a Commodity in the Low Land.s, and leave these Kingdoms too much in the Power of Foreign Imports for supplying the fame: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration, and give such Relief therein, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Petition.

That in the said Bill, it is stipulated, that fishing in the said Rivers shall be confined to the Daytime only; and that so much of an Act, passed in the Thirtieth Year of King Charles the‘Second, for Preservation of Fishing in the River Severn, as relates to the Pilnishment df Persons destroying Fish, or the Spawn or Fry of Fish, in the said River, within ffie Limits in the said Act mentioned, is, by the said Bill, intended to be repealed; and that great Quantities of Spawn of Salmon, called Samlets, are taken and destroyed by Angling and laying of Lines in the said River, which Practice will be authorized by the said Bill; and that Fishermen cannot carry on their Occupations in the said River, unlefis they are permitted to fish at the Flow of every Tide, which happens Twice, with a Variation as to Time, in every Twenty-four Hours; and that there are other Parts of the said Bill, which the Petitioners apprehend are oppressive, and likewise unnecessary: And therefore praying, That they may be heard by themselves, or Counsel, against the Whole of the said Bill.

A Petition of several Persons residing near the River Severn, and interested in the Fishqj’ies therein below Gloucester Bridge, was also presented to the House, and read; likewise taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, in the Preamble thereof, the only greatPublic Utility thereby avowed is to extend the Powers and Provisions of an Act of the Thirt ieth of King Charles the Second, Tor Preservation of Fishing in fjjpe River Severn, with rofpeft to the length of Nets, and Size of Meshes, to Inch Parts of that River as lie in the Counties of Stafford and Montgomery, and in the Counties of the Cities of Gloucester and H'orcester, (Two Places generally covered with Coal Barges) all which Places must be included within the River Severn wherever it runs; and also for extending the same Provisions to the River Verniew, which runs into the River Severn (at or very near the Head thereof) a Length of about 150 Miles Distance from the Entrance or Mouth of the Severn, and where the Regulation of Nets and Meflies directed by the said Act cannot operate to any Effect, nor can bewanted, as there are general Laws already for Punish-inent of other Offences, by taking or destroying the Spawn or F ry of Fish; and that, for these Objects so avowed, the Petitioners observe, that, by the said Bill, ihe Provisions in the said Act of the Thirtieth of Charles the Second, for Punishment of Persons destroying the Spawn and Fry of Fish, is repealed, but the Regulations of the Length of Nets and Meshes, used below Gloucester Bridge, are enforced, although, from absolute Necessity, the Length of Nets, and (in the Mouths of February, March, April, and May, when ’Lampreys, Twaits, and Shads, come up the River) the Size of the Melhes also have never been observed, nor ever can be observed, in those Months, if those Species of Fish are to be taken, Which must be done with Meflies -not larger than Five Inches and an Half round; and that, by the said Bill, it is intended to take away the greatefr Part, and, in some ‘Instances, the Whole, of private Property in Fisheries below Gloucester Bridge, quite down to the Sea, an Extent of above 50 Miles; videlicet, First, by prohibiting totally the Putt Fisheries, and by limiting the Size of Pouchins, and consequently the ‘Quantity of Eels to be taken; Secondly, by prohibiting Fishing, unless from Sun-rising to Sun-setting, though very few Fish can be taken in the Day-time, in Proportion to the Night; Thirdly, by prohibiting Fishing by Day and Night for Three Months (March, April, and May) the moll valuable Season for Fishing, and Three of those Four Months, in which only the Lampreys, Shads, and Twaits, come up the River, though there are already by Law Three Fence Months and

'(Jcldber) besides in the Year; Fourthly, by prohibiting taking Elvers (the Brood of Eels) which come up the River in the said Three Months of March, April, and May, m inwnenfe Quantities, though, if they were not taken, they would dellroy the Spawn and Fry of other Fish, and Lamperns in particular; and though Elvers and Lamperns are the great Support of the neighbouring Poor; but, indeed (as Religion is often a Cloak for Injustice) Fishing is proposed by the Bill to be prohibited 011 Sundays, that all Persons may attend to the YVxxrfli ip of Almighty God, which Regulation (if not already observed elsewhere) is observed below the Bridge, in the County of Gloucester: And therefore praying, That the said Bill, so injurious to privatePro-perty, and whereby no public Good cun be proposed or obtained, may notpafs into a Law.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Common Council, of the City of Bath, in Common Council assembled, under their Common Seal, was also presented to the House, and read; likewise taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth. That it is intended thereby to rest rain Persons from using Nets in any Part of the River Severn but of certain Dimensions; from fixing or laying Putts in the same River, and from taking Salmon therein, between certain Days in the Months of March and May, and of July and November; and that the Markets for Fish in the City of Bath are supplied with Salmon and other Fish by the Fisheries in the River Severn, and great Quantities of fine feasonable Salmon are usually brought to the said Markets in the Months wherein those Fisheries are, by the said Bill, intended to be restrained; and that large Quantities of Plaise, Flounders, Soles, Whitings, Herrings, Sprats, Eels, Tumblin, and Shrimps, are taken in the River Severn, below a certain Weir* called Hock Cribb, otherwise Hook Cribb, in the Parish of Frethem, in the County of Gloucester, and from Time immemorial have been so taken, of a proper Size (and without destroying the Spawn) by Putts; and, from the Nature of the River, such Fisheries cannot be carried on, so as to afford an ample Supply to the Markets, in any other Manner; nor can Salmon be taken in large Quantities below the said Weir, but by Nets of a peculiar Construction, and of different Dimensions from those intended by the said Bill; and therefore, should the same pass into a Law in its present Form, the usual Supply of Fish would be much lessened, to the greajt and manifest Injury of the Inhabitants of the said City, and the Nobility and Gentry who resort thereto: And therefore praying. That the Provisions of the said Bill may not extend to the Fisheries in that Part of the said River Severn which lies below the said Weir or Place called Hock otherwise Hook Cribb, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises as shall be thought just and reasonable.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Sheriffs, and Common Council, of the Gity of Gloucester, in Council assembled, being Proprietors, on behalf of themselves, and other Proprietors of Fisheries in the River Severn, below G loucester Bridge, was al so prefen ted to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Fisheries in the River Severn, below Gloucester Bridge, quite down from the Coal Wharfs within the City of Gloucester, to the Mouth of the said River into the Sea, an Extent t>f 40 or 50 Miles, are private Property, and as such have been immemorially held and enjoyed by the Proprietors and Owners thereof, and their Tenants; and that great Quantities of Fish come up the said River, and afford a great ‘Supply to the Inhabitants of the adjacent Places, and the Public in general; and that, by Two Acts, passed in the First Year of Queen Elizabeth, and the Thirtieth of King Charles the Second, the Length of Nets, to be used for fishing in the River Severn below Gloucester Bridge, is limited to 60 Yards, and above Gloucester Bridge, where there is no private Property, to 50 Yards, and the Size -of the Meflies is limited to Ten Inches round, or Two Inches and an Half from Knot to Knot; and that at the Time of passing the said Acts, there were many Weirs in the said River below Gloucester Bridge (the Remains whereof still appear) from which Fishermen were enabled -to take Fish with Nets of that Length,; which Weirs being destroyed, and the Width of the River considerably increased, that Regulation with respect to the Length of Nets has never fiuce been observed, but Nets of several Lengths have been used, in Proportion to the Breadth of the River, at the several Fishing Draughts, winch Breadth at the Time of Tides is in the narrowest Parts about as wide again as -the Length of Sixty Yards, and m many Places Four Times as wide; and that

Nets cannot be put in across the River, but are drove by the Current obliquely down, and thrown out of Boats rowed with Oars, which cannot reach within a considerable Distance of the opposite Bank; and that for Three or Four Days, upon the Height of the Spring Tides, Fishermen are prevented from fishing for at lead Thi ee Hours during the Flow and Return of the Tides, and in Times of Floods, which happen frequently every Year, they cannot fish at act, and in general for Four Days or more in the Neap Tide, in the Spring of the Year, they fish only in the Night} and that the Tides do not flow with any considerable Head, but very little higher up than Tewkesbury, about Ten Miles above Gloucester, and the Fishing is therefore interrupted (if at all) but for a very short Time above that Place, and the Breadth of the River in general is much narrower, and more confined, above than below Gloucester Bridge, and, besides, in the broader Parts above, there arc many Shoals and Sand Banks on the Sides, or in the Middle, of the River, which operate as natural Weirs, and have the like Effect to confine the Current to a narrow Passage; and that in the Months of January, February, March, April, and there are Lampreys and Shad*, and great Quantities of Twaits, come up the said River, which cannot be taken by Nets with Meshes of the Dimensions limited by the saidA&s; and that by Two Acts, passed in the First Year of King George the First, and the Thirty-third of King George the Second, for the Preservation of Salmon, and of the Spawn and Fry of Fish, proper Penalties and Modes of Conviction, for setting up any Bank, Dam, Hedge, or Net, across any River, or any Part thereof, and for destroying, having in PofiefBon, or exposing to Sale, any unfizeable or unseasonable Fish, or any Spawn or Fry of Fish, are directed and appointed; and further setting forth. That a Bill is depending in the House, for preserving the Salmon and other Fish within the Rivers Severn and Verniezv, by which Bill so much of the said Act of King Charles the Second, as relates to the Punishment of Persons unlawfully destroying Fish, or the Spawn or Fry of Fish, in the said River Severn, within the Limits of the said Act, is intended to be repealed, and a great. Deliru6tion of the Fry of Salmon is intended to be allow ed; which Fry, if permitted to go down to Salt Water, would, in Three Months, return of a considerable Size; but the length of Net and Size of the Meshes are avowedly intended to be restrained, as by the Acts of the First of Queen Elizabeth, and the Thirtieth of K'ingCharles the Second, although the Weirs below Gloucester Bridge are destroyed, and the River widened, and although no Lampreys, nor any Shad or Twait, but of the largest Size, can (during the said Months, when only they come up the River Severn) be taken by Meshes of that Dimension; and fishing by Night is also thereby intended to be totally restrained, although the Tide flows, at different Times, Twice in every Twenty-four Hours; and that, by the said Bill, new Offences are intended to be created, new Regulations and Re-ftri6lions made, and new unreasonable and oppressive Powers and Penalties unnecessarily given; the Whole therefore, of the said Bill, if it should pass into a Law, would be highly injurious, and indeed almost totally destructive, -to the Fisheries of many of the . Proprietors, from the Mouth of the River , up to Gloucester Bridge, who would thereby be deprived of great Part of their private Property, without any Compensation for the fame, or any public Utility; and the Inhabitants of the Cities of , and

A Petition of the (gentlemen, Clergy, and principal S*m« Inhabitants, of the City of Glouc, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; taking Notice of the Bill for repealing so much of Two Acts, passed in the First Year of Queen Elizabeth, and Thirtieth Year of King Charles the Second, as relates to the Size of the Meshes of Nets, and to the Length of the Nets, to be used in the River Severn, below Gloucester Bridge, and for better regulating the Fisheries, and preserving the Spawn and Fry of Fish, in the said River; and Setting forth.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Montagu and Mr. Leeds:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act Commirnonen to enable His Majesty to appoint Commissioners, with

sufficient Powers, to treat, consult, and agree, upon America, the Means of quieting the Disorders now subsisting in certain of the Colonies, Plantations, and Provinces, of North America; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act American for removing all Doubts and Apprehensions concerning Declaratory Taxation, by the Parliament of Great Britain, in any Bl of the Colonies, Provinces, and Plantations, in North America and the West Indies;and for repealing so much of an Act, made in the Seventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, as imposes a Duty on Tea imported from Great Britain into any Colony or Plantation in America, or relates thereto; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act Massachuset’s for repealing an Act, passed in the Fourteenth Year of r Bay His present Majesty’s Reign, intituled, "An Act for 0 ernn,e " the better regulating the Government of the Province of the Massachuset's Bay, in New England;" without any Amendment.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

A Petition of the Trullees appointed to carry into execution a certain Act of Parliament, for enlarging the Term and Powers of an Act, made in the Twenty-ninth Year of his late Majesty King George the Second, for making a Road from the East Side of the Parish of Saint Matthew Bethnal Green, in the County of J'e.r, to the East End of Church Street, and to open a Way into Shoreditch, and for repairing, paving, and regulating. Old Cock Lane, Neiv Cock Lane, Church Street, and the Road on the West Side of the Opening into Shoreditch, and for removing Nuisances and Obstructions therefrom, and preventing the same for the future, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by an Act, passed in the Seventh Lear of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for " completing the Bridge cross the River from

" Binckfriars, in the City of London, to the opposite

" Side, in the County of Surrey, and the Avenues " thereto on the London Side; for redeeming the Tolls " on the said Bridge, and on London Bridgefor rebuilding the Gaol of Newgale, in the said City; for " repairing the Royal Exchange, within the same; for " embanking Part of the North Side of the said River, " within certain Limits; and for further continuing, " towards those Purposes, the Imposition of Six Pence " per Chaldron or Ton of Coals or Culm imported " into the Port of the said City, established by an Act " of the Fifth and Sixth Years of the Reign of King " William and Queen Mary-, and also for carrying on " the new Pavements in the City and Liberties of Westminster, and Parishes adjacent, and in the Town and

" Borough of Southwark; and for other Purposes " therein mentioned," the Sum of £. 156,000 was allowed to be borrowed, for the Purpose of carrying on the several Public Works therein mentioned; and, in order to establish a Fund for the repaying of such Sum, the Duties on Coals and Culm imported into the Port of London were further continued to 1831;

and further Setting forth, That it appears, by the Votes, that the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, have petitioned for Power tfi raise a further considerable Sum of Money, upon the Credit of the Surplusses to arise from the said Fund charged on the Duties on Coals and Culm, to be applied in completing the rebuilding of Newgate, building a Sessions House, and doing other public Business, alleging, that the whole Debt charged upon the Coal Duties will nevertheless be paid oft’ long before the Time allowed by the said Act of the Seventh Year of His present Majesty; and that, after the Appropriation of the Sum of £. 40,000 to the Uses pray'ed by the Petition of the said City of London (if the House shall think proper to comply with the fame) there will still remain a considerable Surplus arising out

of the said Fund; and that, by* virtue of the Acts of Parliament for which the Petitioners are Trustees as aforesaid, they have paved the Streets and Places in the Parish of Saint Matthew Bethnal Green, in the County' of Middlesex, therein mentioned, and such

Streets and Places are now in great Want of Re-paving, which will be attended with a large Expence, and when re-paved will be very beneficial to the Public; but that the Petitioners have not Money fuftieient to defray the Expence of carrying into execution, and completing, the said useful Purposes; and that a considerable Part of the Duty on Coals arises from the Consumption of that Article within the Limits of the Places so to be re-paved as aforesaid, and consequently the Duty thereof is paid by the Inhabitants there, who at present are burthened with numerous Taxes, more than they' can well bear: And therefore praying, That a fuftieient Part of the Surplus to arise out of the aforesaid Fund, after Payment of the Monies already charged thereon, may be applied in Aid of the Purposes for which the Petitioners are Trustees as aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Alderman Wilkes, Sir Herbert Mackworth, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Nicholas Walton, being examined, said, That the said Commissioners and Governors are Owners of certain Messuages, Lands, Tenements, Tythes, and Hereditaments, situate in the Parishes of and

Warkworth, in the County of Northumberland., which are inconveniently fituuted with respe' l to their other Estates; but. that they are very convenient to the Ef-tates of his Grace the Duke of Northumberland, who is willing to exchange Part of his Lands at for the fame, which Exchange will be for the mutual Advantage of both Parties. Then,

An" Act, passed in the Eighth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, intituled, "An Act for the Application " of the Rents and Profits of the Estates forfeited by the Attainders of James late Earl, of Derwentzo " and Charles Raddijfe" was produced, and read; whereby it is enacted, That the said Commissioners and Governors should give Six Months public Notice in the London Gazette, for letting the said Eftat.es; and that no Clause should be inserted in the Leases, giving Power to the Lessees to commit Waste.

And another Act, passed in the Eleventh Year of his said late Majesty, for explaining the last mentioned Act, was also read; reciting the said Act, and also reciting. That there were many Mines of Lead, Coal, and other Minerals, under the said Estates, which would probably^ turn to great Profit to the said Hospital; but as the Working the same might be deemed to be committing Waste within the Meaning of the former Act, a Power was given to His Majesty (in whom the Eliates then were) to authorize the Commissioners and Governors of the said Hospital, to demise and grant all and every of such Mines and Minerals, so'r any Number of Years not exceeding Twenty-one, reserving the bell Rents that could be rcnfonably gotten for the fame. Then Mr. Nicholas Walton, being examined, said. That it would be of great Advantage to have the above Restrictions taken o(F, because, otherwise, the several Lessees would only carry on such Works as were necessary during the Continuance of their respective Leases; whereas, in case the Commissioners and Governors of the said Hospital were enabled to grant Leases without advertising, they would not only have it in their Power by that Means to give such due Encouragement as will induce the several Adventurers to expend larger Sums of Money, to render their Undertakings more permanent and complete, but it will be a certain Means of bringing all Discoveries to light. And he further said, That there are Lands so connected with the Mines, that it will be very inconvenient that they should be in the Occupation of different Tenants; for it is necessary that the Persons occupying the Mines, should have such a Quantity of Land with them as will be sufficient to maintain the Horses and Cattle necessary for carrying on the said Works.

A Petition of several Owners of Fisheries in the River Severn below the Hook Crib, situate in the Parish of Frethern, in the County of Gloucester, on behalf of themselves and many others alike circum-staneed, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners are seised in Fee, or of some other good Estate, in divers Rocks^ Weirs, Shoals, and Slimes, in the said River; in the Parishes of Henbuf-y, Reilicick, and Northivick, Aujt, Littleton upon Severn, ThornburyOldbury upon Severn,

Rockhampton Hill, and Berkeley, in the County of Gloucester, in which, from Time immemorial, they have Cxerciied the foie Right of taking at all Times, by certain Methods called Putts, all manner of Fish usually taken in the said River; and that the Petitioners apprehend, the Two Bills now before the House, re-fpoding the Fisheries in the said River, if passed into . Laws in the present Foi*m, will prove greatly injurious to the Petitioners in particular, and to the Public ih general; for that One of the said Bills will, as they apprehend, entirely deprive the Petitioners of such Mode of Fishing, and of the Benefit of their said several Fisheries, as there can be no other Way of catching Fish in those Places; and by the other Bill, the Petitioners apprehend, their Property will be greatly lessened, by the proposed Restraint in the Months of March and April; and that the said Bills will, in their Effects, distress great Numbers who are now supplied from thence with Fish by the above Mode of Fishing only, as all other Methods will there prove ineffectual: And therefore praying. That the Provisions in the said Bills, or either of them, if passed into Laws, may not extend below the Hook Crib aforesaid, or that the House will yield the Petitioners such Relief as may seem meet.

Prayers.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Merchants, Traders, and others, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are impressed with the deepelt concern, on perceiving that the War in which we have for Three Years been involved with our Brethren in North America, has been attended with Successes from which we derived no Advantage, and Disasters which admit of no Remedy; that, in the present miserable and uncertain State of our Affairs, the only Circumstances of which we have no Doubt are. Burthens intolerable, and impending Ruin; that it is no longer from any speculative Opinions we had formed of the Rights of either Party in this unhappy Dispute, or of the Nature and Extent of their respective Resources, that we are led to condemn the Cause or Conduct of this War, since it now stands con-sessed, that the very Authors of it themselves, convinced of the Error or Impracticability of their Measures, have abandoned the Objects which first gave Rife to the Contell, and appear anxious to conciliate the Enemy they affected to despise; that the Petitioners are too felicitous for the Reltoration of Peace, on any Terms which will insure the permanent Happiness of the Two Countries, not to rejoice at the Oiler of any Propol’als which profess that for their

Object; and they rely on the timely Care of this Honourable House, for ripening these hopeful Appearances into Fruits of lading Amity and Union; and at the same Time they lament, and, lamenting, must strongly condemn, that fatal Delay, which hath reduced this Country to the necessity of attempting to recover Half an Empire, which common Prudence might have preferred; that we have fought to subdue Provinces we had not the Wisdom to retain, and we are now negotiating to regain, by Concession, what we have not Ability to conquer by Arms; that the Petitioners give the fulled Credit, even to those by whom the Nation has been betrayed into this didress- ful Situation, for their present Repentance, whether it is the Effect of Necessity or of Conviction; but, can never forget, that, by their Misconduct, Thirteen flourishing Colonies are loft; nor can they ever be persuaded, that what remains of this disjointed Empire is safe in the Hands of Men so intemperate, so iueon-fiftent, and so incapable; finally, the Petitioners think it their Duty to re present the Apprehensions they en-

tertain, that the Concetlions now proposed may prove too weak an Inducement to a People, whole Confidence we have lorfeited, to relinquish Engagements into which they may have been driven; and to implore the House, by every motive of Duty and of Justice,.to inditute an immediate Enquiry into the Nature, the Extent, and Dates, of those Engagements, and, by a full and ntcellkry Exertion of the high Powers with which this Honourable House is inveded by the Conditution, ito pursue, in due Time, to Shame and Punidimcut, those who, by betraying the Honour of the Crown, and degrading the Character of this once glorious Nation, have justly incurred the Resentment of a dil'eredited, declining, and much injured People.

The Lord North acquainted the House, That he had a Message from His Majesty to this House, signed by His Majesty; and he presented the foihe to the House; and it was read by Mr. Speaker (all i he Members of the Hoyjfe being uncovered) and is as followeth; viz.

GEORGE R.

His Majesty, having been informed, by Order of the French King, that a Treaty of Amity and Commerce has been signed between the Court of and certain Perfopsemployed by His Majesty’s revoked Subjects in North America, has judged it necessary to direct, that a Copy of the Declaration delivered by the French Ambassador to Lord Viscount Weymouth, be laid before the House of Commons $ and at the same Time to acquaint them, that His Majesty has thought proper, in Consequence of this Oifenfive Communication of the Part of the Court of France, to fend Orders to His Ambassador to withdraw from that Court.

His Majesty \s perfpaded, that the Justice and good Faith of His Conduct towards Foreign Powers, and the Sincerity of His Wilhes to preserve the Tranquillity of Europe., will be acknowledged by all the "World; and His Majesty trusts, that he shall not stand responsible for the Disturbance of that Tranquillity, if he fhoqld find himself called upon to resent so unprovoked and so unjust an Aggression on the Honour of His Crown, and the essential Interests of His Kingdoms contrary to the most solemn Aflu ranees, subversive of the Law of Nations, and injurious to the Rights of every Sovereign Power in Europe.

His Majesty, relying with the firmed Confidence on the geaJou8 and affeClianate Support of His faithful People, is determined to be prepared to exert, if it shall become necessary, all the Force and Resources of His Kingdoms; which he.trusts will be found adequate to repel every Insult and Attack, and to maintain apd uphold, the Power and Reputation of this Country.

G. R.

The Lord North preifenfed to the House, by His Majesty’s Command,

Copy of a Paper delivered to Lord Viscount Weymouth, by the Marquis dg Noailies, the 13th March, 1778; and Translation.

And the Titles of the said Copy and Translation were read.

And the said Translation was also read The said Copy is preserved amongst the other Papers of this Session; apd the said Translation is as followeth; viz.

The underwritten Ambassador of his Most Christian Majesty has received an express Order to deliver to the Court of London the fallowing Declaration: zi

The United States -of North America, which are in foil Poftelfion of the Independence declared by their Act rof the 4th July 1776, having caused a Propofol -to be made to the King, to consolidate, by a,formal Convention, the CouneCiions that have begun to be established between the Two Nations, the respective Plenipotentiaries have signed a Treaty of Amity and Commerce, intended to serve as a Rafis for mutual good Correspondence.

His Majesty, being resolved to cultivate the good Understanding fulfilling between France and Great Britain, by all the Means compatible with his Dignity, and with the good of his Stibjects, thinks that be ought to impart this Step to the Court of,

and declare to it, at the same Time, that the contracting Parties have had Attention not to stipulate any exchifive Advantage in Favour of the French Nation; and that the United States have preserved the Liberty of treating with all Nations whatsoever, on the same Foot of Equality and Reciprocity.

In making this Communication to the Court 01 London, the King is firmly persuaded, that it will find in it fresh Proofs of I lis Majesty’s constant and fin-cere Dispositions for Peace; and that His Britannic Majesty, animated by the same Sentiments, will equally avoid ever}' Thing that may interrupt their Harmony; and that He will take, in particular, effectual Measures to hinder the Commerce of his Majesty’s Subjects with the United States of North America from being disturbed, and to cause to be observed, in this Respect, the Usages received between trading Nations, and the Rules that may be deemed fub-filling between the Crowns of France and Great Britain.

In this just Confidence, the underwritten Amhafla-dor might think it superfluous to apprize the British Ministry, that the King his Mailer, being determined effectually to protect the lawful Freedom of the Commerce of his Subjects, and to sustain the Honour of his Flag, his Majesty has taken, inconfpquence, eventual Measures, in Concert with the United States of America.

London, 13 March, 1778.

(Signed) M‘* de Noailies.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed. That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, to return His Majesty the humble Thanks of this House, for the Communication of the Paper presented to the Lord Viscount Weymouth, by the Order of the French King; and for acquainting this House, that, in consequence of this Offensive Declaration, His Majesty has thought proper to order His Ambassador to withdraw from the Court of France:

To assure His Majesty, that it is with the utmost Difficulty this House can restrain the ftrqngeft Ex-prefiions of the Resentment and Indignation which they feel for this unjust and unprovoked Aggression on the Honour of His Majesty’s Crown, and the essential Interests of His Kingdoms, contrary to the Law of Nations, and injurious to the Rights and Poflessions of every Sovereign Power in Europe.

That the good Faith and Uprightness of His Majesty’s Conduct towards Foreign Powers, and the Sincerity of His Intentions to preserve the general Tranquillity, must be acknowledged by all the World; and His Majesty cannot be considered as responsible for the Disturbance of this Tranquillity, if His Majesty should find Himself called upon to relict the Enterprizes of that reiiless and dangerous Spirit of Ambition and Aggrandizement, which has so often invaded the Rights, and threatened the Liberties, of Europe.

That we should be wanting in our Duty to His Majesty, to our ConilRuents, and to ourfehea, if we

Resolvetd, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, to return His Majesty the humble Thanks of this House, for the Communication of the Paper presented to the Lord Viscount Weymouth, by the Order of the French King; and for acquainting this House, that, in consequence of this Offensive Declaration, His Majesty has thought proper to order His Ambassador to withdraw from the Court of France:

To ashire His Majesty, that it is with the utmost Difficulty this House can restrain the strongest' Ex-prelfions of the Resentment and Indignation which they feel for this unjust and unprovoked Aggression on the Honour of His Majesty’s Crown, and the essential Interests of His Kingdoms, contrary to the Law of Nations, and injurious to the Rights and Posselllons of every Sovereign Power in Europe.

That the good Faith and Uprightness of His Majes-tv’s Conduct towards Foreign Powers, and the Sincerity of His Intentions to preserve the general Tranquillity, must be acknowledged by all the World; and His Majesty cannot be considered as responsible for the Dif-turbance of this Tranquillity, if His Majesty should find Himself called upon to refill the Enterprizes of that restless and dangerous Spirit of Ambition and Aggrandizement, which has so often invaded the Rights, and threatened the Liberties, of Europe.

That we should be wanting in bur Duty to His Majesty, to our Constituents, and to ourfelvej, if we did not give His Majesty the strongest Assurances of our moll zealous Assistanee and Support; and that this House has the firmeli Confidence, that, in every Demonstration of Loyalty to His Majesty, and of Love to their Country, His faithful Subjects will vie with each other; and that no Considerations will divert or deter them from Handing forth in the public Defence, and from fuitaining, with a Heady Perseverance, any extraordinary Burthens and Expences which shall be found necessary, fur enabling His Majesty to vindicate the Honour of His Crown, and to protest and maintain the just Rights and efi’ential Interests of these Kingdoms.

Gentlemen,

I return you my hearty Thanks for this very dutiful and affectionate Address: I make no Doubt, that, assisted by the Advice of My Parliament, and supported "by the Spirit of My People, I shall, under the Divine Providence, be enabled to repel every Insult on the Honour of My Crown, to maintain the Rights of My Subjects, and to defend all My Dominions.

Rej'olved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That every Person who shall keep any Office, or Place, for buying, felling, insuring, registering, disposing, or otherwise dealing in, any Tickets or Chances, or Parts thereof, or on the Numbers of any Tickets in any Lottery whatsoever, or shall, by writing, or printing, publish the setting-up or using such Office or Place, shall first take out a Licence for that Purpose.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

Mr. Ralph Heron and the said Mr. French, being examined, said, That the Ford near the Place, where, by the said Articles, it is proposed to build a Bridge, is extremely dangerous at Times of Floods, which frequently happen after Rains; that, at such Times, the Bottom of the said Ford is shifted by the Violence of the Current, which renders the Passage through it always uncertain, and frequently impracticable; and that the building a Bridge, with proper Avenues to it, at the above aescribed Place, would not only be exceedingly convenient for the said Town and Neighbourhood, but of great public Utility.

The Lord North acquainted the House, That he had a Message from His Majesty, to this House, signed by His Majesty; and he presented the same to the House; and it was read by Mr. Speaker (all the . Members of the House being uncovered) and is as followeth; viz.

GEORGE R.

The French King having concluded a Treaty of Amity and Commerce with His Majesty’s revolted Subjects in North America, and His Majesty having 'received Advice, that the warlike Preparations in France become every Day more considerable; His Majesty thinks that, in this critical Conjuncture, He should not act consistently with the Care and Concern, which He always feels for His Faithful People, if He omitted any Means in His Power that may contribute to their Defence: Therefore, in pursuance of the Acts of Parliament, enabling His Majesty to call out and assemble the Militia, in the Cafes therein mentioned, His Majesty has thought it right to make this Communication to the House of Commons; to the End that His Majesty may, if He shall think proper, chuse the Militia to be drawn out and embodied, and to march as Occasion shall require.

G. R.

Refulved, Nemine eontradicentc. That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, to return His Majesty the humble" Thanks of this House, for His most Gracious Message; and to express the just Sense we have of His Majesty’s Goodness, and of His paternal Care of His People, in providing every Means in His Power that may tend to their Defence, and in H is Intention to call out and assemble the Militia, if it shall be found necessary for that Purpose.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to His Majesty by such Members of this House as are of His Majesty’s Moll honourable Privy Council.

A Petition of Thomas Moore, Esquire, Lord of the Manor of Mere, in the County and also

Owner and Proprietor of all the Tithes arising within a certain Common called WMoor, lying within the said Manor, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioner perceives, by the Votes, that a Bill is depending for dividing and inclosing the above-mentioned Common; and that, in a printed Copy of the said Bill shewn to the Petitioner, he is not Hated to be, although he really is, the folc Lord and Proprietor of the said Manor, and of the Tithes of the said Common; and there is no Provision, in the said Bill, "for allotting unto the Petitioner a certain and express Proportion of the said Common, in Compensation for his Manorial Rights and Tithes, which the Petitioner apprehends ought to be particularly provided for in the said Bill; and that there are several Recitals and Clauses very injurious to the Petitioner’s Interest, inserted therein: And therefore praying. That he may be heard, by himself or' his Counsel, against the said Bill; and that it may not be permitted to pass into a Law asit-now Hands.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill for dividing and inclosing a certain Common, or Tract of Commonable Land, called or known by the Name of Westhay Moor, within the Parish and Manor of in the County of Somerset, is committed; and that the: Petitioner be heard, by himself or Counsel, before the said Committee, upon, his Petition; if he thinks fit.

The Order of the Day being read, for the Second The Small* Reading of the Bill to enable the Corporation of Trinity bight House. House of Deptford Sfrond to establish and maintain a Light House on the Rocks called the Smalls, in Saint George's Channel;

A Petition of the Merchants, Mariners, and Trades-men, of the Port of Lancaster, was presented to the House, and read; taking Notice of the said Bill, and Setting forth, That the Utility of the said Light House has not been proved and ascertained; and that ihe Petitioners apprehend the erecting a Light House upon the said Rocks will be so far from being useful to Navigation, that very great Danger will arise therefrom to the Shipping, Lives, and Properties, of His Majesty’s Subjects, and a considerable Duty will beimpoled upon all Ships passing through Saint George's; and that

no Benefit can arise to such Ships by the erecting of the said Light House; and that, exclusive of the Danger to which such Ships will by this Means be exposed, they will be Hill subjected to a further Inconvenience; for, if the said Bill should pafc into a Law, and a Duty thereby be laid upon Trade, it may be the Cause of preventing the erecting of Light Houses in other Parts of Saint George's Channel, which might be of public Utility: And therefore praying. That the said Bill may not pass' into a Law.

„ a Petition of the Mailer, Wardens, and Assistants, of the Corporation of Trinity House of Deptford Slrond, declaring their Intention of causing a Light House, said to have been erected on One of the Rocks ly ing in Saint George's Channel, called the Smalls, to be repaired, or

k new one inllead thereof to be erected upon such of the Rocks as they shall adjudge to be moil beneficial to Navigation; and that certain Letters Patent, containing a Grant of the said Rock to John Phillips, Esquire, for a Term of Fifty Years, are now vested in them, the said Mailer, Wardens, and Assistants, for the Refulue of the said Term, by the Consent of the Pa- tentee and others interested therein; and praying for Leave to bring in a Bill, to enable them to collect Duties on Ships, and other Vessels, passing within certain Limits* and for vetting in them, their Successors, and Assigns, for ever, the said Rocks of the Smalls; and that the Petitioners have sufficient Cause for doubting whether a Light House can be supported on the said Rocks, every Attempt hitherto made having been frustrated by the Violence of the Winds and Waves; and that the Utility of a Light House upon those Rocks, if possible to be erected and supported there, is dubious and indeterminate, not likely to extend beyond a partial and uncertain Advantage, chiefly to Coalling Vessels; and that the enormous Sums already collected under the Denomination of Light Duties are a grievous and unnecessary Tax upon the Commerce and Navigation of these Kingdoms: And therefore praying, if it shall appear reasonable to the House, to impose, at this Time, a new Tax upon Shipping, for the Support of the fiijd intended Light House, when completed, that no Ships or Vessels bound to, or going from this Port to, any Part of Ireland, Africa, or America, may be chargeable with the Duties to be imposed for the Maintenance thereof, that such Duties may be reasonable, and payable only whilll the said Lights are well and conflaritly kept up, and that the said Duties may not be made perpetual, but totally cease, in case the intended Building should be dellroyed or rendered useless as a Light House.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Twenty-third Year of his late Majesty, for the more easy and speedy Recovery of ftnall Debts within the Toiver Hamids, was read. And,

Mr. John Duplex, being examined, said, That the Commissioners appointed by virtue of the said Act have, ever since the Commencement of t lie said Act, determined upon Debts for Rent under Forty Shillings; but that the Court of King’s Bench having lately determined that the present Act giwes no Power to proceed in Cafes of Debt for Rent, the Commissioners have since declined taking Cognizance of lech Debts, to the very great Prejudice of the Inhabitants in general.

Mr. Thomas Dykes, being examined, said, That great Inconveniences have arisen from the present Method of enforcing Appearances, w here the Parties omit to attend upon Summonses; and the Act has been found defective in some other Respects.

And the Witness further said, That the present Court House, for transacting the Bufir.els of the Court, is held at the Will of the Landlord, and is very incommodious; and that the late Act hath made no Provision for building Court Houses and Offices.

That the present Clerks are willing to raise a competent Sum upon the Credit of their Fees, lor the above Purposes, with the Assistance only of the following Increase of Fees; viz.

Upon, every Summons, which is now only gd. the additional Sum of id.; and upon every Hearing, which is now only 3d. the further Sum of id. And the Witness said. That, w'ith the above Increase, the Fees of this Court w ill still lie lower than the Fees of any other Court of the like Sort in or near the Cities of London and
