Mr. Gascoyne, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Six thousand Four hundred Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, to be paid to Mr. Edioard Moore, as a final Compensation for his

Pains, Trouble, and Expence, during an Employment of Thirteen Years, in compiling a General Index to the Journals of the House of Commons.

Iiefolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Three thousand Pounds,' be granted to His Majesty, to be paid to the Reverend Mr. Forjler, as a final Compensation for his Pains, Trouble, and Expence, during an Employment of Eight Years, in compiling a General Index to the Journals of the House of Commons.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Three thousand Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, to pe paid to the Reverend Doctor Roger Flexman, as a final Compensation for his Pains, Trouble, and Expence, during an Employment of Nine Years, in compiling a General Index to the Journals of the House of Commons.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, that a Sum, not exceeding Five hundred Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, to be paid to Mr. Cunningham, in Part of his Payment, for his Pains, Trouble, and Expence, in compiling a General Index to the Journals of the House of Commons.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One Million Four hundred Six thousand Nine hundred Twenty-three Pounds One Shilling and Four Pence and One Farthing, be granted to His Majesty, towards defraying the extraordinary Expences of His Majesty’s Land Forces, and other Services, incurred between the Thirty-first Day of January One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-seven, and the First Day of February One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-eight, and not provided for by Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, that a Sum, not exceeding Eighteen thousand Eight hundred Ninety-five Pounds Five Shillings and Two Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge of several Augmentations to His Majesty’s Forces, from their respective Commencements, to the Twenty-fourth Day of December One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-eight.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Six thousand Nine hundred Ninety-eight Pounds Twelve Shillings and Five Pence, be granted to His Majesty, upon account of the Expences of the new Roads of Communication, and building Bridges in the Highlands of North Britain, in the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-eight.

The Four first Resolutions of the Committea being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

A Petition of the Free BurgcfTes, Freeholders, and V01,. 36.

Inhabitants, of tile Tofvn anil County of upon

Tyne, was presented to the I Joule, and read; Setting forth; That, deeply affected with the present public. Distress, and apprehensive of the imminent Danger, if not total Ruin, of our political Constitution, we look up to you, as the only proper Guardians of those Rights and Privileges, whiph we have committed in Trim to your Defence and Protection. We have long beheld, with Concern, the growing Incroaehments of Ministerial Power, and that Power and Influence given to interested Men, whose avowed Principles are diametrically opposite to the Spirit of our excellent Constitution, which accomplished the Exclusion of Tyranny, by the late glorious Resolution, and the subsequent Elevation of our present moll Gracious Sovereign’s illustrious Family to the Throne of these Realms. After a long Train of unredrefied increasing Evils, we find ourselves involved in an imneceflary, expensive, and ruinous. Civil War; many Thousands of our brave Countrymen hate"' been loft; many Millions of the public Tieafure expended;1 our Taxes daily increasing; our Trade and Commerce declining; many of our Resources cut off; 0141* National Credit sinking; and all (without the least Prospept of public Advantage) perfified in by our Ministers, against the most humble Petitions and just Remonstrances, until repeated ill Success, and the Prof-petit of a Foreign War, have at length convinced them of their Error and Mifeonduft, and compelled them inconliftently to solicit (probably too late) for those Terms which Reason and Truth had long ago sued for in vain: We therefore pray. That the Wisdom and Attention of Parliament may be leriously engaged to in-veltigate, and effectually root out, the Cause of these Evils, to establish the Peace and Happiness of Society, by humbly addreiling His Majesty, to remove front. His Presence and Councils, for ever, those Men, who from Motives of Interest, or vindictive Ambition, may have destroyed this Peace, interrupted this Happiness, and forfeited the Confidence of the People; and, to prevent succeeding Delinquents from being mifled by the flattering Hopes of Impunity, we pray, that legal, but rigorous and exemplary, Punishments may be impartially inflicted upon any who are found to have betrayed the jult Rights, and sacrificed the Welfare, of their Country; that such effectual Check may be given to Vice and Corruption, and such Countenance and Encouragement to public Virtue, as may unite a free and generous People upon the solid Bafts of Loyalty and mutual Affection, and enable us, with that prevalent Assistance which depends upon the Divine Approbation, to escape the Wiles, and repel the Assaults, of our natural, insidious, and powerful Enemies.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr.- Edward Hare,-being examined, said, That there is a large Tract of Land in the Fens in Lincolnshie, which has been drained at a great Expence, and is proper for the Cultivation of Oats, which is the Grain usually sown — That upwards of 30,000 Acres, under BlackSluice Drainage, have been drained, and are chiefly cultivated with Oats (exclusive of another Part under the Witham Drainage Act, which is 30,000 Acres more) — That upwards of £.40,000 has been laid out, besides the Annual Rates for general and interior Drainage.

Mr. Joseph Newman, being examined, said. That the Average Weight of Oats is about Thirty-three Pounds and an Half-a Bushel — That a large Quantity of less Weight is grown — That Oats weighing Nine Stone Ten Pounds a Coomb, is good middling Oats, and fit for Horse Com — That the Weight of the best he has seen, is between 11 and iz Stone per Coom !> — That Upland Oats weighing iz Stone is reckoned very good — That in a dry Year, the Medium of Oats will be better than in a wet Year, which Medium varies as the Season does, and that the Oats vary from Year to Year — That under the Witham Act, upwards of zo, oooo Acres has been inclosed, which is properest for Oats — That the Average Price of Oats, one Year with another, is about Half a Guinea a Quarter at ton — That the Expence of bringing the Oats from Boston to London, is near Three Shillings per Quarter — -That he has calculated the Expence of cultivating' the Oats, which (exclusive of Rent) is about £. 2 per Acre, as follows; Ploughing, Sowing, and Harrowing, Seven Shillings an Acre; Seed, Nine Shillings an Acre, whereon are generally sown between Four and Five Bushels j Weeding, One Shilling and Six Pence; Reaping, Ten Shillings and Six Pence an Acre; Carting, Stacking, and Thatching, Four Shillings; Thrcihing, Three ShiJ-lings ;carrying to Market and Porterage, ThreeSh ill in gs; and Assessments One^ Shilling and Six Pence — That the Average Produce is about Six Quarters upon an Acre

Mr. Thomas Cockfedge, being examined, Laid, That

he is a Corn Factor i n London- — That the Two Persons who by the Law make the Affidavit to the Quarter Session, never have, or do pay the least Regard to the Average Price of Oatsr-ihat they think they are di-rested by the Act to find out the Price of middling Oats, but not the general Average Price of all Oats, which is the constant Practice in London — That the Two People (who aft as Volunteers) always think themselves jutlified in their Affidavit, if they fix upon such Sort of Oats as are middling according to their Idea of the Quality, totally rejeftingany Consideration of other Oats then at Market, let the Prices be whatever they will, by which Means it has often happened, that for the Fortnight preceding the Application to the Sessions, many Thousand Quarters of Englrih Oats, of the middling Quality, have been sold at Prices not exceeding Fourteen tb Fifteen Shillingsper Quarter, when the Affidavit has been presented to the Sessions, that the Price of middling Oats is then above Sixteen Shillings — That in his Opinion aliout 400,000 Quarters of Oats are fold in the Port of London in a Year — That he thinks they have received from the Ports of Spalding, Lynn, and Wifoeach, about 120,000 Quarters per Annum, for these Four or Five Years past —

That there are often great Quantities of that Corn at Market, when the Ports are opened — That the Average Weight of the Fen Oats is-about Thirty-three Pounds to Thirty-four Pounds a Bushel — That the Average Weight of all other English Oats (exclusive of the Fen Oats) is about Thirty-six Pounds a Bushel — That Foreign Corn is better than Ours in all the Degreen — -That

55,000 Quarters of Oats have been imported into don, within the last Three Weeks — That about Fourteen Shillings a Quarter ha* been paid at an Average for that Corn — That the Weight of Foreign Oats, in his Opinion, is from about Thirty-two Pounds to Forty Pounds a Bushel, and the Average Weight is from Thirty-six to Thirty-seven Pounds a Bushel — That the Average Price of the Home Oats is now about Thir-, teen Shillings and Six Pence a Quarter — That the Importation of Home Oats has been increasing in the Port of London near Ten Years. And the Witness being asked, Whether it would be a Remedy to the Evil complained of, if there was some regular Mode of ascertaining the Port Prices of Oats? he said, He thought if such a Mode was found out, it is all that is wanted to answer that Purpose — That the Port has often been opened, without the least Attention to the Prices of Oats from the Fens — That this Matter was Once so flagrant, that he attended the Sessions when the Affidavit was produced, apd the Certificate granted to the Custom House, with Mr. William Morley, who is a Corn Factor, and has large Dealings in Corn from the Fen's, and they offered to prove to the Court, that no Oats which either of them had fold for the preceding Month, had reached near Sixteen Shillings, and that he imagined they had fold between them 10,000 Quarters in that Time — That the Sessions refused to pay any Attention to them, and said, all that was to guide them in their Determination, was the Affidavit — That there is a Species of Oats called Poland Oats, which, though they weigh no more than Thirty-four Pounds per Bushel, fell for One Shilling a Quarter more than the other Oats, upon Account of the India Trade.

Taylor*; A PETITION of several Master Taylors, residing ^^rtiming^ within the Cities of London and or

within Five Miles thereof, was presented to the House, and read; taking Notice of the Bill to explain, and amend, and reduce into One Act of Parliament, the Law s now in being for regulating Master and Journeymen Taylors within the Bills of Mortality, and within the Distance of Five Miles thereof; and Setting forth. Vox.. 36.

That the Petitioners conceive that the said Bill, so fat* from answering the good Purposes pretended thereby, will be very mischievous, and subject the M afters to Extortions, Misbehaviours, and other Inconveniences from the Journeymen, will promote Combinations amongst the Journeymen to demand exorbitant Wages, and prevent Masters from distinguishing and encouraging Merit; and that the Petitioners apprehend, the Laws now in being are, and will be, very sufficient for regulating both Masters and Journeymen, W'ith the following Amendments; viz. To allow and compel the Party giving or receiving unlawful Wages, to give Evidence against the Party receiving or giving such Wages, and to acquit the Party giving such Evidence of the Fast, so far as relates to himself: And therefore praying. That they may be heard, by themselves, or Counsel, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law, but that the Amendment aforesaid may be made to the Acts, now in being, for regulating Journeymen Taylors.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Stirling A Petition of James Francis on be-

Highways. half of himself, and in the Names, and by the Authority, of several Freeholders, Heritors, and Commissioners of Supply, in the County of was presented

to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner has perused the Bill for repairing the Highways and Bridges in the County of Stirling, as the same has been amended by the Committee, to whom thefame had been committed, and begs Leave to observe, that the said Bill, as it now Hands, makes further Alterations upon the Road Laws of the said County than was known to have been intended when the Counsel for certain Petitioners against the said Rill were heard at the Bar of the House; and that the Bill, as it Hood before going in- to the Committee, deprived such Heritors as had not Lands valued in the Cess Books of the County at £. ioo Scots, of the Right of assessing the County, in what was necessary for the Repair of Roadsand Bridges; as it now fiand6, it deprives Freeholders of that Right, as well as the lesser Heritors; and that the execution of this Act being put into the Hands of certain Trustees named by the Committee, deprives the Justices of Peace and Commissioners of Supply of the Power before vested in them, of making and repairing the Roads within the said County that are not Turnpike Roads, and likewise takes away from the Trustees of the Turnpike Roads the Power of repairing the fame; and that certain Lands within the County of Stirling are not valued in the Cess Books of the said County, though of more real Value than others that are valued; and the ' Proprietors of the said Landis (of whom the Petitioner’s Brother is One) will, by the Bill as it now Hands, be deprived of any Voice as to the Repair of the Roads going through the said Lands, which will be left at the Mercy of others not interested therein, and that the Bill, as it now Hands, interferes with the Rights and Privileges of the Town of Stirling, the Managers of which have had no Notice given them ef any such Attack, and conficlered theijiselves as secured therefrom by

Promises of the Promoters and Agitators of this Bill; they think it peculiarly hard to be thus attacked in the Absence of their Representative in Parliament, who has been suffered to remain in Captivity since the Commencement of the American War, though it is well known and acknowledged this Misfortune happened to him by no Fault of his own, and that every other Field Officer in His Majesty’s Service, who was taken, has been exchanged; and the Petitioner thinks it incumbent upon him to represent to the House, that there are upwards of Forty thousand Inhabitants in the County of Stirling, all of whom, except the Thirty Petitioners for the Bill, desired, that if an Act muH be made, the Damages done in Consequence thereof to Individuals might be ascertained by Juries, or by Arbitrators, as directed in the Act for Preservation of public Highways in that Part of Great Britain called England: And therefore praying. That he may be heard by his Counsel, against the said Bill, why the same may not pass into a Law.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Fourth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act for granting an Allowance upon the Exportation of British-made Gunpowder," which was to continue in Force for Five Years from the 24th Day of June 1731, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, and which, by several subsequent Acts, made in the Tenth, Sixteenth, Twenty-fourth, and Thirty-first Years of his said Majesty’s Reign, and the Fourth and Twelfth Years of His present Majesty’s Reign, was further continued until the Twenty-ninth Day of September 1778, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the'Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Ninth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act for further encouraging and regulating the " Manufacture of British Sail Cloth, and for the more " effectual securing the Duties now payable on foreign " Sail Cloth imported into this Kingdom," which was to continue in Force from the 24th Day of June 1736, for the Term of Five Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, and which, by several subsequent Acts, made in the Thirteenth, Twenty-fourth, and Thirty-first Years of his said Majesty’s Reign, and the Fourth and Twelfth Years of His present Majesty’s Reign, was further continued until the 29th Day of Septembei' 1778, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

A Petition of Sambrooke Freeman, of Berkeley in the County of Middlesex, Esquire, Thomas Rajhleigh, of j BartletsBuildings, London, Gentleman, Executor of

the Will of Doctor William Battie, deceased, Anne Penning, of Great Rujfel Street, in the said County of Middlesex, Spinster, Anne Battie, of the same Place, Spinster, and other the Creditors under and by virtue of an Act of Parliament herein after more particularly mentioned; intituled, "An Act for improving and completing the " Navigation of the Rivers Thames and Isis, from the City of London to the Town of in the County of Wilts," whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That an Act was made in the Twenty-fourth Year of King George the Second, for better carry* ing on and regulating the Navigation of the Rivers Thames and Isis, from the City of London West ward, to the Town of Cricklade, in the County of Wilts, which being found ineffectual for the Purposes intended, another Act was made in the Eleventh Year of His present Majesty, for improving and completing the Navigation of the said Rivers, from the City of London to the Town of Cricklade, in the County of

Wilts; and that the Commissioners, authorized to put the said last mentioned Act into execution, are impowered to make Orders and Constitutions for purchasing of Locks, Ferries, and Lands, for the Use of the said Navigation, and to purchase and make Towing Paths,

] ►ailing the said last mentioned Act, the Petitioners, or those whose Adignecs, Trustees, or personal Representatives they are, upon the Credit of the said Act, and with-a view to alfift in carrying the Purposes thereof more speedily into execution, have advanced several Sums of Mouey, after the Rate of Four and an Half per Cent, which are dill owing to the Petitioners; and that the Improvements necessary for completing the said Navigation, according to the Intention of the said last mentioned Act, are not yet iiuished, although nearly the whole of the present Fund, arising from the Money advanced by the Petitioners, is nearly exhauded by the several necessary and expensive Works already made upon the said Rivers, and great Pains have been taken by the Commissioners under the said last mentioned Act, to render the Navigation of the said Rivers complete, and to reduce the Price of the Freight of Goods conveyed thereby; and that the Profits arising from the said Navigation, are barely sufficient to keep down the Intered of the Money borrowed; and, if the Duties arising therefrom should be advanced, will be greatly injurious to the Public, and mult totally defeat the Intention of the said last mentioned Act; and farther setting forth, that the Petitioners have lately perused a Bill, depending in the House, for making a Navigable Canal from the Town of Bajingsioke, in the County of Sout/iampton, to communicate with the River IVey, in the Parish of C, in the County of

Surrey, whereby it appears, that the said Canal is meant to pal's through or near the several Places therein mentioned; and that the Conveyance of Goods and Merchandize between the said Places by or through which the intended Canal is meant to pass, and between 4he said several Places, and the Towns of Reading and Aldermaston, in the County of Berks; and from the said several Places by or through which the said intended Canal is meant to pass, and the said Towns of Reading and Aldermajton, to the several other Places with

which the Navigation of the said Rivers Thames and Isis have any Communication, principally contributes to the Support of the Navigation of the said Rivers; and that, in case the said Bill should pass into a Law, not only the Conveyance of Goods from and between the said several Places by or through which the said intended Canal is meant to pass, but also from and between the fame, and the said Towns of Reading and Aldermajton, will in a great Meafare be diverted from -the said Rivers Thames and IJis to the said intended Canal; by Means whereof the Profits arising from the Navigation of the said Rivers must be greatly reduced, and the Commissioners impowered to carry the Purposes of the said Act for improving the Navigation of the said Rivers into execution, will not only be rendered trnable to procure such other Sums of Money as may be required for completing the fame, but the Tolls, Freight, and other Emoluments, arising from the Navigation of the said Rivers, will be insufficient (after keeping the several expensive Works which have been erected and made upon the Banks of the said Rivers -in repair) to keep down and answer the accruing Inhered upon the Petitioners said respective Debts, to the 17

great Detriment of the Navigation of the said Rivers Thames and IJis, and coul'equently to such of the Pub-

lic as derive any present Advantage therefrom, and to the irreparable Loss of the Petitioners, as the Security given to them, under the Faith and Credit of the said Act, will be effectually destroyed: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pais into a Law; and that the Petitioners may be heard, by theiff Counsel, against the fame.

A Petition of several Owners and Occupiers of Locks and Winches on the River Thames, below the Influx of the River Kennett, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Locks and Winches on the River Thames were erected, and are still kept up, for the Benefit of the Navigation of the said River; and that, by Two late Acts, made in the Twenty-fourth Year of King George the Second, and in the Eleventh Year of ' His present Majesty, for better carrying on the Navigation of the said River Thames, the Owners or Occupiers Of the said Locks and Winches are obliged, under severe Penalties, to keep up and reiiair the same (which are very hazardous and expensive Works) for the Benefit and batter carrying on of the said Navigation; and that, to enable the said Owners and Occupiers to defray the Expences of keeping up and repairing such Works, the Commissioners empowered to execute the said Acts, have allowed to the said Owners and Occupiers a certain Toll on every Barge passing through or by the said Locks; and that the Petitioners observe., by the Votes, that Leave hath been given to bring in a Bill for making a navigable Canal from the Town of Basingstoke, in the County of Southampton, to communicate with the River Wey, in the Parish of Chertsey, in the County of Surrey; and conceive, that if such Canal should be made, great Part of the Trade now passing the Thames Navigation will be diverted into another Channel, and the Tolls arising from such Trade no longer be paid to the Petitioners, greatly to the Diminution of the Income established by the Legifla^ ture for keeping up and repairing the said Locks and Winches, notwithstanding which, the Petitioners will still be obliged to be at the same Expence in keeping up and repairing the said Works; and that, should the said Bill pass into a Law, it will very much injure the Petitioners, and greatly reduce the said Fund established by the Legislature, and even render the same inadequate to the Purpose intended of keeping up and repairing the said Works: And therefore‘praying. That they may be heard,' by themselves or Counsel, against the said Bill passing into a Law, or that they may have such other Compensation or Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report, which was made from the Committee, to whom the said Bill was committed, be taken into further Consideration; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said BHl, against the said Petition.

Duncan Campbell, Esquire, informed your Committee, That he was appointed, by the Justices of the Peace for the County of Middlesex, Ovorfeer of the Convicts, in July 1776 — -That he was directed to provide a Ship of 240 Tons to receive the Convicts, to the Number of 120 — That he provided a Ship called the Jufiitia, of about 260 Tons — That there were no particular Orders given him about the Maimer of fitting it out — That he adopted the Mode uled in Transjiort Vessels, which are employed in conveying the d roops which Government send out, by trying Two Tier of Beds, one above another, Five Feet den Inches between each Tier — That in Transport Vessels only Five Feet are allowed between each Tier — That he allowed the Men Eighteen Inches Width each, which he believes is the Allowance in Transport Vessels — That lie soon found that Mode of laying them was not proper, and he was adviseil to alter it, and to endeavour to give the Men more Iloom; he then pulled down the Cabins, and adopted One general Platform on each Deck, which is the Plan that now exists, only inliead of allowing Eighteen Inches Width to each Mhn lie allows Two Feet — -That he adopted the Plan of Matting, but when the Mats were loose the Prisoners pulled them about, and were carclcfs of them; upon which he ordered them to be nailed upon the Platforms —

Your Committee then called Dr. who in-

formed them. That he was on board the jujlitia Three Times last Year; the First Time was upon the 17th of June, the Second in July or Au and the Third in Augujlor September; and that he was Once on board the Cen/or — That the Hold in which the Convicts

were kept, was very airy, inso much as to allow them every Thing necessary for their Health — That he thought there was all possible Care taken of them, except in one Instance, which was that of the Manner in which they were placed to sleep — That there were Platforms provided all round the Ship, and Six were to sleep in each of those Platforms — That they lay very close together, so that, in his Opinion, there was too little Room for each of the Men — That the Beds were placed against the Sides of the Vessels, allowing about 18 or iq Inches Width for each Man to lie upon — That tire Vessel was very clean, there was no bad Smell, except near the Necessary; but the next Time he was there, the Funnel of that was altered, in Consequence, as he apprehends, of his Advice, and other Gentlemen’s of the Royal Society, who were on board with him; in all other Respects' lie thought they were well provided for — That in regard to their Clothing it seemed to him to be good — That the Friends of the Convicts sent some, and some was sent by Government — That their Bread was good, but not the finest Wheat Bread' — That he took some of it to the Tavern, and that he, and the Company with him, preferred'it to other Bread — That the Convicts had a Mat to lie on, and one Coverlid to cover them; the Mat was upon the Boards, and Coverlid over them; the Beds were hard; they compared them with the Beds used by the lower Part of the People at Modi //‘a-r-That it was Summer when he was on board — That some of the Convicts undressed themselves to go 10 Bed — That there were very few lick; there were Physicians with him, so that he did not attend to them

They are pnntlhed with a Cat of Nine Tails, for refuting to work; their Labour did not seem so hard as that of common Labour in other Places; but he saw them getting up the Ballast, which is harder than common Labour — That he can’t speak with Certainty as to the Beds, but that the Convids lay too close together; a Partition to divide Man from Man would be mnch better, as each Man then would endeavour to keep his Place clean — That he thinks it would be a great Improvement to have a Space between the Beds and the'Wall.

That his Second Visit on board the Hulks was on the 26th of January 1778 — That he went first to the

— That they left Work between One and Two o’Clock, and came for their Dinners, and did not return to Work any more that Day — That he was informed they went to the Warren a little before Ten, and re- turned about Half pall One — That there were only 103 employed in the Warren — That when they worked there, they had a Pint of Strong Beer each Man —

It appears also, That the Number of Convicts at present under Contrail to be maintained is 380; and that the Yearly Average of the Felons, who were ordered for Transportation during a Period of Six Years and an Half, from the ift of November 1769 to the ift of May 1776, amounts to 960, of which a Fourth being deducted for Women, which is nearly the Proportion that appears from the Accounts given to your Committee of Persons transported in the said Six Years and an Half, there remain 720 Males liable to the Pu-ndhment of hard Labour on the River , except

such as from bad Health or Weaknefe may be deemed unfit for it.

It further appears, That Three several Contracts for providing for Convicts sentenced to hard Labour have beer, made by the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury with Mr. Campbell, the First being at the Rate of 38 a Man by the Year; which, for 120 Convicts, amounts to the Sum of £. 4,560.

The Second, at the Rate of £.26. 15*. lofrf. per Man, by the Year; which, for 130 Convicts, amounts to the Sum of £.3,483- 7

The Third, on the same Terms as the Second, for 130 ConviCls, from January 1778 to July 1779.

It also appears. That the Value of the Labour done by the ConviCls in Woolwich Warren, in making a Wharf, a Proof Butt, digging Ditches, and other useful Works, amounts to £.3,350; and that the Value of their Labour in railing Ballast is computed at £> 2,703. 12 s.6d.

Upon the Whole, your Committee have come to the following Resolutions:

- Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That from the Beginning of the Institution of the Hulks, there has been a progressive Improvement in the Accommodation, Food, Employment, and Means of preserving the Health of the Convi6ls sentenced to hard Labour on the River Thames, and that the said Hulks are at present convenient, airy, and healthy.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it will be proper, by a new Bill, to continue the present Mode of punching Convicts on board the Hulks, by hard Labour, for a certain Time.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into further Consideration upon Friday Fortnight, the ift Day of May next.

A Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Burgesses, of the Borough of Wigan, in the County Palatine of caster, was presented to the Hgufe, and read; Setting forth, That the Trade of the said Borough, as well as of many adjacent Parishes and Townships, hath for several Years chiefly confilied, and now eonfifts, in the weaving and manufacturing of White Cloths, Canvafe -or Sail Cloth, Checques, and other Linen Cloths, or Cotton and Linen mixed, for the Consumption of this Country, as well as for Exportation; and that the greatest Number of the Inhabitants of those Places having been brought up in the said Manufactures, and having served Apprenticeships to the fame, are thereby rendered unable to pursue any other Business, so as to support themselves and Families; and that the said Manufactures being chiefly made of Yarn imported from Jr eland, subject to a Duty there, and to a considerable Charge for Commission for buying, and for Freight and Insuranceupon the same to England, the Petitioners have

yet do they (although in the most dutiful and respectful Manner) beg Leave to represent, that, even upon the most liberal Principles, the Commercial Privileges of Great Britain ought only to be extended to those Parts of the Empire where the People pay Taxes in Proportion to those levied upon the Inhabitants of;

and, if the Petitioners are not very much mistaken, the Taxes paid by the People of Ireland bear but a fmaJl Proportion to those established in Britain; and therefore, by passing into Laws the Bills now depending, an Encouragement will be given to the Trade and Manufactures of Ireland, not only ruinous to those of Britain, but which the People of Ireland have no Title, either in Justice or in Policy, to receive: And therefore praying, not only that the Bills now depending may not be passed, but that no Indulgences, which may be detrimental to the Commerce and Manufactures of Britain, may be allowed, until, by bearing their proportional Share of the National Expence, the People of Ireland shall become, in Justice and in found Policy, Entitled to an unlimited Freedom in Commerce and Manufactures; and that the Petitioners may be heard, by Counsel, against the Bills above mentioned.

A Petition of the Committee of the Company of Merchants trading to Africa, being offered to be presented to the House;

The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recom-. mends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners have laid before the House, an Account of the Money granted for the Year 1776, examined and passed by the Curlitor Baron of the Exchequer, as required by an Act of the Twenty-third of George the Second, intituled, "An Act for extending and improving the Trade to Africa and that they have invdted the Money, granted in 1777, for the Support of the Forts and: Settlements on the said Coast; and that the Forts and Settlements on the said Coast having been delivered to the Petitioners in a very bad State by the Royal African Company, and the Sums annually granted by Parliament being nearly expended in the Civil and Military Ellablillnnents, leaving very little for the Repairs of the said Forts, Several of them still remain in a very ruinous Condition; and that the Petitioners find, by the Books of Accounts received from Africa, ending the 31st of December 1776, that there was, at that Time, due and owing to the Officers and Servants there a Debt of £.24,694. 14.?. urf. Coast Money, which, according to their Method of Calculation, amounts to the Sum of 16,463. 3.?. o llerling; and the Petitioners have too much Reason to apprehend, that the said Debt is considerably increased since that Time, owing, in some Measure,' to the Supplies sent out being considerably lessened by the additional Expence of Freight and I(durance; and that the Petitioners, being sensible of the great Regard fiiewn by the House for the British Forts and Settlements on the Coast of Africa, therefore pray the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant such Sum for the necessary Support and Maintenance of the said Forts and Settlements, for repaying the Officers and Servants the several Sums of Money advanced by them, and likewise for the Repairs still wanted, as shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

AN ingrossed Hill to Amend an Act, passed in thd Twenty-sixth Year of King George the Second; more effectually to enable the Parishioners of the Parish of Christ Church, in the County of , to purchase, hire, or erect, a Workhouse, for the employing and maintaining the Poor of the said Parish, and for the more effectual Support and Employment of the Poor therein, was read the Third Time.

An ingrossed Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, by way of Ryder, declaring, that the Churchwardens thall take Security of the Treasurer.

And the said Clause was Twice read, wdth a Blank; which being filled up, the said Clause was read the Third Time; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill, by way of Ryder.

Another ingrossed Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, by way of Ryder, for allowing the Annuitants and Contributors to inspect and take Copies of the Books; and inflicting a Penalty in same of Refusal.

And the said Clause was Twice read, with Blanks; which being filled up, the said Clause was read the Third Time; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill, by way of Ryder.

Another ingrossed Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, by way of Ryder, for allowing an Appeal to the Quarter Sessions.

And the said Clause was Twice read, w’ith Blanks which being filled up, the said Clause was read the Third Time; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill, by way of Ryder.

Then the Amendment following was proposed to be made to the Bill; viz.

Pr. 21. 1. 21. After " Parish" to insert " to be " sued for, and recovered, in the " Name of the Treasurer, for the " Time being, in the Court of " Requests for the Tower Hamlets aforesaid."

And the said Amendment was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House; and the Bill was amended at the Table accordingly.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be, An Act to amend an Act, passed in the Twenty-sixth Year of King George the Second, more effectually to enable the Parishioners of the Parish of Christ Church, in the County of Middlesex, to purchase, hire, or erect, a Workhouse for the employing and maintaining the Poor of the said Parish, and for the more effectual Support and Employment of the Poor therein.

Ordered, That Mr. Alderman Harley do carry the Bill to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence.

A Petition of the Mayor and Capital Burgesses the Borough and Foreign of Walsall, in the County of Stafford, and the several other Persons whose Names are thereunto set and subscribed, M anufaftu rers of Biafs and Iron at and nea* the Borough aforesaid, on behalf of themselves, and other Manufacturers of Brass and Iron in this Kingdom, was presented to the House; and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Bill is depending for opening a free Trade between Ireland and all the Set-

tlements; and that, should such a Law take Place, it will deprive great Numbers of Manufacturers, in this Kingdom, of the Means of maintaining themselves and numerous Families, or otherwise cause such Emigrations of Manufacturers from this Country to Ireland (where Labour and Provisions of all Sorts are cheaper) as will enable that Kingdom, in a few Years* to rival the Manufactures of England: And therefore praying. That such Bill may not pass into a Law.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Citizens, and Manufacturers of Gloves, in the City of Worcester, whole' Names are thereunto subscribed, was also pre* fented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that Bills have been, read, for opening a free Trade between Ireland and the British Plantations and Settlements; and that, should such Laws take Place, the same will deprive great Numbers of Manufacturers, in this Kingdom, of the Means of fubfilting themselves and Families, particularly in the Gloving Branch, or otherwise cause such Emigration of Manufacturers from this Country to Ireland (where Provisions of all Kinds are cheaper, and from w’hence Skins are exported for this Market,' which pay a heavy Duty) as will enable that Kingdom, in a few Years, to rival the Manufactures of England: And therefore praying, that such Bills may not pass into Laws.

A Petition of the Mayor, Burgesses, and Commonalty of the City of Bristol, under their Common Seal, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that Five Bills are brought in, for opening a free and direct Trade between the Kingdom of Ireland and the British Plantations in America, and the Settlements belonging to Great Britain on the Coast of Africa, and to permit the Importation of certain Goods of the Manufacture of Ireland into this Kingdom Duty-free; and that the Petitioners apprehend, if such Bills were to pass into a Law, they would prove destructive to that great

System of Commerce, Manufacture, and Revenoe, happily adopted at the Establishment, of those Plantations and Settlements, and which has ever since been pursued with Success, and would be highly injurious tb Thousands of Manufacturers, who now maintain themselves by honell Industry; and the Petitioners conceive, that it would be moil unequal to grant a free Importation into Ireland from the said Plantations*and Settlements, or to allow the Manufactures of Ireland to 'be imported into this Kingdom, except under the like Regulations, and the same Duties, as the People of this Country are subject to: And therefore praying. A Petition of the Mailer, Wardens, and Commonalty, of the Society of Merchants Venturers of the City of Bristol, under their Common Seal, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners have seen Five several Bills brought into the House; One to permit the Importation of certain Goods from the British Plantations in America, or the British Settlements on the Coal! of Africa, into

the Kingdom of Ireland; another, to permit the Exportation of certain Goods therein mentioned, directly from Ireland into any British Plantation in , or

any British Settlement on the Coast of Africa; another, to permit the Exportation of Glass, manufactured in Ireland, from thence to any Place whatsoever except Great Britain -,another, to permit the Importation of

Cotton Yarn, the Manufacture of Ireland, into this Kingdom, Duty-free ;and the other, to permit the Importation of Sail Cloth and Cordage, of the Manu. facture of Ireland, into this Kingdom, Duty-free; and that the Petitioners apprehend, if such Bills were to

Safe into a Law, that great Syltcm of Commerce and Revenue, which has been established with so much Consideration, and at so much Expence, would be at once overset, and a Torrent of Mischiefs unthough# of, and unforeseen, Would be poured in upon this Kingdom; and that the Duties payable in Ireland, on almost every Article of Trade which concern the Bills in Question, are vastly below the Duties paid on those Articles in Great Britain; that Provisions are cheaper in Ireland than in England, and the Labourers and Manufacturers of Ireland are not subject to the same Taxes as those of Great Britain, all which Circumstances will furnish Ireland with such Advantages over Great Britain as cannot be withstood; and that the Landed Interest of this Kingdom, ever benefited by the flourishing State of Trade and Manufactures, will also be greatly injured by the Means aforesaid; for, besides other Circumstances, Thousands of Artisans, who now maintain themselves by honeit Industry, would be deprived of the Means of their Subsistence,' and mult beqome burthensome to their Parishes; and the Petitioners apprehend, it would be most unequal to grant such Advantages to Ireland, not paying the same Taxes, or being subject to the same Duties, as the People of this Country; and that great Numbers of Ships and Men are now employed to carry from this Kingdom to Ireland the Produce of those Countries, to which the Bills in Question would admit, them to a free and immediate Trade, all which would be thereby Tendered useless, and consequently the Strength of t,he Nation be diminished: And therefore praying, That the Bills in Question may not pais into a Law.

A Petition of the Merchants, Importers, and Manufacturers, of Hemp, Iron, and Steel, of the City of Bristol, in behalf of themselves and others, the Manufacturers of those Articles in Great Britain, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that Bills are depending, to permit the Exportation of Goods (Wool and Woollen Manufactures only excepted) being the Produce or Manufacture of Ireland, directly from thence to North America, the West Indies, and any British Settlements oil the Coast of Africa, and for. allow-

ing the Importation of Cordage into this Kingdom Duty-free; and the Petitioners conceive, that, should the same pass into a Law, the Iron, Steel, a.nd Hemp Manufactures of this Kingdom, will sustain the mult fatal Injury, and the Export Trade of their capital Manufactories be. nearly ruined, if not wholly annihilated; and that, as the Duties on the raw Materials of Iron, Steel, and Hemp, now stand between the Two Kingdoms, and from the Vicinity of Ireland to the Markets, the Cheapness of Pfdvisions and Labour, with other local Advantages, in that Kingdom, the Petitioners, notWithstanding all their Skill ill manufacturing, will be undersold at every Market, and the Furnaces, Forges, Mills, and other expensive Erections, to the Amount of Millions, will be greatly reduced in Value, and some rendered totally useless; and that the baneful Effects of these Bills will not rest solely oft the Merchants and Manufacturers, but will extend in a very material Degree to the Landed Interest of this Kingdom, the Wood Lands and Collieries will be exceedingly reduced in Value, and the Poor’s Rates in many parts of this Kingdom will be greatly inereased, by the Thousands of poor Labourers thrown on their respective Parishes, for want of that Employment now afforded them by the Iron, Steel, and Hemp Trade, and their Dependencies; and that the Petitioners apprehend, the Import Duties on the rough Materials aforementioned, will lessen in Proportion as the Irish Manufactories increase, and such Diminution ‘of the Revenue creating a new Demand,.will be the more grievous Burthen on the Public at large, as it will be produced by Measures tending to bring on an Inability of supportiftg their present increasing Taxes: And therefore praying. That they may be heard, by themselves or Couhfei, against so much of these Bills as affects them, and that the House will grant them such Relief as shall seem meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Merchants and Manufacturers of Trade of Aberbrothock, was presented to the House, and read; IreUnd. Setting forth, That the Five Bills now depending in Parliament, for the Enlargement of the Trade of Ireland, will, one or aH of them, if passed into a Law, prove most destructive and ruinous to the Trade and Manufactures of Great Britain in general, and of this Town and County in particular: And therefore praying the House, to take the Trade and Manufactures of Great Britain into their most serious Consideration and Protection, and not suffer any of the above-mentioned Five Bills to pass into a Law.

A Petition of the Merchants, Tradesmen, and Ma- Ditto, nufacturers, of Wolverhampton, in the County of Stafford, was also presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth. That the various Iron Manufactories of the said Town, and its Environs, are now brought to the greatest Perfection; and that the Petitioners, with the deepelt Concern, observe a Bill is before the House, for opening a Free Trade between Ireland and all the British Settlements; and that, should such a Law take Place, Thousands of our most ingenious Manufacturers, now the Support of themselves, and of many numerous Families, will be deprived of a Maintenance, and thereby be induced to emigrate to Ireland for Employment, to the manifeil Injury of the English Trade:

And therefore praying, That such a Bill may not pass into a Law.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Merchants, Traders, Ditto, and Manufacturers, of the County Palatine of Lancaster, whose Names are subscribed, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe* by the Votes, that Bills are depending, to permit the Importation of Sail Cloth and Cordage, of the Manufacture of Ireland, into this Kingdom, Duty-free; to permit the Importation of certain Goods from the British Plantations in America, or the British Settlements on the Coast of Africa, into the Kingdom of Ireland-, to permit the Exportation of certain Goods therein mentioned directly from Ireland into any British Plantation in America, or any British Settlement on the Coast of Africa; to permit the Importation of Cotton Yarn, the Manufacture of Ireland, into this Kingdom, Duty-free; and to permit the Exportation of Glass, manufactured in Ireland, from thence to any Place whatsoever, except Great Britain; and that the Petitioners apprehend, and are allured, that, in case the Bills should pass into a Law, the same will be highly detrimental to the Revenues, Commercial Interefis, and Navigation, of this Kingdom in general, and tend to the utter Ruin of the Manufactures and Mercantile Interefis of this County in particular, and also greatly affect the Landed Interest therdbf: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves or their Counsel, against the said Bill or Bills respectively passing into a Law.

A Petition of the Burgesses, Manufacturers, and Ditto, principal Inhabitants, of the Borough of Newton, in the County of Lancaster, was also presented to the House, atidread; Setting forth, That the Petitioners having observed, by the Votes, that a Bill is depending for opening a Free Trade between Ireland and all i\\o Bridjh Settlements; and, as they are thoroughly convinced that such Bill is pregnant with Consequences highly prejudicial to the Interel'ts of the Kingdom in general, and of the County of Lancaster in particular; therefore praying, That such Bill may not pass into a Law.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and Inhabitants, of the Town of Warrington, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, was presented to the House, and read;

That the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

A Petition of the several Manufacturers of Sail Cloth in and near the Towns of Warrington, Lancaster, Preston, Kirkham, Liverpool, Prefcot, Farmoorth, Wigan, and Ulverftone, in the County of Lancaster, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are much alarmed and concerned to fee, by the Votes, that a Bill has. been brought into the House, to permit the Exportation of certain Goods therein mentioned, dire6Uy from Ireland into any British Plantation in America, or any British Settlement on the Coail of Africa ,* and the Petitioners conceive, that the said Bill Is meant to allow the Exportation of Irish Sail Cloth; and that the establishing the Manufacture of Sail Cloth within Great Britain, both as a Branch of Manufacture, and as a Naval Store for the Safety of the State, has been considered by the Legislature as an Object of great National Importance; and that the fluctuating Situation of the Sail Cloth Trade subjects the Manufacturer to many Losses and Inconveniences, from which other Branches of Manufacture are free; and that, in Time of Peace, their principal Dependence and Support arises from the Export Trade to the British Plantations, and the Settlements belonging to Great Britain on the Coail of Africa; but, if the proposed Bill should pass into a Law, the Petitioners conceive, that the Sail Cloth Manufacture of this Kingdom would be greatly prejudiced, and the British Navy thereby reduced to the Necessity of depending upon Ireland for a Supply, which iu Time of War

will be subject to the Depredation of our Enemies, as well as to many other Disappointments: And therefore praying. That the said Bill may not pass into a Law as it now (lands; and that they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the fame, or so much thereof as can affect the Article of made Sail

Cloth.

A Petition of the Merchants and Manufacturers of the Town and Neighbourhood of Preston, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Bill is brought in for the Exportation from the Kingdom of Ireland, directly into any of the British Plantations in America, or the West Indies, or into any of the Settlements belonging to Great Britain on the Coast of Africa, in Vessels which may lawfully trade to and from those Places, any Goods, Wares, and Merchandizes, being the Produce or Manufacture of Irela Wool and Woollen Manufactures only excepted) and all Goods and Commodities, of the Growth, Produce, or Manufacture of Great Britain, which have been, or may be, legally imported from thence into the said Kingdom of and all Foreign Certificate Goods which have been, or may be, legally imported from Great Britain into he-land;and alleging, that the Linen Manufactures, which have been at great Expence established, and are now carried on in the Town and Neighbourhood of will be greatly injured, if not altogether ruined, should the said Bill pass into a Law, the Advantages to which the Manufacturers have, by their Labour and Industry, entitled themselves, will be thereby taken from them, the Poor will be deprived of the Means of (up-porting themselves and Families, and the Value of Land in that Part of the Kingdom, which depends on the Prosperity of Trade, will not only be extremely reduced, but the Inhabitants will be rendered unable to support the great Weight of Public Burthens to which they at present so amply and cheerfully contribute: And therefore pray rng, That they may be heard, by themselves or their Counsel, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law; or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief, as to the House shall seem most expedient.

A Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Common Council, of the Borough and Corporation of Liverpool, was also presented to the House, and read; taking Notice of the Bill to permit the Exportation of certain Goods, therein mentioned, directly from Ireland into any British Plantation in America, or any British Settlement on the Coast of Af; and Setting forth. That great Sums of Money have been raised and expended, by virtue of several Acts of Parliament, for the making of Docks, erecting of Lights, and rendering the Port and Harbour of Liverpool as fafo and commodious as possible; and that, relying on the Faith of the House, several Persons have been induced to advance considerable Sums of Money, for the making and erecting such Docks, Lights, and other Improvements, for the Conveniences of Commerce, on the Credit of the Duties arifrng and payable by virtue of such Acts; and that, in Consequence of such Conveniences and Improvements for the Benefit of Trade, Numbers of Foreigners, and others, have re-fopted to, and settled there, for the Purposes of carrying on different Branches of Commerce, to the great Increase and Emolument of the Town of and the Revenues of this Kingdom; and that the Number of Ships and Vessels, which, for these Seven Years last past only, have foiled or been employed in the Trade from hence to the British Plantations in America, and to the British Settlements on the Coast of Africa, amounts, on an Average, yearly, to 230, or thereabouts; and that the Number of Ships and Vessels, which, for these Seven Years last past only, have failed or been employed in the Trade from hence

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Merchants, Mariners, Traders, and Manufacturers, of Liverpool, whose Names are subscribed, was also presented to the House, and read; likewise taking Notice of the said Bill, and Setting forth. That such an Infraction of the Act of Navigation, and a Change so important in that System, by which the Commerce, Manufactures, and Revenue, of this Kingdom have been so long and so successfully regulated; would, as the Petitioners apprehend, occasion much immediate Mischief, and be productive of very fatal Consequences in more distant Times, to the Revenue, Population, Landed Interest, Naval Force, Manufactures, and Commerce, of Britain: And therefore praying. That they may be heard, by themselves or their Counsel, against the said Bill.

A Petition of the Tallow Chandlers and Soap Boilers of the Town of Lancaster, was also presented to the House, and read; likewise taking Notice of the said Bill, and Setting forth, That the Petitioners are employed in the manufacturing of Candles and Soap, which they dispose of for Exportation to the West India Islands, and are in a great Measure supplied with Tallow, necessary for carrying on their respective Manufactories, from Ireland, where they pay a Duty on the Exportation thereof to England, and also are subject to the Freight, Premium of Insurance, and other Charges accruing thereupon; and that Ireland, by being exempt from these Charges, will come at the Materials for those Manufactures upon much cheaper Terms, and would, in case the said Bill pass into a Law, entirely engross the Export Trade thereof to themselves; and that the Irefs of this valuable Branch of Business would be extremely injurious to the Petitioners, as it is the natural and only Vocation by which they have supported themselves and Families, and employed Numbers of People, to the Benefit of the Community in general: And therefore praying. That they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Bill passing into a Law.

His Majesty, relying on the experienced Zeal and Affection of His faithful Commons, %pd considering that, in this critical Conjuncture, Emergencies may arise, which may be of the utmost Importance, and be attended with the most dangerous Consequences, if proper Means should not be immediately applied to prevent or defeat them, is desirous, that this House will enable Him to defray any extraordinary Expences incurred, or to be incurred, on account of Military Services, for the Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-eight, and to take all such Measures as the Exigency of Affairs may require.

The Lord North presented to the House, by His Majesty’s Command,

Copy of a Treaty between His Majesty and the Prince of Anhalt Zerhjl, concluded and signed at Stade,

the 23d April 1778; and Translation.

And the Titles of the said Copy and Translation were read.

The fair! Copy is preserved among!! the other Papers of this S.ffion, and the said Translation is as-followeth; viz.

Translation of a Treaty between His Majesty and the Prince of Anhalt Zeconcluded and ligned

at Stade, the Twenty-third Day of April 1778.

Be it known to those whom it may concern. That H is Britannick Majesty having thought proper to accept a Corps of Infantry of the Troops of His Moll Sceene Highness the Reigning Prince o,

to be employed in the Service of Great Britain, the high contracting Parties have caul’ed their Orders for this Purpose to be given to their respective Ministers; to wit. His Britannick Majesty to Major General Fauci! t, and the Moll Serene Prince of Anhalt, to the Colonels De Davier and De Kef ritz, who, after the Exchange of their respective full Powers, have agreed upon the following Articles.

Article ift.

The Moll Serene Prince of Anhalt Zerhjl yields to His Britannick Majesty a Corps of Infantry of Six hundred Men, according to the annexed Lift, which shall be at the entire Disposal of the King, with the foie Exception, that they shall not be employed against the Emperor or Empire of Germany.

Article 2d.

The Moll Serene Prince engages to equip this Corps completely, and they shall pass in Review before His Majesty’s Commissary at the Place oflheir Embarkation.

Article 3d.

The Mod Serene Prince engages to furnish the Recruits annually necessary for this Corps, which fludl be delivered to His Britannick Majesty’s Commissary, disciplined and completely equipped, at the Place of Embarkation, at such Time as His Majesty shall appoint.

Article 4th.

This Corps shall be provided with Two Pieces of Field Artillery, with the Gunners, and other Men, and the Train thereunto belonging.

Article 5th.

The King’s Service and the Safety of the Troops equally requiring that the Commanding Officers and Subalterns should be well skilled and perfect in the Service, l lis Moll Serene Highness will take due Care in the Choice of them.

Article 6th.

The Most Serene Prince engages to put this Corps in the belt State possible; and no Men shall be admitted Vo L.36.

therein, but such as are fit fof Cftrrtpaign Service, and so acknowledged by His Britannick Majesty’s Com* midary.

Article 7th.

This Corps shall be provided with Tents* and all the

necessary Equipage.

Article 8th.

The King grants to this Corps the ordinary and extraordinary Pay, as well as all the Advantages in Forage, Provisions, SCc. SCc. which the Royal Troops enjoy; 4nd the Molt Serene Prince engages, to permit, this Corps to enjoy all the Emoluments of Pay which His Majesty allows them. The lick and wounded of the said Corps shall be taken Care of in the King’s Hospitals" and shall be treated in this Respeid as the' Troops of His Britannick Majesty; and the wounded, not in a Condition to fen e, shall be conveyed to Europe, and be sent back into their own Country, at the King’s Expence.

Article gth.

There shall be paid to His Most Serene Highness, as Levy Money for each Foot Soldier, Thirty Crowns Banco, the Crown to be computed at Fifty-three Sols Of Holland, and valued at Four Shillings and Nine Pence Three Farthings. This Levy Money shall be paid in One Month after the Signature of the Treaty; provided always, that Thirty Crowns Banco shall be retained for each Soldier, who, without being lick, shall be deficient in the said Corps on the Day of their passing in Review before His Britannick Majesty’s Commifliiry; which ThirtyCrowns Banco shall, neverflieless, be paid as soon as the Soldiers deficient, shall afterwards join their respective Corps.

Article 10th.

If it should happen that this Corps, in the Whole or in Part, should fuller any very extraordinary Damage, whether in a Battle or a Siege, or by any uncommon contagious Distemper, or by the Loss of any Transport Vessel in the Passage to America, His Britannick Majesty shall make good, in the most equitable Manner, the Loss of the Officer or Soldier, and defray the Charge of the Recruits necessary for completing the Corps which shall have fuitained such extraordinary Damage.

Article nth.

The Moll Serene Prince reserves to himself the Nomination to the vacant Offices, as well as the Admtnil-tration of Justice. His Britannick Majesty, moreover, will cause Orders to be given to the Commander of the Army in which this Corps shall serve, not to require from this Corps any extraordinary Service, or which may exceed their Proportion with the rest of the Army. This Corps shall take the Oath of Fidelity to His Britannick Majesty, without Detriment to that which they have taken to their Sovereign.

Article 12th.

The English Pay shall commence Seven Days before this Corps of Troops began their March, which \\as the 2ill of February in the current Year; ami from the Time of their quit ting their own Country, all the Transport Charges shall be borue by His Britannick Majesty.

Article 13th.

His Britannick Majesty grants to His Most Serene Highness the Prince, while this Corps of Troops shall be in His Majesty’s Pay, to be computed from the Day of the Ratification of this Treaty, an Annual Subsidy of Twenty-two thousand Five hundred Crowns Banco; which Subsidy shall be continued for Three Month,s after the Return of the said Corps into the Dominions of His Moll Serene Highness; and the Troops shall enjoy the Pay to the End of the Month in which they shall arrive in the Territory of His Molt Serene Highness.

Article 14 th.

This Treaty shall be ratified by the high con*

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Common Council, Merchants, and principal Inhabitants, of the City of Exeter, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners being informed, that several Bills are depending before the House, granting an Extension of the Trade of Ireland-, and notwithstanding the Petitioners conceive the Exceptions prohibiting the Exportation of Woollens are to continue in force, yet they beg Leave to express their Fears, that, should the said Bills pass into Laws, the clandef-tine Export of IrifiiWoollens will greatly increase; and the Petitioners are very apprehenlive, from a comparative View of the Prices of Labour and Provisions, and the Difference of the Taxes in both Kingdoms, that such Laws will be productive of many other Evils, and occasion iuexpressible Injury and irreparable Loss to this Nation: The Petitioners therefore, dreading such fatal Coufequences, but sincerely wishing their Sifter Kingdom may have every Relief this Country can properly grant, pray, That the further Prosecution of the said Bills may be deferred until next Session of Parliament, that, in the mean time, Objects so important and extensive may be thoroughly examined and digested. *

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

After which, His Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne, to both Houses of Parliament, as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

After so long and laborious an Application to the Public Business, 1 think it proper at this Season of the Year to give you some Recess. I come at the same Time to return you My particular Thanks for the Zeal you have lliewn in supporting the Honour of My Crown, and for your Attention to the real Interests of all My Subjects, in the wife, just, and humane Laws, which have been the Result of your Deliberations, and which I hope, will be attended with the moll salutary > Effects in every Part of the British Empire.

Vol. 36.

My Delire to preserve the Tranquillity of Europe has been uniform and sincere: I reflect, with great Satisfaction, that I have made the Faith of Treaties and the Law of Nations the Rule of My Conduct, and that it has been My conllant Care to give no just Cause of Offence to any foreign Power; let that Power, by whom this Tranquillity shall be disturbed, answer to their Subjects and to the World for all the fatal Couse-quences of War.

The Vigour and Firmness of My Parliament have enabled Me to be prepared for such Events and Emergencies as may happen; andl trust that the experienced Valour and Discipline of My Fleets and Armies, and the loyal and united Ardour of the Nation, armed and animated in the Defence of every Thing that is dear to them, will be able, under the Protection of Divine Providence, to defeat all the Enterprizes which the Enemies of My Crown may presume to undertake, and convince them how dangerous it is to provoke the Spirit and Strength of Great Britain. ';

1 Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I. thank you for the Cheerffilness with which you have granted the large and ample Supplies for ^he Service of the current \ear, and foryoun Care in raisipg them in- a Manner the moll effectual and the least burthensome; and My warmest Acknowledgments are due to you for the Provision you have enabled Me to make for the more honourable Support of My Family.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

Your Presence in your respective Countries may, at this Time, be of great public Advantage. It is unnecessary for Me to recommend to you to do your Duty in your several Stations: On My Part, I have no other Wiffi or Object but to deserve the Confidence of My Parliament, and the Affections of My People.

And afterwards the Lord Chancellor, by His Majesty’s Command, said.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

It is His Majesty’s Royal Will and Pleasure, that this Parliament be prorogued to the 14th Day of

July next, to be then here holden; and this Parliament is accordingly prorogued to the 14th Day of

July next.
